It is a simple tool but it is very useful, and in the hands of someone who needs to better stabilize a video recorder it will be more useful still. As I mentioned above, it won’t work absolute miracles, but it reduces the camera shakes enough to make a noticeable difference.

My son participates in an online meeting weekly, and he needed a new webcam to replace the one he was using. The old one worked but was not of good quality. Based on the asking price for this webcam I was not especially hopeful. That said, it has proven to be better than either of us expected.

It's easy to set up - plug it in and let the OS configure it. It's easy enough to use, too, by selecting the camera desired if there's more than one.

We have seen no issues with clarity or audio/video quality, which have both been solid and reliable. In his meeting, others have commented that his feed seems to be the clearest and most glitch-free.

At least one other reviewer noticed issues with lag and skipping. This has not been an issue for us and so far this little camera has performed well without incident.

The model we received did not have the mini tripod. However, it has a standard mount for a tripod and those little tripods are easy enough to find. If you already have a tripod of any size, this webcam will mount without issue.

Could it be better? Sure. But, improvement would drive up the cost, and the quality is good as it is. For the asking price, this is a great little webcam.

Crucial is one of the first names that comes to mind when I have needed reliable RAM for my systems in the past. I have a Crucial 500MB SSD in one of my systems and it has served me well over the years so I was interested in this SSD as a back-up option for pictures and data. It has proven to be a fine solution for my needs.

Right up front – yes, it works with Linux right out of the box. I plugged it into my Peppermint Linux system and the kernel immediately recognized the drive and made it available. It was on me to mount the drive, but this was a simple matter and I was able to access the file system and see drive statistics. Obviously it works with Windows so I won’t go into that.

This is a physically small device, slightly less than half the size of a cell phone (iPhone 6s is what I used for comparison). It will easily fit inside the change pocket in my jeans and can tuck just about anywhere. This is a double-edged sword. On one hand it is convenient to have something this small and easy to store, but it is also easy to misplace or even lose. If this stays in your laptop bag or briefcase it should be secure, but if you are in a habit of keeping things in your pockets instead be cautious.

Transfer speeds are good. I have not done benchmarks on this drive but I copied thousands of pictures (average size about 8mb per file, some more and some less) and it was significantly faster than the USB drive I have been using for a while and faster than many of the thumb drives I have been using for backups. I have no complaints.

This is a small and fast drive that just works. It works with Linux which for me is important, and it is small enough to tuck in my camera bag for making backups in the field.

I selected this keyboard after doing a bit of research. I already have a solar keyboard (a Logitech) on my Windows system, and I needed a keyboard for my Linux system. I was a little hesitant to buy because I did not see any definitive information that it would work with Linux. I've had it several days, and I can say with some authority, it definitely works correctly under Linux.

The system in question is a Dell laptop running Peppermint Linux hosting a CentOS 8 VM. Most keyboards (with one notable exception) work on this system so I was hopeful it would work well, and it does. It behaves virtually identically to the Logitech keyboard and so far has given me no trouble.

Build-wise, this is a solid keyboard that should hold up to some abuse. It is sturdy and does not flex when I am typing. I like the fact that the dongle is held to the back of the keyboard magnetically so it can be transported with less concern of being misplaced when not in use.

One of the major issues I have with keyboards is that I have the hands of a gorilla and I frequently run into issues with hitting multiple keys at the same time, particularly with flat keyboards like this one. The keys are slightly bigger than average with this one, though, and hitting muliple keys simultaneously is less of a problem. This was an unexpected and welcome surprise.

Aesthetically, I love the feel of this keyboard. Most of the keys are concave and feel pleasant to the touch. Oddly, a good number of the keys on the bottom row are actually convex. While this is no issue at all, I do find it puzzling.

It is priced competitively against the Logitech too.

If I could change anything I would include some kind of indicator of how much charge this keyboard has at any given time. So far I have not run out of power, but eventually I expect to have a situation where there has not been enough light to keep it at a full charge and it would be good to know how much power it has retained.

I'm pleased with this keyboard. It works well under Linux and I don't need to replace batteries or plug it in. I really can't ask for much more than that.

I selected the OctoPad as much out of curiosity as out of need. I have a weighted platform that looks similar that I use for my GPS navigator in the car, and that has proven to be one of the best ways to support that device. I expected a similar experience from the OctoPad, and it has proven it’s worth. I would, however, stop short of calling it perfect.

The concept is simple. It is a weighted (sand-filled) pad with a non-skid bottom. It has a ball joint with a threaded mount attached, and the mount can accommodate a camera, selfie stick, smartphone harness, or even a harness for another device if it supports the thread. It serves the same base purpose as a miniature tripod but is more versatile as the flat, rubber base is designed to prevent slipping on smoother surfaces.

It is the non-skid base that stands between this being a good product and a great one. The rubbery material is thin and feels quite fragile, and I believe it is a matter of time before it either breaks down or just rips. Because of the material of the upper portion that covers the sand I believe a new base can be sewn in place when this happens but that is inconvenient at the very least.

Other than my reservations about the no-slip base, this has proven to be a valuable tool for me. I have a selfie stick permanently mounted on it and I use that to mount a small COB light, which all together provides me with a very useful mobile light source when I need to angle a light in a tight spot. It is not ideal but it brings me much closer than when I hand-hold the light. It also is more stable when the surface on which I put it isn’t quite level.

This is a useful tool in my photography arsenal. It works as designed and it provides me with some options when I need a mount that I can put almost anywhere. I would change the base material and make it more durable, even if it increased the cost a bit, but otherwise I have no complaints and am pleased with the OctoPad.

Note: There are multiple products attached to this listing. I am specifically reviewing the vertical mouse.

I have used a variety of trackballs, mice, writing tablets and more in my search for the most comfortable pointing device. My weapon of choice has been a higher-end trackball for the last couple of years, and I have a relatively cheap vertical mouse I use on occasion when I need to use that trackball on another system. I've used Kensington trackballs in the past and have had good experiences with them, so I was optimistic about this vertical mouse. So far, it has not disappointed me.

I have the hands of a gorilla so finding a mouse, trackball or any other pointing device usually requires some searching. What fits my hand is often too big for others and what I find too small is usually just right for everyone else. This vertical mouse seems to hit the sweet spot - it's comfortable in my hand and quite usable but it is also good for people with smaller hands. I will say that it is still slightly on the small side for me, and when I use it my pinky finger rests on the desk at the base of this mouse, but it is not uncomfortable and is a step up from others I have used.

In terms of the contour and fit, it is arguably one of the most comfortable vertical mice I have used. My thumb, index and middle fingers rest properly on it and I have no trouble controlling the mouse at all. I do not need to stretch to reach the buttons, but also I do not need to scrunch my hand either. It's a good balance.

Operation is smooth and easy. It is very responsive, it is not loud when the buttons are clicked, and it has a reasonable amount of range.

Considering the cost, it is as close to perfect as I have used. That said, there are a couple of things I would change if I had the opportunity to do so, though the cost would increase. First, I would add the ability to connect via Bluetooth and provide for switching between two connected systems. I have that ability with other peripherals and I like it, though it's a convenience feature. Second, I would add the ability to recharge it instead of replacing batteries. This is a double-edged sword, though - the difference between being up and running with replaceable batteries and rechargeable can be the difference between a minute and a couple of hours.

Because of the nature of vertical mice, it is not switchable between right and left hands. This is very much a right-handed mouse. If you are left-handed, you can use this mouse but it will be very awkward.

One odd thing occurred when I set it up under Windows 10. When I plugged in the receiver it reported it as a wireless keyboard. However, operation has been fine so this is a weird cosmetic issue and I assume that it is because it uses a common receiver.

I like this mouse and am pleased with it. It isn't absolutely perfect and there are some ways in which it could be improved, but to do so would increase the cost appreciably. At the price point, this is one of the best vertical mice I have used.

Most of the headphones with which I have worked have been active noise canceling (ANC) phones which have their strengths and weaknesses. I have a few pairs of nice non-ANC phones, some of which are excellent for studio work, but this is my first pair of true studio phones. After working with them, I am very pleased with them. They are comfortable to wear for long periods of time and they sound great with a very balanced sound profile.

These are over-the-ear phones, not on-ear, and I prefer that. They do not pinch or press my ears and I can wear them for several hours without them getting uncomfortable. The pads are soft and do not irritate as some phone pads sometimes can. The pads do not breathe, though, so after some time they do eventually get a bit warm.

If using these as Bluetooth phones, operation is simple – turn them on. They’re immediately ready to pair and my system discovered them and paired without incident. The Bluetooth range is good and I was able to get between 30’ and 50’ with walls in between before the sound began to stutter a little.

If you prefer to use them corded, that works too and these come with several audio cords with which to connect. Speaking of the cords: these do not use a standard audio cable with a standard connector on the phone side, so you can’t simply use any audio cable with them (though they will work with extension cables). Bear this in mind.

Volume can be controlled by touching the connector on the left side – flick up to increase volume, flick down to decrease.

The most important aspect of any headphones is the sound quality and these definitely deliver. The highs are sharp and crisp without being piercing. The midlevels are full and warm, and the base is strong without being overdriven. Most headphones anymore are tuned to overdrive the bass at the expense of the midrange making music sound hollow while pounding the listener to a headache. It is refreshing to listen to music that is properly balanced without needing an equalizer to get the sound right. I would not call these audiophile phones, but they’re better than many headphones I have used that cost much more.

If I could change one thing… I prefer a headphone set that clamps down on my head and fits snugly. These are not as snug as I’d like, but they are better than some I have used. When I turn my head and look down, they remain in place without slipping which is an issue with loose-fitting phones. Since these don’t slip, I’m satisfied.

I’m happy with these phones and based on my experience with them I am pleased to recommend them. They sound great and they are comfortable enough for extended use.

Anymore, an emergency radio has been largely replaced by smart phones for getting emergency updates and it is not a common item that people frequently buy or have around. That said, having a radio like this is useful when traveling and either cell service is bad or using a phone is impractical. In such cases a radio like this is a really good resource. For us, while not a necessity this radio sees daily use as a weather radio.

One of the things that has been around our house for many, many years is a weather radio. We are in range of two weather stations and we have a dedicated emergency weather radio that provides us emergency notifications as well as current conditions and forecasts around the region. The difficulty we have had with it is that reception is not the greatest and we often have static over the broadcast. We have a secondary weather radio that has even worse reception that our main one.

I did not have high expectations of this radio at all. We tuned it to the closest station with the expectation of hearing a lot of static and interference. Much to our surprise, the broadcast is clear and uncluttered. We tuned to the other station and got the same – a clear broadcast. What was a real surprise for us is that we could suddenly pick up a third station. We had no idea we were close enough to any other station to hear their broadcasts. It’s not as clear as the others, but it is clear enough to be understood.

As a weather radio, this unit is excellent. We have no complaints.

Most of the other features we have tried though do not use regularly. It has a flashlight built in that is bright enough to navigate through the house during a power outage and it has a couple of different modes such as SOS flash that make it useful in different emergency situations. It has different charging modes so it is ready to go when needed, the most frequent of which we use is the solar charging but it can be plugged in and it also can be hand-cranked to generate enough power for emergency use. A particularly helpful emergency feature is the ability to charge your phone, and the battery is sufficient to give one full charge to a smaller smartphone with power to spare.

If I could change one thing I would make it more ruggedized. It is good in that regard and should be able to handle getting dropped or jostled and bumped, but there is definitely opportunity to go farther. This is by no means a show-stopper or even a complaint, but a data point – if you need something that can handle a lot of abuse, this isn’t it, though in the price range it would be difficult to find better.

This is a nice emergency radio and my family really likes it. Though designed and marketed as an emergency radio, it actually sees daily use solely on the basis of how well it performs as a weather radio.

I selected this light after doing some research on continuous LED lights. I had a situation where I had only a strobing light available to me and it made getting even a still exposure without banding very difficult. My requirements for a continuous LED were that it had to be compact, bright and have variable color output. This light met those requirements, and in addition I found some favorable write-ups of this light online. Though on the pricey side, I took the plunge and so far I have no regrets.

I will state right up front that this is not marketed as a general purpose light and it is not a proper substitute for such. There are less expensive and more practical lights available if you need general lighting. Yes, it will work as a general purpose light source, even as a flashlight in a pinch, but that’s akin to using a blowtorch to light candles when a simple match will do.

This is a very small light, about the side of a king-sized candy bar. Even after reading the description and reviews, I was surprised at just how small this light is. That’s good for me because it fits perfectly in my camera bag and can go with me without taking up extra room or requiring space in the car or luggage. When stored in the case it takes up about as much room as a small jar of peanut butter.

The light has ten brightness settings as well as a boost mode which makes it almost blinding. The lowest setting is quite dim but usable, and the brightest outside of boost mode is bright enough to illuminate a 10’x10’ space reasonably well. The light color is constant unless using the color “gels” (more on that in a moment). When using boost mode, it remains in that mode for a period of roughly a minute before switching back to one of the normal settings. It takes some time before boost mode can be used again, likely a safety measure due to increased heat output.

Included are several color “gels” that are more like hard plastic plates that fit in front of the light array. These allow for some adjustment in color. The colors tweak the color range to be warmer or colder. I used the darkest orange to give a scene a warmer, golden glow that worked remarkably well. These plates are held in place against the array with a clip-on harness that fits over the front of the unit.

Also included is a silicone diffuser that reduces the harshness of the array. When the clip-on harness is in place it is difficult at best to attach the diffuser.

There are several effects modes to emulate different lighting situations, including a flickering light, lightning strike, glow from a television and more. While these are interesting and some will find these modes useful, particularly for video, they do not serve my purposes.

What I did not realize is that this light has a mounting hole on the bottom that allows for attaching it to any standard tripod or even a monopod/selfie stick. I attached it to a higher-quality telescoping monopod with a swivel base and was able to get the exact lighting angle I needed. With a tripod it becomes hands-free.

Though it is waterproof I have no intention of using this in water.

It includes a couple of patches that allow it to be semi-permanently attached to a surface. I am contemplating building a large light box and attaching this light inside.

This is a really excellent and versatile continuous LED light. It is as bright or dim as you need it, it includes some color plates for adjusting the color output, it includes some special effect modes and it is small enough to fit in my bag without any trouble at all. This is a very easy light to recommend if you need a continuous LED light.

I use canned dusters for a variety of purposes, from cleaning keyboards to cleaning up my electric shaver. These sometimes leave residue behind, so I was interested in trying this electric duster to see if it would cut down on residue and save money in the long run. I will confess that I was not very optimistic and thought it would be underpowered. However, it has proven to be as effective as a canned duster in cleaning keyboards and other equipment, without leaving any residue and without losing power like canned dusters tend to do as they get cold.

This device is smaller than a tea kettle and relatively light. It requires an AC outlet so it does need to be plugged in when you want to use it. I was hopeful I had missed something on the description and that there was a rechargeable battery but unfortunately this is not the case. This was me being hopeful, not a confusing write-up.

It comes with a few attachments to help direct the air flow over the surface of what you’re trying to clean. The most helpful attachment, to me, is the round nozzle, but all of them have their uses.

I took it to my office where we have an abundance of dirty keyboards that need to be cleaned, and I set to work. I was expecting it to do a mediocre cleaning job, but it gave me a very pleasant surprise and blew air with plenty of force to clean out the clumps of dust that collect under the keys. More importantly, though, the power didn’t diminish like what tends to happen with canned dusters as they get cold, and there was no problem with frost buildup either.

So far, this is proving to be a useful and helpful tool. It produces enough force to get the job done without losing power, and it leaves no residue behind.

I bought this set of filters to fit a 77mm Fujinon lens. I needed a UV filter, and I wanted a CPL filter. I bought a separate variable ND filter so I really didn’t need the ND4 filter but it’s a good addition to this set. So far I have been pleased with the set and am happy to recommend it.

The UV filter is useful as a basic protective cover for a lens, but it also does filter out UV light. This is a lot less of a problem when it comes to digital camera, as UV light was harmful to 35mm film. UV light can make images hazy and this filter can reduce that. In very specific situations, there can be reflections between the lens glass and the filter, so there are occasions when using the UV filter is not advisable.

I had the opportunity to use the CPL filter on a sunny day at a lake and I used the filter to cut through the reflections on the water. It worked well and I was able to get a picture of things on the bottom. That’s all I could really ask.

I have not used the ND4 filter.

This set comes in a nice carrying case that protects the filters when they’re not in use. The case is small enough that it fits inside my camera bag without any issue.

This is a decent filter set and I am pleased with it. The filters I have used have worked well for me.

I selected these macro filters to go with a 77mm Fujinon lens. I have used these types of filters with an older camera and wanted a set for my new camera, and after researching available options I chose these. These are decent macro filters though there is some room for improvement.

These are about as basic as it gets. They’re not fancy, they’re just screw-on filters designed to fit lenses with a 77mm thread. They fit my lens just fine and I have had no trouble removing them when I am done. These are straight glass and with the exception of the +10 filter there is little distortion. The +10 filter has a lot of edge distortion but clarity in the middle, which is very much like other sets like these I have used.

There is a problem with the +1 filter in my set. The glass is loose in the ring and it actually rattles when I handle it. It doesn’t seem to be loose enough to come out of the ring. It does concern me that it could come out, though. I would be more concerned about this if I used this particular filter more, but that’s not the point.

This is not a bad set, but the quality is not as good as it should be. The filters work well enough, but I am concerned that the glass might separate from the ring, based on one of them in my set. So far it hasn’t happened.

I have worked with a lot of different sets of headphones and ear buds and have gotten a good feel for what sounds right and what doesn’t. Specifically with ear buds I pay attention to the fit as well as the sound, which are two areas where many manufacturers get it wrong. Anker did a good job with these though there is a soft spot in the sound profile.

I used these with an iPhone 7, and initial pairing was very quick and painless. The buds found each other (another issue I have seen with other sets on occasion), and these paired without much fanfare or issue at all. That’s really all you could ask.

These fit like a dream. The package contains several silicone plugs of different sizes so you can get just the right fit for yourself, but I found that the ones already on the buds were actually a perfect fit. I popped these in, gave them a turn to lock them in place and they sealed perfectly. I am especially happy with how well these fit in my ears and actually stay there.

The sound isolation is on par with what you’d expect. When not powered on and streaming music they are the equivalent to a cheap set of ear plugs – enough to block out some sound but not completely silence the world.

The sound quality is very good but the sound profile could use a tweak. The bass is strong but not overdriven to the point of causing headaches. There is a tendency to overdrive the bass, so having good bass that’s not overpowering is nice. The highs are bright and clear too. The midrange is another matter and feels weak (though not non-existent). Music played through these buds lacks the warmth and fullness that the midrange brings to the table (and if it was overdriven everything would sound like it is coming through a tunnel). I would rather have under-driven midrange than overdriven, but it’s still soft enough to be noticeable.

They case in which these buds are stored also serves as the charger. What is interesting about these is how the case itself is charged. Instead of MicroUSB, this case uses a Type C connector which is not unwelcome but up to this point is unusual for this kind of device. There is a cable in the box so there’s no issue.

These are good ear buds and they have some nice features. They fit superbly and they pair to a source without problems. The sound profile is imperfect, though not terribly so, which is the only complaint I have with them.

For the most part I have had good fortune with Logitech peripherals. As I write this I am using an MX Ergo trackball which is the best mouse/trackball I have ever used. I looked to the MK470 mouse/keyboard combination with the idea of using it with a laptop running Linux. I had high expectations for the keyboard but lower expectations for the mouse due to the size and shape. Both failed me, but in completely different ways.

I will start with this: this combo does not use a unifying receiver so if you want to use another peripheral with this combo you’ll need either another USB port or connect via Bluetooth. That’s all right as long as you recognize that up front. It’s a mild disappointment, but it was clear up front so this was not a surprise.

The mouse and the keyboard both have the batteries installed already. The keyboard takes 2 AAA batteries and the mouse takes one AA battery. I question the logic behind using different battery sizes.

I plugged the receiver into my laptop running Linux with the latest kernel, and both peripherals were immediately usable. That’s a plus.

The first problem I have is with the mouse. The mouse works just fine but is such a low-profile device that it is uncomfortable for me to use. I have a travel mouse that actually fits my hand a little better and that says a lot. For someone with very small hands this one will serve acceptably as a basic two-button travel mouse. To be fair, I knew this ahead of time so I cannot complain too much. It does work correctly and in a pinch I can work with it.

The keyboard is a completely different matter entirely. It works just fine – except for the “P” key. For that specific key, I have to bear down very hard to get it to register at all. I tried leaning the keyboard on its side and tapping it gently in case something was caught in the switch and I have tried my best to clean it without disassembly. No matter what I have tried, the “P” key continues to be insensitive to the point of rendering the keyboard unusable.

I really wanted to like this keyboard, and I knew the mouse would be small. Unfortunately, because the keyboard I received doesn’t work properly I can’t use it and can’t rate it favorably. It’s a shame – I imagine I got a bad unit (it happens), but I cannot recommend a product based on an assumption.

UPDATE 10/31/2019:

I popped off the "P" key and looked at the mechanism underneath, since the keyboard was not otherwise useful. It does not appear to be broken, damaged or obstructed in any way. For this particular key, the plastic key cover needs a small bead in the center underneath to push down the silicone membrane to make contact. Using a very small piece of tape and a tiny ball (about the size of a pin head) I was able to add such to the key cover to get it working without damaging any parts, without changing the feel while typing, and without spending any money. However, this should not have been necessary as this should have been tested properly before pack-and-ship; my review and rating stand.

This is the first digital picture frame with which I have worked so I do not have any basis of comparison with others to know if it compares well against other ones or not. That said, it does what it is supposed to do, it does it well and I am happy with it.

Setup is simple and easy. If you have your media ready to go, copy it to the included SD card and pop it in.

On a side note, the card that came with it is 32GB which is huge. That can hold literally thousands of full-resolution images from a digital camera. Assuming that the average high-resolution JPG image is 8mb (which is what comes off my mirrorless camera) it can hold about 4,000 pictures. That all said, this frame can also play back video and sound, so there is more to it than just showing pictures. In that light, the size of the card makes a lot of sense.

The frame is approximately 10” of viewing area. The images are bright and clear which should please most users.

The unit handles a number of audio, video and image formats. The list is not exhaustive, but it does handle the main types in each category.

Included is a little remote. The remote isn’t fancy but it is sufficient for changing settings, moving to the next media element, power on/off, etc.

There’s really only one negative, and that’s the documentation which is written in very poorly-translated English. I would lower my rating of the overall package on this basis except that the product is so self-explanatory and easy to use/understand that the documentation isn’t necessary.

Overall, we are happy with this frame. It works well and it is very easy and straightforward to understand. It handles a lot of formats and can play back audio and video in addition to showing still images.

I selected this camera to mount on my front porch, with the intention of keeping a watchful eye on the front of the house. I was very skeptical of this camera because of the price and assumed that it would be a budget-grade solution as a result. It has proven to be better than I anticipated.

This is a single-camera solution with no dedicated monitoring station. It connects via the WiFi network and it can be monitored via phone which is handy when you’re away. It includes a power supply and all of the mounting equipment (minus the tools) to set it all up for outdoor use.

All of that sounds great, but as I write this the camera sells for under $40.

It has not performed like a $40 camera. It has been rock-solid so far – it’s stable, it has remained connected except for when I have had router issues, the image in the daytime is excellent and the night-vision mode is far and away better than I expected – I can read license plates on cars in the driveway at night.

This is not a complete security solution but rather is a single camera for zone security. There are more complete systems that offer more features and capabilities, but these cost a lot more and cover broader areas with multiple cameras. If you just need a single camera to monitor a fairly small area, and you have a wireless network to connect it to, this is a very affordable solution.

Of the three main GPS receiver manufacturers - Garmin, TomTom and Magellan - I have had the most success with TomTom devices. My first GPS was a TomTom and it served me well for years until the map outgrew the memory. I was excited to have the opportunity to try this one; so far, it has been a good unit, though I do not care for the menu system.

This is a larger unit than the original one I had, upgrading from a 4.3" to a 6". I like the screen real estate. For all that screen space, TomTom has made good use of it, maximizing the visible map and keeping the interface clean and uncluttered. One area where I am slightly disappointed, though, is in the speed display which is a little small - it's good to keep it out of the way but it's a little smaller than I like and it a bit harder to read. If you use your GPS for watching your speed, this could be a problem.

Navigation is easy. I like the way this unit routes me to my destination yet does not nag me when I go off the chosen route. Others I have used (including my old TomTom) would badger me to make a U-turn for a while before deciding that there was another way to get where I was going. This unit does make that point sometimes, but it also is smart enough to reroute when I have multiple similar routes.

The biggest plus for this unit (and it seems to be a TomTom thing) is that the voice very clearly enunciates without distortion or the unit buzzing. I have had this issue with every other unit of every other brand, but my old TomTom was clear and understandible even at higher volumes. Since this one is the same, I believe TomTom has a better understanding of how to build a unit that sounds right.

Navigating from work to home is usually a straight shot down the interstate for 40+ miles and a little bit of backroads. To test, I instead took a long, out-of-the-way route that I use when there is heavy traffic volume. Knowing it would try to put me on the interstate, I set the farthest point as a first leg, then set it to take me home from there. The route it chose was actually only slightly different than the one I had chosen already, and the difference was that I accounted for rush hour traffic.

Speaking of traffic... This unit gathers traffic data without relying on mobile data. I greatly prefer this to having to run an app on my phone and letting it gather traffic info from online. So far I have not had it report a reroute due to traffic; I will come back here and update when it does.

The main complaint I have about this GPS is the menu system. WIth TomTom's older units, the menu system was fairly traditional and was smiliar to that of a PC application menu system (sorta). The new interface has a scrolling row of icons that lead to more icons. I am not a fan of this type of interface and is the one thing I would change about this unit if I could.

When this unit is first powered on and set up it downloads a hefty amount of data to update the map. This is unavoidable, unfortunately. Do not be discouraged by this - it will be up to date and ready to go when it finishes.

I have not had any real issues with this unit so far. It works well and I like how it navigates. I don't like the menu system and find it very awkward, but it gets me where I want to go with little fuss.

I am on-the-go a lot and I have been looking at decent solutions for reliable storage when in transit. I was hopeful that this disk would be a good option. It’s a good drive that’s plenty fast with a good bit of storage, but it isn’t anything particularly special – it’s a disk in an aluminum enclosure with a rubber bumper. The price, though, makes it an attractive option.

This drive is smaller than I expected, though I say that having an 8TB backup drive on my desk in front of me. The other drives I have used that are similar to this one are small like the older WD Passport drives. This one is somewhere in between. It’s small enough to fit in a laptop bag without any trouble and it is large enough to not get lost like a thumb drive.

In the most basic sense this drive is a small HDD in an aluminum enclosure with a removable rubber bumper. The bumper is suitable for reducing shocks from bumps and short drops, though I question if it’s sufficient for a serious drop (3’+). On the plus side, the bumper has a port cover to make the drive mostly weather sealed.

The interface is USB Type C which is great for speed. Included in the box is a cable for the drive as well as an adapter to make the drive work with a standard USB port.

Of course it works with Windows, but I am a Linux user. Running an Arch-derivative with the latest kernel and drivers, I plugged the drive into my Linux laptop and the kernel saw it immediately. So, I can say this drive works with Linux without issue. The question becomes if it will be used under Linux full-time, in which case it might be helpful to rewrite the file system to make better use of the space.

This is a decent external drive with some weather sealing and shock-reduction. It’s affordable, spacious and it works with Linux.

I have worked with GPS navigators from several manufacturers, including Garmin, Magellan and TomTom. Each unit has its strengths and weaknesses. My favorite GPS unit up this point has been another TomTom, an old Start 40 which served me well for several years. I was interested to see how much the series has changed since I got that older model. It has changed quite a bit – more than I expected. I like this navigator, though I can see a few things I’d change.

First off, I have the 6” model which is a beast. I am used to a 5” GPS which I have been using, and it took some time to adjust to the larger screen. This is not to say it bothers me; it just is enough of a difference to require getting used to it. If you are upsizing like that, be aware that it takes up more physical space and placing on the windshield might require replanning.

Out of the box, I powered it on, connected it to my WiFi network and downloaded over 6GB of updates. That’s a huge update. The map it holds is obviously the largest component to be updated, and it covers all of the US, Canada and Mexico. While it is nice to have all that coverage, I personally do not need that much map and would have liked the option of only having the US map on-board. That would cut memory requirements. My older model was limited in memory and the map grew until it could no longer fit; I can see the potential for that happening again.

For navigation, up to this point I have stuck with the default settings, except with the 2D/3D map setting.

My first trip with this unit was to work. I did not use it to navigate, I only used to to show the map as I drove. It found my fix quickly (one of the reasons I like TomTom navigators) and when I was driving it updated the map smoothly and quickly as I reached new features. It displayed road names, it showed the placement of certain POIs like gas stations, and because I was driving at sunrise the map switched from night mode to daytime so I got to see both maps.

I’ll state for the record, I am not fan of the daytime map’s default color scheme. I almost always use the 2D map, not the 3D one, and it uses a set of pastel colors that might be somewhat soothing on the eyes but they’re quite drab. I’d rather see a bolder map that makes features stand out more. Another thing this unit does not show is road symbols like the interstate shield, instead opting for just small-print words. I can live with that but I do prefer the symbols.

On the way home from work, I used the unit again, but this time to guide me on an alternate route. Friday afternoon traffic in this area is typically awful, and the route home is almost always snarled by at least one accident (sometimes as many as 4-5). I chose to follow a route I knew would take two hours to get home, though it moves the whole time. I loaded the first point into the GPS and it dutifully guided me there, taking me on a fairly optimal route. When I got there, I then told it to take me home and I was quite surprised – every other GPS unit I have used has tried to make me take a U-turn to go back the way I came to get back on the interstate (the source of the problem), but this one did not, instead taking me on a route that would connect me back to the interstate about 20 miles south. Knowing this was also a bad route traffic-wise, I made a planned turn in the middle of the route, skipping another 20 miles of interstate. Instead of insisting I turn around, the unit again adjusted my route and took me on almost the exact route I had planned to take anyway.

What impressed me is how quickly the unit rerouted me without trying to put me back on the original route it chose. This is quite different from most units. Normally I get “turn around when possible” or “recalculating” over and over – not this time.

I finally did let it put me on the interstate, about 5 miles from home. When I reached my exit is showed very clearly what lane it wanted me to use, and it was very obvious when I was to turn.

I use the American female voice that reads street names. She enunciates very clearly and is easy to understand. Many GPS units sound tinny or have a buzz when the voice is active, but this one does not. My old Start 40 sounded clear too and did not buzz. I think perhaps TomTom does a better job with designing their units for sound.

One thing I use my GPS for is speed tracking. When in an area where there are no posted speed limit signs, it is nice when the GPS shows the speed limit and your current speed. For this one, though, the speed display is very small. It’s out of the way which is good, but I’d prefer a larger display or at least some ability to make it bigger. If there is a setting for that I have not uncovered it yet.

My primary complaint with this GPS is actually the menu system, which I find to be very clunky and odd. I don’t like it, and preferred the older menu system. It is workable, regardless.

Most GPS units that offered traffic do so through a special antenna or attachment in the power connector. Rather than offer this, this unit instead gets traffic updates via your phone through a Bluetooth connection. This is a double-edged sword. On one hand, it does not require that the unit be plugged in all the time and it becomes much more portable. On the other hand, it means that it pulls data and if you’re in an area where there is no data connectivity your updates aren’t available. I’m still deciding if I like this arrangement or not.

This is a good GPS with a little room for improvement in a few areas. The screen real estate is nice, and it navigates very well (better than most others I have used). It enunciates clearly and updates en route smoothly and quickly. The menu system is a little clunky, and there are some display settings I think could be better. Overall, though, this unit gets the important things right. It’s a good unit at a competitive price.

I prefer messenger bags to backpacks so I selected this bag for myself to go with my laptop. I prefer leather to canvas bags, so this one is a good fit for me. There is one thing about this bag I would change, but otherwise I am pleased with it.

The leather used for this bag is something I have heard referred to as "distressed" or "ruined" leather, though neither are indicative of quality but instead refer to the appearance. It is made to look battle-worn and older than it is, but it's actually in very good condition. I looked this bag over for issues - loose stitching, cuts and tears in the leather, uneven seams and the like, and I found nothing. Overall, this is a well-made bag that has been assembled with some care.

The main compartment is divided and is large enough to handle my laptop as well as a couple of books. I have been able to cram in a few accessories as well and still close the zippers and closures without issue.

The main flap folds over the main compartment and uses a pair of snaps to fasten the flap down. The snaps are hidden behind false, decorative buckles. I am no fan of the type of fastener that was used, as I have had those break unexpectedly when I have caught the strap on something without realizing it. I would have preferred either a magnet which would break away easily or a real buckle which would hold tighter.

I like this bag and expect it to last for years to come. It looks great (if you like the "ruined leather" style) and it is made very well. The one thing I could change is the flap fasteners because of past experiences, but otherwise I have no complaints.

This bag arrived just before we went out of town for a trip, and the timing couldn’t have been better. My wife has a 13” laptop that she loves and uses daily, and this bag was the perfect solution for carrying it on the trip. It isn’t necessarily the most fancy bag but it gets the job done and it seems to be made well. I would make one alteration to make it better, based on experiences I have had with similar bags in the past.

This is a smaller bag, not designed to hold 15.6” or larger laptops, so it is not going to help people who have “standard” laptop sizes unless this is going to be used as a book bag instead. If you need a bag that fits a laptop that is 15.6” or greater, this one will not work for you. That’s okay as it is very clearly marketed as such so it should come as no surprise. Being for smaller computers doesn’t make it useless though; it does work very well as a book bag and an organizer, so even if you need a larger one for your computer this one has its uses.

This is a leather messenger bag. The leather is a style I have heard referred to as “ruined leather” though that’s not an indicator of the quality. On the contrary, this bag is well made and I can’t find anything about it to suggest that it is made with less care and quality than the price dictates. In spite of the appearance, the materials are quality and I cannot find any blemishes or cuts, the stitching is straight and all the clasps and zippers work properly.

There are plenty of pockets to store your items and keep organized. Of course there this the main compartment which is designed to hold a computer, but there is room for books as well in the main compartment. There are zippered compartments inside the bag as well as outside, and these are good for carrying your mouse, pens and pencils, passport, maps and other important items.

The flap that covers the main compartment secures to the rest of the bag with straps that fasten with a pressure snap behind a fake decorative buckle, and this represents the one thing about this bag I do not like. If you are not careful and you catch one of the straps on something will walking, you can break the snap and damage or ruin the bag. I have had this happen with other bags using this kind of fastener. I would rather see a magnet used instead which will let go when pulled, or get rid of the decorative buckle and replace it with a real buckle which will hold regardless.

I like this bag. It is well made and it should last for years with proper care. It has room for your smaller laptop as well as books and other supplies. I don’t like the way the flap secures, mainly because if problems I have had with similar bags using similar fasteners, but for the majority of users this is a good solution that is worth consideration. It’s a little more expensive than a canvas bag, but it should last longer.

I have worked with a large number of computers by various manufacturers, and I can say that each one has had its strengths and weaknesses. I was really intrigued by this one with the 8th generation i3 chip – I didn’t even realize that the i3 was still being developed or produced. My experience with this laptop (and its chip) has been a mix of positive and negative, though the positive does outweigh the negatives I see.

I will start by addressing the elephant in the room. This system comes with only 4GB of DDR4 RAM. Why? The standard anymore is 8GB unless all you’re doing is surfing the web and writing documents. I am not sure what possessed Dell to release a machine with that little RAM running Windows 10. So, my first order of business was popping the case open and expanding to 8GB, which was easy with a single 8GB stick. There are two slots in there, and 8GB works in one slot, so I am hopeful I can bump it to 16GB.

While I was in there, I was in for a surprise. There is a hard drive bay, and it’s empty. The system registers 256GB in a solid state flash, which is elsewhere (I did not see it but I know it's in there).

Oddly enough, the Dell software does not recognize the increased RAM though Windows and the system BIOS definitely see it. That’s a minor issue, not a real concern. It does need to be kept in mind though – it could be confusing for the unaware.

This is an UltraBook system, meaning that some shortcuts were taken to keep things light and small. The main thing missing is a CD/DVD drive which is hit or miss on UltraBooks. There is HDMI for video output but no other video output interfaces. Surprisingly, there is no USB type C port, but there are three type A ports. There is also an audio jack and an Ethernet port, as well as an SD card reader. The power button doubles as a fingerprint reader.

I booted the system, set it up and was on the network downloading updates within about 10 minutes. I was presented with a fairly clean desktop and not too much extra fluff n’ stuff. The system was a bit sluggish for the first hour as things were updated and cached, but it has settled down now and things are reasonably peppy. I have done little with the graphics beyond loading a video and looking at image files, though I expect it will handle light gaming and graphics work like photo editing, though the latter would definitely benefit from having 8GB instead of 4.

Windows did not activate automatically and I needed to run the troubleshooter before it activated. I am not sure what went wrong there, but it was a temporary issue and very quickly and easily resolved. I suspect there was a network issue.

The screen is slightly less bright than that of my Acer and Toshiba systems, though that’s not necessarily a bad thing. The screen is not as harsh to look at, and the resolution is good, so I would consider this a plus. Pictures and image files look clear and sharp with good color.

The real surprise is the sound, which is much better than I expected and is great for watching videos without requiring headphones or speakers. I will still use BT output when I want to listen to anything important (music or a movie), but the built-in speakers are more than adequate.

I like the keyboard, though I do not care for the touch pad. The pad is on par with most, neither better nor worse, and I am not a fan of touch pads. It’s nice that it can be turned off, and it is nice that it’s available if it’s needed.

The system comes pre-installed with McAfee which is unfortunate but not unexpected. I stripped that joker off in a hurry and installed something for which I already have a full license. There’s also the trial for Office 365 which I unceremoniously uninstalled. Other than those two, there isn’t much bloat on the system.

So, my main major complaint is that Dell went cheap and only put in 4GB of RAM instead of 8. Adding 4GB is very economical – less than $30 – so I fail to understand why that shortcut was taken. It’s easy enough to add after the fact, though, and the overall cost of the system is quite reasonable. This is not a heavy gaming rig by any stretch of the imagination, it’s instead a multimedia and light-duty graphics workstation which is what I need the majority of the time. I’m satisfied with this system in spite of the skimpy RAM (which can be fixed cheaply). If you need a system that isn’t for heavy graphics or gaming, this one is a reasonable choice.

I prefer messenger bags to backpacks when it comes to toting my laptop anywhere, and I had high hopes for this one. I have a 15.6” laptop and the bag is marketed to handle laptops of that size. My laptop does fit it but it’s a tight squeeze; otherwise, I am very pleased with this bag.

I won’t go deep into the number of pockets, compartments and whatnot as the product description does a sufficient job of explaining all of that. I will say this, though: the main compartment has a divider in it, and the “laptop side” has a restraint to hold the laptop in. My laptop does not quite fit in that compartment, but fits [tightly] in the other area in the main compartment. I am not sure if the bag just needs to be broken in before my laptop will fit better or if it will always be tight, it’s hard to say at this time.

I like the leather material as it makes the bag fairly waterproof.

Unlike other messenger bags I have used, this one does not rely on magnets or snaps to hold it closed but uses actual buckles. This is less convenient but it also is more secure as I have had both magnets and snaps fail.

My particular bag is a nice caramel color. I expect it to darken with use.

I looked the bag over for blemishes and manufacturing defects and I have not found any. The leather is free of cuts and pocks, the stitching is tight and straight and the fasteners and accents are tight. There does not appear to be any loose threads either. Overall, it’s a well-made bag and I expect it to hold up for a long time.

I am satisfied with this bag. It looks great, it smells nice, and it seems to be made well. A little more room so that my laptop fit in the bag properly would make it even better.

I am best described as a skilled amateur when it comes to photography and I am always looking for ways to get better and to build my knowledge and ability. I am not a professional by any means, but I know a lot more than the average selfie-taker. I have wanted a ring light for a little while and I was delighted to have the chance to get to use this one. It does work, in the right circumstances, but it is definitely aimed at the base consumer market and is priced accordingly.

Thought it can be used as part of a professional set-up, it is designed and marketed as a consumer-grade unit. There are a number of obvious design decisions that make this more than just a little apparent. The tripod is good, but the mounts are designed for smartphones and will not work for DSLR cameras, mirrorless cameras or video cameras. That’s ok, as it is clearly marketed that way. The unit uses a USB power source which is an important point – the light itself isn’t especially bright like one that uses a normal AC power source. To be effective, the light needs to be fairly close to the subject. If a dim directional light is needed, a regular desk lamp is more than adequate in most cases. The upshot is that using USB power makes it much more portable for travel (more on that in a moment).

The remote allows for making a few adjustments to the light itself. There are three color modes and ten brightness modes, all of which can be (rather, must be) set through the remote. The adjustments are sufficient for this grade of light, though I would have found more colors and a more smooth graduation in brightness to be more useful. That’s more of a nitpick than a criticism considering the price point.

Build-wise, this unit is acceptable. It should hold up well enough in the studio or home office. What is lacking is a carry case to protect it when travelling. Considering the target audience (social media producers), this is an oversight that I think is important. To transport this light, it should be well secured and the only recourse as sold is to put it back in the original box, and that’s just unwieldy. Plan accordingly if you choose to transport this light.

This is an adequate unit for its target audience but will leave the aspiring professional underwhelmed. If you are looking for something that will work sufficiently for making posts to social media this is a reasonable unit; if you need a serious ring light for photography, consider other options. The main problem with this light is the fact that it is designed for portability but comes with no carrying case; keep this in mind.

I have worked with a lot of headphones, in particular active noise canceling (ANC) phones though I have several pairs of regular phones as well. One of the things that really bugs me about headphones these days is that there is a strong emphasis on bass, and most “bass enhanced” headphones overdrive the bass to the point that it destroys the rest of the sound profile in the process. This pair is one of the very few I have used that boosts the bass and gets it right.

Well, let’s get right to it – the sound profile is the most important feature of any headphones. If the sound is off, music will sound terrible and even straight speech can sound weird. These headphones tout their bass response, and I was a little apprehensive at first. However, unlike most, the bass on these is not so overdriven that it gives me a headache or interferes with the midrange. This is very unusual. The bass is definitely strong, but what is interesting is that it is actually detailed and not just a pounding low-frequency noise. I can hear details in the bass range that I usually can’t hear. A bass guitar sounds like a bass guitar, not a heavy noise frequency that is lost in distortion even at lower volumes. Even more interesting is that the bass, while stronger than the midrange, does not overpower it and drown it out, and the midrange sounds right. The highs are nice and clear too, without being bitingly sharp. Overall, the manufacturer did a very good job getting the sound profile right. It’s not exactly balanced because of the enhanced bass, but the enhancement is done well enough to make music still sound very natural.

Another area of surprise for me is that these are quite comfortable to wear for a little while even though they’re on-ear phones and not over-the-ear phones. I usually prefer over-the-ear phones that fit snugly, and these are the opposite of that. They’re on-ear and fit lightly, though tight enough to stay on when I tilt my head down and they do not pinch. These still have a little sound leakage when the volume is turned up a little, though it isn’t too bad at all.

These are Bluetooth phones and I was able to get them to connect to my phone very quickly and easily. Reconnection is quick and effortless.

Would I change anything? Yes – I would make these a tighter-fitting over-the-ear headphone. However, that’s a personal preference.

Overall, I am hard-pressed to find much about which to complain with these headphones. They get the bass enhancement right and sound really good. If you like headphones with a good bass response but still sound good, these are a good choice to consider.

I prefer to use a camera that is separate from my smartphone in most cases (though having a camera on my phone does come in handy). My DSLR also has a video mode but again I’d rather keep that separate, in this case because of the SD card capacity. I was interested in this video camera, mainly because it has the features I need in a video camera and it is relatively inexpensive. So far it has proven to be worth its asking price. It is not a high-end camera by any means but it is fine for general use and it is priced reasonably.

I’ll start with listing what’s in the box: the camera, a remote control for the camera, the microphone with foam wind guard, a cable to connect the microphone to the camera body, batteries for everything (3 different kinds), a carrying case, a 32GB SD card (not sure what class), a USB cable, an HDMI cable and a user’s manual for the camera as well as the microphone. Everything you need to get started is already in the box.

The camera is very lightweight, more so than my Sony camera which is more solid and heavy. The Sony also cost several times more. The light weight and plastic housing makes this camera feel somewhat cheap, though that is more cosmetic. The weight is actually an advantage as it helps with one-handed filming where a heavier camera would cause fatigue faster.

This is a 24MP digital camera and while that is not the best resolution available it is better than I would expect at this price point. Video comes out clear and smooth for the majority of projects. If you really need a higher resolution (in which case you’re probably doing more professional work) you likely will need to spend much more.

One area of disappointment for me with this camera is the lack of optical zoom. The zoom is purely digital and in my experience a digital zoom solution is never as clear and accurate as an optical zoom. This camera is no exception and I find the digital zoom to be almost useless to me. It has some uses when not zoomed far, but when zooming in closer and closer it becomes clear that the image quality suffers.

The camera does have a fairly comprehensive menu system and is easy to navigate. I did find the user manual mildly helpful in better understanding what the camera can do for me.

Overall, this is a decent little camera, especially when considering that the cost is quite low. It is not a top of the line camera and it does lack an optical zoom, but for the price point it is a decent consideration if you need a video camera suitable for taking on vacation or for class projects.

I have had good fortune with Verbatim products in the past, particularly blank CDs. I was excited to try this thumb drive and it has worked out well for me so far. The biggest plus is the size of the whole unit.

This is a 32GB drive which is a good size for most things anymore. It is good as a mass storage device but it also is suitable as boot media if you need to use it for recovery media, OS replacement or other things. There are bigger thumbs drives out there, but this one is big enough for most.

It comes preformatted with a FAT32 file system which makes it easy to read by practically all modern operating systems. My Linux system is able to mount it and read it, and Windows 10 opens it automatically. I likely will reformat it though for a better-performing file system to use primarily on my Linux system.

I looked on the drive for hidden files and found only the system volume stuff.

I did not make notes on the read/write speeds but it seems to perform on par with other name-brand drives I have. I have worked with drives that are quite slow when copying larger files like ISO images; this one seems about average when compared to Sandisk and PNY drives.

Where this drive really distinguishes itself, though, is in the very small size, which is good but also could be a problem. It folds up to about the size of a nickel (approximately) and easily fits in a change pocket. This keeps it out of the way and makes it easy to toss in a bag, purse, pocket or backpack even when it’s full. However, it also means it can easily find its way into the laundry.

So far, I have no complaints with this drive and am happy to recommend it. It performs well, it is easily recognized on different platforms and is small enough to go just about anywhere.

My experience with JVC up to this point has been with video equipment and televisions. My experiences have been positive so I hoped that this would be a good set of Active Noise Canceling (ANC) phones. I have worked with a lot of ANC phones – Bose, Sennheiser, Sony, Philips and more. Almost every set I have used has had some flaw, either in the ANC or in the sound profile. These JVC phones are interesting in that regard. The sound profile is nearly spot on, but the ANC is on the conservative side.

I’ll go over the ANC first. This is not a real competitor for the high end Sony or Bose sets and if the main thing you want from a set of ANC phones is noise elimination then these are far from the strongest or most aggressive. I have a fan that I use as the main test for ANC phones, and with the most aggressive phones the fan is almost completely wiped out. The JVC phones do cancel a good bit of noise, but it leaves a good bit of sound behind that Bose in particular eliminates. Now, that said, ANC headphones that can cancel more than these are almost universally much more expensive, often by double the price. These are what can probably be called “good enough for most”. For me, I like a more aggressive headphone, but these cancel enough ambient noise that when I am listening to music I don’t hear much else.

Many ANC phones fiddle with the sound profile to compensate for some of the lost frequency response, usually in the bass range and at the expense of the midrange. These phones are very unusual in that they don’t really seem to impact the sound profile much at all. And, the sound is very balanced. The bass is good, not overdriven (if you have ever used Dre Beats or Monster phones, you know exactly what I’m talking about). The midrange is warm and music sounds like it has the right depth as a result. The highs are clear and vocals sound very clean. The sound profile does not seem to be different between when the ANC function is on or off, though turning on the ANC does enhance the volume (which you can observe by having the headphones off when you activate the ANC in the middle of playback.

The ear cups are comfortable and I can wear these for a while before I need to take them off for comfort reasons. They don’t seem to get too warm when wearing for a while which is good. They’re not the most comfortable phones I have used, but they are better than many.

They connect via Bluetooth and I had no issues pairing and connecting them to my phone.

My favorite feature is that there is an independent volume control on the headphones themselves that does not change the volume setting on the source device. This is a feature that is a bit unusual; often, when the phones have a volume control on them it impacts the system volume when adjusted.

So, there is one thing about these phones that I think needs some improvement. Included with them is a cloth bag for protection, and that’s just not going to cut it, particularly in this price range. A bag prevents the contents from getting dirty but provides no damage protection. For the asking price (presently $149) these should have a hard case that at a minimum provides crush resistance.

I am very pleased with these headphones, more than I expected to be. They sound great, though the ANC is passable. My biggest issue isn’t with the phones themselves but with the lack of a suitable protective case. Hopefully JVC will resolve that issue in the near future. If you want a good set of ANC phones without spending north of $300, these are worth a look.

I have worked with a lot of active noise canceling (ANC) headphones, from a large variety of manufacturers. Every set I have owned, from the top-of-the-line to the weakest and cheapest, has had its strengths and weaknesses. Until recently, Bose was the one to beat when it specifically came to the ANC function, though many others have a better sound profile. My favorite ANC phones are a set of Sony in-ear buds that rival Bose in ANC and trounce them in sound quality. When I found out that Microsoft had made an ANC headphone as well I did not have the highest of expectations – I expected mediocrity with the ANC and a reasonably good sound profile. I was dead wrong in both presuppositions – these are incredible headphones and are worth every penny of the asking price. They’re not absolutely perfect, but they’re better than one could reasonably expect.

I’ll start by saying that I am sorry in advance for the lengthy review. I have a lot to say on these, and I would much rather give far too much information than not enough. The present asking price as I write this is $349 and that’s a lot of money to drop, so more information is better.

Right out of the box these are relatively nondescript and don’t jump out as either flashy or gaudy. The controls that are visible and obvious are limited – a power button and a mute button, as well as the USB Type C power jack and a 3.5mm audio input jack. There are more controls, though, and it takes a quick glance at the documentation to get a feel for what’s there. There are two dials, one on each can, for controlling the level of ANC and for controlling the volume, L and R respectively. The flat portion of the cans facing outward are multi-function touch controls that allow you to play/pause, skip forward and backward, handle calls and also interact with your digital assistant. I will come back to that last point a little farther down.

I powered these on and they immediately announced that they were ready to pair. I paired them to my iPhone and they connected and were usable quickly, faster than most Bluetooth devices I have used. I put them on, tapped once on the right ear and Pandora immediately started up. That was easy!

The sound quality is very good though I will stop short of calling it audiophile level. The bass is good and not overdriven. I don’t care for deep, pounding bass and that is a problem with a lot of ANC phones I have used (Dre Beats being among the most aggressive in that regard). It softens as the volume level is dropped and that is very normal. The midrange is actually quite good with the proper amount of depth, so music sounds full and warm and not like it’s being piped through a tunnel. The highs are bright and clear though not piercing. Overall, these are among the most balanced ANC headphones when it comes to the sound profile. I cranked the volume and they don’t distort.

The ability to adjust the ANC is not new; however, the way these headphones do it is very innovative and unlike anything else I have seen. The dial that controls it gradually lessens the amount of ANC that is applied when listening, in small but perceivable steps, until the ANC is turned off. With the central air on in the house, I gradually went from no ANC to maximum and it very gradually wiped out all of that sound. When at the maximum level the ANC is almost as aggressive as Bose, with a lot less of the the weird pressure sensation on the ears.

A unique feature of these phones is integration with Cortana. When paired to a device running Cortana, simply saying “Hey, Cortana” gets its attention and you can interact with the same types of commands you use on the command line or the search window. It does require that Cortana be properly configured. I have Cortana installed on my iPhone (yes, you can do that and it works well), and the integration with the headphones when connected is good. I had a Windows Phone when they were still available and I would have liked to try this with that phone.

There’s some debate on whether these are on-ear or over-the-ear phones. These are very definitely over-the-ear phones unless your ears are huge. The cups are buttery soft as is the head band, and these are very comfortable. I am able to wear them for long periods of time without fatigue. They do get warm after a while, so keep this in mind.

One area a lot of headphones skimp on is the carrying case. The case with these phones is better than average. It is crush resistant and provides good protection for the phones. Included within is an audio cable for input as well as a USB charging cable.

These headphones bring a lot to the table and were quite a shock for me. I had much lower expectations, for the ANC function in particular but also for the sound profile. Both exceeded my expectations and the comfort factor is the cherry on top. These are excellent phones and I am very pleased with them.

I have a teenage son who likes gaming on the PC and he has been wanting a new microphone for a while since his headset failed. I was given the opportunity to check this one out, and so far it has worked well. I do have complaint with it, though it’s not a deal breaker.

This is a USB-based microphone so it does not take up the audio jack when plugged in. This is good as it does not preempt a standard headphone set when it’s plugged in. Windows 10 detects it and it is immediately available as an audio input device. No special set-up and no driver downloads are required – it’s plug and play.

In use the sound quality has been good considering the price. In a two-way chat, those who have been on the other end of the discussion have told us that they can hear what is being said more clearly and there is less static than the previous microphone we were using, one that was quite a bit more expensive but still not high-end. That’s really all we could ask.

The one issue I have with it is that the base is not weighted well at all and it is very easy to tip it over or knock the microphone from where it sits on the desk. It’s easy enough to fix by either attaching it to a heavier base, using double-sided tape or even Velcro to secure it to the desk, or some other rigging to anchor the microphone assembly to the workspace. In the grand scheme of things, this is a minor issue; that said, I would rather spend slightly more and have a weighted base that isn’t as easily toppled.

For the price this is a good microphone that works better than could be reasonably expected. There is some room for improvement that would increase the cost slightly, but it would make the difference between being a good product and being a great one.

I use my smart phone for an alarm clock and in that capacity it works well and is all I need. However, when I check the time in the night it requires fumbling with the phone, then being half-blinded by the screen when I turn it on long enough to check the time. I looked to this alarm clock to resolve this for me and in terms of timekeeping it’s exactly what I hoped. As a radio, though, it leaves much to be desired.

The main feature of this clock that makes it worth the cost is the tremendous display. The numbers are huge and are red which does not ruin night vision. And, being always on all I have to do it look at it and know the time without fumbling in the dark for my phone. The projection on the ceiling is also great and I like being able to flip it at the touch of a button. For me, this is all I need.

However, where it fails is in the audio department. The speaker is sub-par and when listening to music to does not do well at all and sounds bad though not awful. I have heard worse. I would rather see this sell for $10 more and have a better speaker in it.

If you choose this alarm clock, get it for the display which is great and is the main selling point. If you are looking for a good clock radio and the sound is important to you, this might not be the best choice. I don’t care about the audio so this is a minor point; others may feel differently.

I have a couple of vertical mice that I use with my various computer systems, and they really do help with wrist fatigue and pressure. I also have a very nice Logitech MX Ergo trackball which is my go-to device for all of my systems. With Logitech releasing this vertical mouse, I was very optimistic that I would have the perfect solution. I was sorely disappointed. This is the worst Logitech device I have used and I can’t recommend it.

I’ll start with the good aspects of it, and then I will get into what isn’t so good.

This device can be connected via wireless USB or by Bluetooth. This is handy for when you want to use multiple systems and want to connect to them, in different ways. If you already have another wireless Logitech device, it can connect to the receiver for that device, reducing the number of wireless ports required. It connects well through either method and I have been able to move it between systems just with the press of the connection button on top.

In operation, it seems to work well as a pointing device. I will say that if you are not used to working with a vertical mouse there is a learning curve that is involved and you will be very frustrated while you make the adjustment. The movement isn’t hard – it’s working with the buttons which even though are worked with the same fingers they feel unnatural at first. This is a problem with all vertical mice, not just this one.

It is rechargeable, meaning no more batteries, and it holds a charge for a good while. I like mice and keyboards that don’t need batteries as in the very long term it saves money. (Logitech has a solar keyboard that is phenomenal and never needs to be plugged in at all – great device.)

I have three main issues with this vertical mouse. The first is the build quality. It feels very lightweight and cheap, and I would call it fragile. It is supposed to be light and maneuverable so it’s easy to use, but it’s so much so that it has a very cheap feel to it that is unsettling. Second, this is a HUGE mouse which for me is great but for most people is unworkable. It fits my hand very well, but I have hands like a gorilla. My wife tried it and found it to be completely unusable because she couldn’t work the buttons well at all due to the size. Finally, this is a very expensive peripheral compared to other vertical mice I have used that I actually prefer. This vertical mouse presently sells here for about $100. I have one that cost around $25 at the time I bought it, feels more solid and is easier to use. My wife and I compared the Logitech vertical mouse with my cheaper one, and we both agreed that the less expensive one was easier to handle and worked just as well. The only thing I lose with the cheaper mouse is Bluetooth connectivity, which in my case is not a deal breaker.

I wish I could rate this mouse more highly but I just can’t. It’s expensive, feels cheap and just isn’t made to fit smaller hands (and usually, it’s a challenge finding mice for larger hands). It’s worth consideration if you need a mouse that can be easily transitioned between wireless and Bluetooth, but if you just need to use it with one system I’d recommend researching other options before making a purchase.

I use laptops at home instead of tower systems, but I still prefer a stand-alone keyboard for most things. I have had very good success with Microsoft peripherals in the past so I had high expectations for this keyboard. So far, it works well enough but I have encountered a couple of snags that make it less than perfect.

This is a slim and efficiently designed keyboard and it is slightly wider than my 15.6” laptop. It’s the right size for me and I am happy with the dimensions when it comes to fitting it in my work space. No complaints there.

Set-up is a little on the tricky side. I tried to set it up for Bluetooth use without following the instructions first and got nowhere. It does not appear in the list of available devices so it could not be paired right off the bat, though my system does handle the Bluetooth standard. The instructions say to connect it via USB first, then turn it on and follow the set-up when Windows detects it. However, the instructions do not say that you must use the cable that came with the keyboard; I used a different one and failed, though the keyboard did work as a USB keyboard with that 3rd-party cable connected.

I’ll answer the very obvious question right now – I was able to get it working under Linux as a USB keyboard, but not as a Bluetooth keyboard. I am not sure if the problem is with the Bluetooth receiver in the system I tested or if the keyboard is just not compatible at all. I have an iPhone as well and it did not see the keyboard in the list of available devices. This is not a failure or a shortcoming of the keyboard – it operates very much in accordance with how it has been marketed, so getting it to work under Linux with Bluetooth would have been just a bonus.
