Interestingly, it says it can be set up to work under the Windows Phone platform which has been discontinued...

When I set it up under Windows 10, it did not go as the documentation said it would go. I did get the toast notification and I clicked as directed. It set everything up and said it was ready to go. It never allowed me to set up the fingerprint configuration and I have been unable to find any setting within Windows to allow me to revisit. So, I have a fingerprint reader that I can’t configure. Considering that this is being used in a home with a private computer with password protection this really isn’t a show-stopper but it would have been nice to mess with this technology.

In operation the keyboard is very responsive and so far I have been pleased with it except for one thing that I cannot seem to reconfigure. I prefer to have the function keys operate as function keys by default, instead of media keys. Without being able to find a keyboard configuration setting in the OS anywhere I have no way to reverse the default operation, which is to require pressing the Function key prior to hitting F1 – F12 to get them to default as function keys instead of media keys.

I do like this keyboard and it works well for my needs. The set-up isn’t bullet-proof though, and there are some behaviors it would be nice to change or reconfigure.

I recently purchased a new [Windows] laptop that has a Type C connector, and I selected this unit to get more USB ports as well as the card reader. So far it has worked out well for me and it seems to work as designed, and with no tweaks or software installation required.

This little unit is small and it easily fits in a shirt pocket though the cord does impact the way it fits in said pocket. It’s a little bigger than a comb but smaller than a candy bar. It feels solid and well-made and so far has shown no signs of fatigue or weakness.

I plugged it in and the fit was very snug so I had to work with it to get it plugged in properly. That’s actually a positive – it should not come unplugged unexpectedly when I move my laptop or plug something else into it, a problem I have had on occasion with MicroUSB devices.

Windows recognized it immediately and it didn’t seem to need any extra device drivers or anything to make it work. It picked up the Ethernet interface as well as the USB hub, and that’s really all I would expect before plugging in anything else. The card reader works and I was able to read images off of the card I use in my camera through this device.

I have not yet tried it under Linux but that’s coming shortly. I also have an Android tablet with a Type C port with which I will try this device as well.

I have not yet tried the HDMI adapter. I have a use for it as my laptop actually does not have an HDMI port on-board and I’d like to attach it to my television to stream video.

Would I add anything? I would have liked to see an integrated wireless adapter or a Bluetooth receiver built in, though I have those built in to my system and adding those to this unit would drive up the cost a bit. I would probably make the unit slightly larger too.

So far, this device has been solid for me. It works right out of the box without any setup required – plug it in and you’re ready to go.

I bought this replacement ball for my Logitech MX ERGO, which worked well for me before I accidentally dropped it and subsequently put a pock mark on the original ball. The ERGO still worked but would occasionally get stuck when the support pegs would catch the pock and cause the ball to resist - not enough to really hurt anything but just enough to make digital drawing difficult and just enough to annoy me. This replacement ball has taken care of that for me and has proven to be a worthwhile expense for me.

The ERGO and the M570 have the same size ball, so this ball can be used in either (I was using the ball from my old M570 in the ERGO while I waited for this ball to arrive). Replacement is a 30-second procedure and requires no special tools, though a pencil does make getting the old ball out a lot easier.

There are two different finish types available, glossy and matte. I chose the glossy in red. Operation has been absolutely smooth with no resistance at all and no catches. I haven’t noticed any operational differences between it and the original gray ball that came in my ERGO. And, in my opinion, the dark red of this ball actually looks a little nicer than the original silver ball as well as the blue M570 ball.

This wasn’t an expensive replacement and so far it has worked out very well for me. It has restored operation of my trackball to what it was before I damaged the original ball, which is really all I needed. Based on my experience with it, this is an easy replacement ball to recommend if you need to replace the ball in either a Logitech M570 or an MX ERGO.

NOTE: There are several models of GoPro cameras attached to this listing. I am specifically reviewing the GoPro Hero.

I have worked with a number of the cheap knock-off sport cameras available and up to this point I have been relatively satisfied with them. I have not worked with an actual GoPro before now, so I was interested in seeing how well this unit would compare to the cheap clones. There’s really no comparison – the GoPro is an order of magnitude better. Yes, it’s more expensive but it’s a higher quality product that works better.

Of the GoPro models available, this is the most budget-friendly I have seen and it doesn’t come with a lot of frills and extras. It does come in a waterproof shell and it does have a clip so you can attach it to a helmet or handle bars, but that’s really about all that comes in the package. There’s no memory card with it, either, so plan on picking up a MicroSD card with the camera.

The usability when compared to the cheap clones is about the same. The menus are a bit different but they do perform the same general functions. That said, where the GoPro Hero sets itself apart from all of those cheaper cameras is in the quality of the product and the resulting pictures and recordings. This little camera is solid and so is the waterproof shell; it will stand up to some abuse and should just keep right on going without batting an eye. It also produces better-quality video than every clone I have tried, which is saying something because some of the cheap cameras actually do a decent job of producing good video.

The size and weight are nice features that make it very highly portable. I have seen motorcyclists on the highways with cameras similar to this one mounted on their helmets, and while that looks funny to the observer it makes for some great videos online and it does give the motorcyclist some backing when there is a traffic incident. For the younger crowd, it’s great for capturing skateboarding tricks in the first person as well as that wild ride down a water tube.

I have not worked with this camera a whole lot yet but I have seen enough to know it’s a big upgrade from the cheaper clones that are available in abundance. The Hero is a budget-friendly option for the user who wants quality results without breaking the bank, in exchange for giving up some of the less critical features like Bluetooth and WiFi connectivity. If you need those features, but you still want the best-quality, you’ll need to look at one of the more advanced and expensive models.

I selected this mouse to be a spare for when I am on the go. Amazon-branded things are often of good quality so I was hopeful for this mouse. I came away a bit disappointed due to a couple of issues I have had with it.

This is a basic wireless mouse, suitable for surfing the web, working on documents or similar tasks. It’s not particularly good for gaming as it is not designed for such. If the goal is to have something that will allow you to casually use the computer for basic tasks, this one will serve. If you need a heavy-duty mouse for frequent use or you need a gaming mouse, spend a little more and get a more solid mouse.

One of the issues I have with mice is that I have huge hands and finding a mouse that fits my hand properly is a challenge. This is a smaller than average mouse, so it really doesn’t work for me. That’s not a big deal; it was designed for the large majority of people with smaller hands, so I can’t criticize this mouse for its size. It’s in that weird in-between size - smaller than the average desktop mouse but larger than a travel mouse.

The real issue I have seen with this mouse, though, is with the DPI setting. After idling for a little while, the mouse has a very nasty and predictable habit of resetting the DPI mode automatically. This is the only mouse I have used that has exhibited the problem. This impacts me when I am doing photo editing or using a graphics program and I need fine control. Sure, I can hit the DPI setting and get it to where I need it to be easily enough, but I should not have to do this over and over, particularly when I need the same setting all the time.

Other than the DPI setting, this mouse works exactly as expected. It is a decent mouse if you do not need predictable DPI settings. If you need a mouse that retains your settings, or if you need a larger mouse, or if you need a heavy-duty device, this is not the right choice for you. It’s fine for travel or casual use.

I use active noise canceling (ANC) headphones all the time and prefer them to normal headphones as I tend to work in noisy environments and I’ve found that with ANC engaged I can play music at lower volumes. I like Sony headphones so I was excited to try these ANC ear buds. They’re a bit unusual in a few ways but they work well and are worth their asking price.

These are truly wireless and have no physical connection between them. Power them both on and they find one another. They pair via Bluetooth to a phone, tablet or PC, and the connection is stable up to about 40’ around corners. This is a good start.

There are several modes to these when it comes to the ANC function and each has its uses. I usually just use full ANC without any of the ambient sound modes turned on as it gives the best music experience. One of the two ambient modes is optimized for speech and voice, the other for more generalized noise. Neither completely cut off noise canceling, but rather they allow different bands of outside noise to come through. In full ANC mode, these are good noise cancellers, though not as aggressive as some others like Bose.

These have proven to be comfortable, and they have the little wings on each bud for keeping them in place in your ear. I used them while working in the yard and never once did I have a problem with slipping or falling out, even though I have the wrong size silicone insert on one of them.

The sound is very good but I would stop short of calling it outstanding. The bass is heavier than I like though not so bad that it gives me a headache unless I pump the volume up too much. The midrange is warm and full, and the highs are bright and crisp without being piercing. The sound can be adjusted a bit in the app that you can download, as it has an equalizer of sorts that lets you tweak the levels or choose a preset.

Ah, the app… This is the primary downside of these. The method to adjust these is either an Android or iOS app, not a physical piece of hardware and there is no Windows equivalent (for those who want to use these with a PC). The app is a little clunky though fairly self-explanatory and it does do what it’s supposed to do. Given a choice between an app or an additional piece of hardware, I would choose the hardware.

These charge up in the carrying case, which has leads that connect to each bud. Pay attention when you put these in the case – it is possible to reverse them, and while it hurts nothing the charging doesn’t work well… The case has some sort of battery in it and it charges the buds without being plugged in itself, though it does require occasional charging. Charging is fast – I charged them from empty to full in about an hour. One thing that could be improved, though: the buds can be popped in the charger while still powered on, and the act of charging them does not make them cut off. So, you can end up with dead buds and a dead charger too.

These are decent wireless sport buds that have good sound and good ANC functions. They’re comfortable and not overpriced. There are a couple of areas for improvement, particularly in charging but also in the app control, that would make these even better.

One of the problems I have seen with the latest crop of notebooks and Ultrabooks that have come out is a lack of USB ports. There's usually a need for more ports than these systems have and it gets frustrating. A small USB hub like this is a good solution. That said, this particular hub does not have a separate power source so some consideration must be made when plugging in power-hungry devices.

From a design stantpoint this is a solid unit, shaped to be accessible without being huge. It has a little weight to it and this is helpful for keeping it stable. The addition of Velcro strips in the package to secure it in one place is a welcome inclusion and makes securing the hub very simple no matter what your configuration is.

The hub provides four USB 3.1 type A ports. Let me state what should be obvious - this will not convert a USB 1.1 or 2.0 port into a 3.1 port, so plug it into a 3.1 port if you want the speed across the hub. For my specific uses, it does not need to be a high-speed hub and I am find with using it as a 2.0 hub, but admittedly that's slightly wasteful.

There is no power port on this hub and there is no DC adapter in the box. So, any power that the hub needs comes through the onboard port into which it is plugged. That's fine for low-power devices like mice, keyboards, memory sticks and so on, but if the intent is to plug in such things as USB hard drives with no external power supply this can cause some headaches. No, one drive isn't going to overload the hub, but if you have multiple drives attached there may be reliability issues when they starve one another for power. When the device plugged in has its own power supply (like a big backup drive), this has little impact on the hub.

The point is, plan carefully how you intend to use the hub.

I like this hub and it does a good job for what it is. It has given me three extra ports on an Ultrabook I use which is all I could ask for. The ability to power this hub with it's own power supply would be the only area for improvement I could find.

The Bluetooth adapter in my main system has failed so I have been looking for a replacement for it for some time. I am familiar with Sabrent as a brand so I was willing to give this little adapter a shot. It works for me, and so far it hasn’t given me any difficulties.

First things first. This is a tiny little device, the size of a USB receiver for mice and keyboards. Be careful when you do not have this plugged in because it is easy to misplace. I don’t mention this as a fault but rather as a point of consideration. If your desk is cluttered like mine, be prepared to misplace this little guy once in a while if you ever unplug it.

I didn’t have any issues setting this unit up. Others have reported that it’s not cooperative during setup and installation but that was not my experience. I plugged it in and Windows 10 saw the dongle right away. I loaded the drivers and it was good to go – simple as that.

I have been able to pair keyboards, mice, and headphones through this adapter and all work like they should. I have observed, though, that the volume seems slightly low when using headphones when compared to the older adapter in the system. I am not sure if this is a function of the adapter or if there is some setting in Windows that I have not found. It’s not enough to bother me, but it is enough for me to notice.

So far, so good with this adapter. It has given me Bluetooth connectivity again on a system where the interface had failed. No complaints from me.

I have worked with a number of trackballs, my most successful being a Logitech M570 which served me well for years. I finally wore it out and after some research I purchased the Logitech MX Ergo to replace it. I have had it about three days, and it has already proven to be exactly what I had hoped and more. It’s not perfect but it’s close.

I was attracted to the fact that it works both as a wireless mouse with a USB receiver as well as a Bluetooth mouse. I have two computers on my desk, one being a Windows 10 system and the other being a Linux (Arch-based) system. My old trackball worked with both though I had to move the receiver between the systems, so I went with the assumption that this one would also work with both.

I connected the trackball to my Windows system via Bluetooth and it has been flawless in operation. It connects without intervention and it works exactly as expected - all buttons work as they should and the operation is very smooth and predictable.

I plugged the USB receiver into the Linux machine, pushed the channel button on the trackball and it immediately started working on the Linux machine, even though it was still paired to the Windows system via Bluetooth. It works exactly as it should and I have had absolutely no issues with the trackball on my Linux installation. So now, I can switch back and forth between the two systems with the push of the channel button and without having to connect or disconnect anything. It simply works, and the switch-over is fast. The take-away for me is that I no longer need two mice on the desk.

I friend came over with his MacBook and there was no issue at all with connecting the trackball via USB. We did not try connecting via Bluetooth.

The trackball has a metal plate on the bottom that is held in place with magnets, and depending on how the plate is attached the trackball can be tilted to ease wrist strain. The plate serves another purpose too - it adds a lot of weight to the trackball. Even without the plate, the trackball is hefty and has some mass to it, but the plate just makes it even more so. For me that’s a positive; others may dislike the added weight.

One of the things I have missed has been a tilting scroll wheel. This trackball has one and I have been enjoying getting used to that feature again.

One thing I did notice is that there is no CD/DVD in the package for loading drivers. This isn’t a big deal, and it’s easy enough to get the drivers from the net. That said, the trackball just seems to work when you attach it, without any issue. For me it has absolutely been plug-and-play, on every system I have tried.

If I could change one thing - I would have made this trackball a little bigger. I have big hands and I struggle to find a trackball that’s an absolute perfect fit. This one is close. For the large majority of people it’s going to be spot on.

I am very happy with this trackball and have no issue with recommending it. It works great, connects easily, when connected to two different systems it switches at the press of a button, it has a bit of heft to it and the tilt is adjustable for wrist comfort. It’s really all I could ask for.

NOTE: This review is written for the Small, Bluetooth edition.

I have been using Wacom Intuos and Bamboo tablets for years, not really for graphic arts but more for digital handwriting and for use as an alternative to traditional mice and trackballs. My present solution is an Intuos 5 medium which seems to be about the right fit for my hands and my work space. The one drawback has been that it’s a wired solution. This new Intuos is a Bluetooth solution and it is definitely a step forward. For me the challenge is downgrading to the small from the medium, but it’s a good fit for me when traveling and when working in cluttered spaces.

To approximate the size, it is roughly equivalent to 7” tablet in size. It’s small enough to tuck away in a corner of a desk when not in use, and when it is being used it does not take up large amounts of real estate. The design itself makes it suitable for use just about anywhere it can be set down and kept stable - one of the reasons I like drawing tablets more than traditional mice.

The Bluetooth connectivity is new to me, and I was pleasantly surprised to find that this unit can connect via USB as well. So, if your system is like one of mine and the Bluetooth doesn’t work, this drawing tablet still will work.

I have it connected to my Windows 10 system. I have not yet made the effort to get it working with my Linux system, though I expect there will be some labor involved to make that work. I’ll revisit that later.

In operation, this is a straightforward drawing tablet though it is an improvement over my Intuos 5 in some ways. Of course the Bluetooth is a step up, but I was surprised by the increased number of pressure levels which is effectively doubled over my old tablet - 4096 vs 2048. For someone like me, this is not a huge difference and I don’t take advantage, but for someone who is very serious about fine digital artwork this can be a huge benefit. For use in handwriting, it is not especially important as even 512 pressure levels (like my original Bamboo small) is more than sufficient.

When you register, you get a choice between three Corel titles, of which you can select two (for the medium you get all three). Some may find the choice difficult - Painter Essentials 6, AfterShot 6 and Clip Studio Paint Pro (2 years) - but for me, having AfterShot is more than enough.

There is a downside to this little tablet, though - the pen is mediocre. There is no comfort grip, changing the nib is a pain, and there’s a very limited number of replacement nibs for it. It’s the one weak spot in an otherwise nice product, and even then it’s not all that bad.

The hardest part for me with this specific tablet is the move from a medium to a small, but this this counterbalanced by the Bluetooth connectivity and the inclusion of the Corel titles, specifically AfterShot. This is a very nice drawing solution and is it priced nicely. I’d recommend the small for anyone either just getting started or experimenting; the medium is a better fit for those more experienced or needing more real estate. I would choose a different pen if available, though.

I normally think of storage media and batteries when I think of Maxell. That said, this is my second pair of Maxell headphones. My first pair is an ANC set that isn’t perfect, but they’re far and away better than I would ever have expected. These phones are not ANC phones, they’re just wireless listening phones. I was hopeful that they would be as good as my ANC phones in terms of sound quality, and Maxell has not disappointed me. They’re not perfect but they’re better than you can reasonably expect from the asking price.

Up front, let me say that I am not a big fan of on-ear headphones, and these fall into that category. I prefer an over-the-ear phone which to me is more comfortable. These aren’t bad for on-ear phones. This comes down to preference. If you are cool with on-ear phones, these will work for you, but if you have to have over-ear phones then you should consider other options.

The pads are soft enough, though they aren’t super cushy like some others I have used.

Being Bluetooth phones I immediately connected them to my phone. The connection went off without a hitch, though the phone was slower to find these than I had hoped. Once connected, they have been stable and reconnecting is much faster.

The real test is the sound profile. On my ANC phones, Maxell worked a miracle and got the sound profile nearly perfect even when the noise canceling is turned on. With these phones, the sound profile is not precise but it’s very balanced and better than average. The bass is strong but not throbbing like most headphones made these days. I like bass, but I don’t appreciate the insistence on pumping it so heavily that it gives me a headache. The midrange is full and music sounds like it has some depth without sounding like it’s playing from the bottom of a well. The highs are bright and clear, though on specific frequency ranges there is the slightest hint of distortion if you really look for it (and since I’m reviewing these, I went looking for it).

I cranked up the music as high as I could, and there was only a hint of distortion in the highs. And I had a headache when I was done.

Build-wise, these are not too bad. I would not pack them in a gym bag or anything like that, but these should work fine for a long while as long as they’re cared for properly. There’s enough flex in them to make them durable enough to survive some rough handling, but at the end of the day they’re primarily plastic - a drop from the right height or being crushed in a book bag will break them.

These phones are under $50 as I write this. What’s really distressing is that I have phones that are north of $200 that do not sound as good as these. Maxell knows how to make a good headphone that competes well with more expensive phones - I have two very different pairs to prove it. It begs the question - why are they only making budget headphones?

I would rate these slightly lower if the asking price were above the $50 mark. But, at the asking price you’d be hard-pressed to find headphones that sound better.

I have built systems with SSDs for the last several years and I have come to see where they have their strengths and weaknesses. Not all SSDs are the same, and some have distinct advantages over others though the gap is definitely narrowing. This is my first experience with Samsung’s SSDs, and so far it has been a very positive experience. It has given me no issues at all and has performed well.

I installed the drive in a Dell Inspiron laptop which was running Windows 8. On the SSD, I installed Linux instead. Installation was very smooth, it was quick and I had a working system up and running in no time. I have now been running the system constantly for over a week (no powering off or hibernating) and the drive has shown no signs of trouble.

I loaded up a virtual machine and ran it on top of the main installation. The VM and the host install both have performed admirably and have not suffered from any noticeable I/O lag. Running smartctl against the drive after the past week of testing, it has reported no errors and a very healthy drive across the board.

Aside from the speed advantages of an SSD over a platter-based drive, this drive is absolutely silent (no surprise there) and so far I have not had any heat issues. It has given me no indications of any trouble in operation and my system is running as smoothly as should be expected.

The one issue I have with this drive, and it’s not a performance or quality issue, is the pricing. It is a little more expensive than most, and so far I have not seen any real justification for it over the likes of Crucial, Kingston or other branded drives. There may be justifiable reasons that reveal themselves later (I do not know how long this drive will continue to work but it should literally last for several years, even under very heavy use), but for now it seems a tad expensive compared to competitors.

Operationally I cannot find fault with this drive. It works well, it’s fast and quiet (as should be expected) and so far I’ve not had heat issues with it. Utilities I have run against it have shown that the drive is very healthy and has reported no problems out of the box. This is a good drive that will serve well. Time will tell, though, if it is worth the slightly higher asking price.

I have had several pairs of Panasonic headphones and I regard them as a budget-grade phone that is better than generic but leaves room for improvement. I was hopeful that these phones would be better and would distinguish themselves as better than average. Unfortunately they do not and they suffer from the same issues I have had with other Panasonic phones in the past. They're certainly not bad, but there is some room for improvement.

First off, these look great, though I would stop short of calling them "retro" in appearance. They're styled to be retro-looking, but they betray their youth in the plastic details. That said, they have the cool factor that they are going for and the will stand out over most run-of-the-miss headphones than you'll find most people using.

One of the problems I have with these is strictly a personal preference. When I use over-the-ear phones like these, I want a phone that clamps down tight over my ear and applies some pressure. This does two things for me - it cuts down on the chances that they'll slip off when I look down, and it cuts sound leakage when I am listening to something. These are a more relaxed, loose fit, and this is not to my tastes. There's a good number of users that will be very happy with the way these fit, and as I said this is a preference, so I cannot say this is a fault. It's something to keep in mind, though. Aside from the tightness (or lack thereof), the pads and band are soft and these can be worn for a long while without issue.

These are Bluetooth phones, so I used them to connect to my Android tablet. They connected very quickly and without any real issues. I have no complaints there. They stay connected once paired and the range is good to at least 20-30 feet from the source which is good.

Where these headphones fail, though, is in the most important area - the sound profile. The highs are slightly muddy though not unacceptably so. The bass is present and not overdriven which to me is a very good thing. But, the midrange is not right at all, and as a result the music sounds like it is coming out of a tunnel when I am listening. Yes, I could fix this with an equalizer, but many people will not think to do that or do not have access to one. This is a familiar issue I have had with Panasonic phones, and unfortunately these do not correct the issue.

For speech, these sound just fine.

These are interesting phones and they look good. For those liking a loose fit, they're going to be very comfortable. However, there is an issue in the sound profile that anyone serious about their music will not be able to help but notice, and at the price point it's a more serious issue than if these were inexpensive (budget) headphones.

I work a lot with smart watches but this is the first health monitor/GPS watch I have used. I was excited to have the
opportunity to work with it, and I was hopeful that it would be a good unit. Epson is a brand I know well from their printers, so out of the gate I had some expectations. This watch has proven to be a mixed bag.

I will start with what I believe are the strongest features. This watch has a much better-than-average charger. Many watches I have used have a magnetic charger that is either poorly constructed or will not stay on the device it'’s charging. This one, however, is a clamp-based charger that does a good job of holding the watch even under its own weight without letting it slip or shift. I would have liked to see other manufacturers adopt this kind of charging clamp.

The battery lasts for a very long time. I charged it up completely and after taking it from the charger I deliberately left it on the shelf to drain. It's rated for 20 hours, and I assume that is for active use. Letting it sit idle, it lasted two weeks for me. It of course drains much faster when it is actively being used so once I started using it I had to charge it again. This is a handy data point if you're traveling - if you're going for a weekend, it holds enough charge to get through in most cases, and if you are an infrequent user it will retain a charge for a while.

The display is very clear and easy to read. I have had no issues at all with the display and I am very pleased with how easy on the eyes it is.

One of the issues I have with most wrist-wear of any kind is getting it to fit properly. I have large hands and wrists, and I found this watch to be a bit snug on even the loosest setting. This is par for the course for me. I was hopeful it would fit a bit better, but it wasn't to be.

The aggravation started when I set up the software and paired the watch to my phone. The Bluetooth pairing did not go smoothly and I tried several times to get it straight. I finally switched over to setting it up through the watch instead of through the phone, and I was able to get it working and connected. While this is an acceptable work-around for someone with patience, it is an aggravation for someone who prefers things to just work the way they're supposed to.

I will say I am not especially impressed with the software app. I think it is a little too overly complex and counter-intuitive, but it does work and it has a lot of features. It does a good job of tracking progress.

So, aside from setup and fit, how does it work? It seems to work well. I am very familiar with sport GPS units so I assumed this one would work about the same, and it does. It acquires the satellites and uses those to report position back to the phone app so you can track yourself. This is useful when you want to see where you went and how far. The speed of acquisition of the satellites seems to be roughly the same as with my hand-held units. The heart rate monitor seems to be good and in measuring manually for comparison it appears to be accurate. The step feature is a good quick measurement and is sufficient to replace a dedicated pedometer.

Overall this is a decent health watch, but there's some room for improvement. It looks great, it works well and it's easy to read. It is hampered by less-than-idea setup and software, and it would be nice if it fit a little better.

I will start by saying that I am typically not a fan of ear buds. I will also say that the very best headphones I have is a set of Sony active noise canceling ear buds. I have always had good success with Sony audio products and I regard the brand as an upper mid-range line. These buds are disappointing in that, while they’re comfortable for ear buds, the sound profile is lacking, specifically in the midrange.

This is a basic set of ear buds that work as you might expect. They do not have ANC functionality, there is no battery or battery pack and there is no Bluetooth functionality. These are straight plug-in audio gear with no fancy features. These will work with just about any device that provides a 3.5mm audio jack.

Most ear buds are uncomfortable to me, but these are surprisingly comfortable and I can wear these for a good bit of time. They come with several inserts of varying sizes so you can find the size that fits your ear canal just right. The included inserts are soft and do not irritate my ears as much as others have done in the past. I still very much prefer over-the-ear headphones which is a personal preference more than anything.

So, where’s the problem? The problem lies in the sound profile which is unbalanced. Having used literally dozens of sets of ear buds and headphones over the past 3-5 years I have developed a good feel for what sounds right and what doesn’t. Most ear buds have one of two issues, either way too much bass or almost none at all. These are surprising in that they actually get the bass just about right, not too heavy and not too light. The highs are very bright and clear, perhaps a touch too piercing for my tastes but not to the point of being unacceptable. The midrange, though, is flat. The result is that music sounds somewhat sterile and lackluster. This is similar to the issue I have seen with my Bose headset. These still sound good, but they fall short of where they could and should be.

Normally I would rate ear buds with a glitch in the sound profile a little higher, as they’re still quite usable and they sound decent. But, these are much more expensive than the average and I have heard less expensive buds with more balanced sound. Sony makes a number of sets of ear buds and headphones, but these are not among their best offerings.

There are two of us in the house that use iPhones with the lightning port and as such we do need extra cables. Lightning cables are great but they do have a tendency to break. Also, not all third-party cables are the same and some are not worth the box they ship in. I was anxious to try this cable and I have found it to be a perfectly acceptable replacement for the one that came with my phone. Actually, it’s better.

First things first - it is important to note that this cable is MFI-certified which is actually a big deal. I have worked with cables that are certified and those that are not. Those that carry certification are guaranteed to work properly with your device, while those that are not certified are a roll of the dice. This cable is certified so it means two things you can expect from it: it will allow you to charge your phone without worry, and it will allow you to connect your phone to your computer without complaining about the cable being unauthorized. It just works.

The cable is shielded in a heavy nylon weave and that is a double-edged sword. On one hand it means the cable is very stiff and not very bendy which may or may not be an issue. More importantly, though, it means it is going to last longer than plastic coated cables which tend to flex and break.

The ends are terminated well too, with a hard plastic sleeve at the end of each plug where the cable connects. This spot is where most cables fail, and it is nice to see that some thought was put into reinforcing the cable at this point.

The weighted ball is interesting but to me it gets in the way. It can be slid up and down the cable which has its uses, but it is large enough and bulky enough to be more of a hindrance to me than a help. That said, if you are putting this cable in an area where it will not be moved and you intend to leave it there for the long term, it does prevent tangles and it allows for keeping gently tension on the cable.

Overall, I am pleased with this cable. It’s a lot less expensive than Apple-branded cables and it definitely is more durable and should last a long time.

I am usually not a fan of ear bud-style headphones as I have trouble finding sets that are either comfortable or have good sound. More often than not, buds have been tuned to have the bass either too strong or too weak and they sound very unnatural. Sony did a good job with these and got them sounding very balanced. They’re not perfect when it comes to comfort but there are ways to remedy this.

These are not active noise canceling (ANC) phones. Sony offers another model that is ANC-capable and they’re excellent but an order of magnitude more expensive. If you need ANC, this particular set of buds cannot do that so consider other options but be prepared to spend more.

These are sport-style ear buds in that they come on a neck harness and they are wireless. They connect easily via Bluetooth though they come with an adapter so they can be corded and used with devices that cannot work with Bluetooth. One concern with this type of phone is that often the cord is a little short between the harness and the buds, meaning a turn of the head pulls the cord a bit and can dislodge the buds from your ears. This particular set has some extra play in the cord so I have not had this issue as of yet. The cord on either bud can be “shortened” on either side by pulling the slack through tensors on the harness to reduce play in the wire.

In terms of use for sports and exercise, these feel a bit more fragile than most and I would caution against using them for doing anything much more active than running. They might hold up just fine, but these are a bit more pricey than most and are not ruggedized. This is probably my main complaint with these.

Comfort-wise, these are not bad. I have had better success with these than most, though I still greatly prefer over-the-ear headphones most of the time. The inserts are relatively soft and pliable and they do fit well, and the set comes with multiple sizes so adjustments can be made to get them to fit just right. In researching, I found that there are plenty of replacement tips; so, they can be swapped out if need be to find something that fits better or is more comfortable.

The main consideration about any set of phones, regardless of price, is the sound. In my mind, Sony has always had good quality products that do a fine job of balancing the sound. These ear buds are very much in line with my previous experiences. The sound profile is very balanced and even and the result is natural sounding playback. The tendency with the majority of manufacturers is to heavily push the bass. The bass in these is present and you can definitely hear it but it is not so pronounced as to dampen or overpower the rest of the profile. The midrange sounds good (particularly for ear buds) and had the right depth, meaning music sounds warm and not like it’s coming out of a tunnel or barrel. The highs are bright and clear but not piercing. I would stop short of saying these are audiophile quality, but the sound is much better than most bud-style earphones.

These are not your typical, cheap set of ear buds. These are better than the average and they are designed to be more comfortable and useful in an active lifestyle. They sound great. My only complaint is the construction - the harness in particular feels fragile. If you don’t need ANC and you don’t anticipate using your phones for heavy physical activity, these are a great choice. If you need something a bit more rugged, you might consider other options.

Most of my experience with Logitech products has been with keyboards and mice, though the company has made products in other segments as well, such as video surveillance systems and Modula-2 compilers. This is the first set of Logitech speakers I have tried and used, and I was expecting them to be a solid mid-range offering. They’ve proven to be better than that.

These speakers are not very large, about as big around as the lid on a container of oatmeal. They’re heavy, though, and in addition to the main speaker they have a bass subwoofer on each. They feel very solid and should hold up under some abuse shy of being dropped on a concrete surface.

My first test was to connect them to my phone via Bluetooth. I plugged them in, turned them on and they immediately started broadcasting their ID. My phone immediately saw them and I was able to pair and connect them without any issue at all. Based on my experience there, the Bluetooth connectivity is excellent. I later tried to connect them to my computer by the audio cable – simple and easy as should be expected.

The main question when using a set of speakers – how do they sound? In a word: excellent. The bass response is solid but not overdriven, the midrange is warm and has good depth, and the highs are sharp and clear without being shrill. I was expecting a more subdued sound profile, but Logitech did a good job with getting these to sound great. I would stop short of calling these audiophile quality, but the large majority of users should be happy.

I bumped up the volume and tried to get these to distort and I was unsuccessful. They remained clear even through the full volume range. I set them in the kitchen, turned up the volume and went to the basement as I was still able to hear the sound clearly – through the ceiling.

I do have speakers that sound better by a little bit, but they cost three times as much and they’re quite a bit larger. Considering the price point and the size of these speakers, these are much better than one could realistically expect.

I have a Samsung NX300 camera and so far the main problem I have had has been the battery life. I can get approximately 250-300 pictures between charges (assuming auto settings with average exposure times) which is very low and it has stranded me without battery power more than once. I was looking for extra batteries and an external charger when I found this one here on Amazon. I decided to take a chance on it and I purchased it, and that has paid off for me.

First things first: the batteries in this pack work just fine in my camera. The size and footprint are the same as the manufacturer’s battery, but the capacity is actually higher. The original battery is 1130mA, but these are 1500mA which means more exposures per charge - in theory quite a bit more. I have not yet drained one of these so I do not know exactly how long they last but initial indicators are strong that I will get more than 300 exposures per charge. So, since there are two batteries in the package and I still have the original battery, I should be able to get 1,000 or more exposures per outing if I have all of them charged up when I start.

The external charger is a big plus for me - no more plugging in the camera itself to charge the battery. It plugs into a standard outlet, but it also has an adapter so it can be plugged into the 12V outlet in the car. That’s handy for road trips. So far I have not used the adapter but I am pleased to have it and will use it at some point. The charger does a good job and I was able to charge up one of the batteries in 3-4 hours (I wasn’t paying attention so I am not sure of the exact time it took).

If there’s anything at all I would add or improve: it would have been nice to have a USB cable to plug into the barrel adapter port, so it could be charged over USB too, even if it took a lot longer. That would be very convenient, but the package does not suffer from not having this.

This is exactly what I was looking for and is exactly what I needed to eliminate my camera’s power issue. I have more than triple the battery power now, I don’t have to plug the camera in to charge the battery and I can even charge it in the car. The fact that the charger and both batteries together cost significantly less than a manufacturer’s replacement battery is just the cherry on top.

NOTE: I am writing this review for the 1TB platter-based Passport drive.

I have a 250GB Passport I bought several years ago and it has served me well, though it has gotten close to full over time (I never imagined at the time that I would fill that thing up). I have had good fortune with it so I expected the same from this 1TB version, and so far I have been right. In addition to the larger capacity, it is very definitely a speed upgrade from my old Passport.

This is a small drive in terms of physical footprint, approximately 4”x3”x0.5” in dimension. That’s a double-edged sword. On one hand, it is small enough to stuff in a shirt pocket which makes it an excellent on-the-go storage solution that’s almost as convenient as a thumb drive. But, that also means it is easy to misplace or lose (or have stolen if left unattended).

It comes with software that allows you to password-protect the drive which is a nice deterrent in the event that the drive is taken. It’s certainly not foolproof, but it’s sufficient to keep the large majority of unauthorized access out. To be honest, since the drive does not leave my home I have not used the software at all.

When you plug in the drive to a Windows or Linux system, the OS immediately recognizes the drive and it is available immediately for use. In the case of Windows, you can immediately explore the drive and read from it and write to it. For Linux, it depends on how you have configured automount and which desktop management software you use, but the kernel does register the presence of the drive and you can display the partition table.

This is a USB 3.0 drive, making it a huge speed upgrade from my older 2.0-based Passport. This is a great solution for storing all of your pictures, movies, important documents, and as in my case large downloads and purchased software packages. With 1TB of space, I don’t think I am going to run out of space anytime soon.

As a bonus, this is a very quiet drive.

I put this drive on a USB power meter to see how much it draws from the USB port. At rest it pulls 0.17A. When actively reading, it peaks just under 0.6A which is surprisingly low. My concern was that this would add some strain on the USB port over a longer period of time but this seems to be an unjustified concern. That said, I am more likely to connect it to a USB hub instead of directly to a USB port.

So far I have no complaints with this drive. It’s a big step up for me from my older Passport, being larger, faster and more quiet. It’s not cost prohibitive either which is just a bonus. If you need a decent backup drive with large capacity and a small footprint, this one is worth consideration.

I have a Dell laptop that has served me well and I also have an older Dell workstation that has been great. I had high hoped for this tower system, and unfortunately it doesn’t quite meet expectations. If you are looking for an affordable gaming system, this one will work on the lower end.

I’ll start with the positives.

It comes with a 7th-generation core i7 processor and it is definitely fast. It is not one of the low power consumption processors, so when you look at the CPU in the device manager you see 8 of them reported - this is a good thing.

Everything is integrated with this system and there are plenty of ports. You don’t need a separate graphics card (though you can add one - more on that in a minute), sound is built in, Bluetooth is built in too and it even has integrated wireless networking.

This is a very attractive system too, and it’s quiet. If you don’t like a noisy system\, this one has you covered.

It comes with 1TB storage. It’s disk-based so it’s slower than an SSD but with that amount of space you have more than enough space for most uses.

And, it’s affordable. It will not break the bank if you already have a monitor and keyboard/mouse combo.

And now for the bad news.

I am not the least bit impressed with the graphics card. With modern games the more graphics memory you have the better, and having only 2GB video RAM is not enough to get it done anymore. My son is an avid gamer and has demonstrated to me that his business-grade laptop gets better frame rates. So, we are shopping for a better and more generous graphics card.

Another area where we will be expanding is the system RAM. The RAM is DDR4 and it’s fast, but the system comes with only 8GB. Our present plan is to double it.

No documentation? I know that the trend is to not include install/recovery media, but come on - there should be more than just a quick start in the box.

This is a decent desktop system that would be find in a business environment, but it falls a little flat when it comes to gaming. It needs a better graphics card (well, at least more video RAM) and it needs more system RAM to be a respectable gaming system.

I have used active noise canceling (ANC) headphones for many years and I have come to expect - and look for - the subtle differences between them. I have worked with ANC phones from Bose, Sennheiser, Monster, Noontec and quite a few more. All of them have their strengths and weaknesses. This is my first experience with Sony ANC phones, and I anticipated good ANC functionality and a solid sound profile. At the price point ($300 as I write this) they need to be excellent to be worth any kind of consideration. These were a huge shock to me: the ANC is nearly on par with Bose and the sound profile is solid, giving better results than I imagined.

I will address the ANC function first, then the sound profile, and afterward I will discuss design and features. I apologize ahead of time for being long-winded, but I’d rather give too much feedback than not enough.

The ANC function is, in a single word, outstanding. Bose is the standard by which I compare others and very, very few headphones get anywhere near the same level of noise cancellation as my Bose sets (QC-15 and QC-20i, by the way). Those that get close usually have the same weird pressure sensation for which Bose is known. My primary test is a loud fan that I use for generating white noise when I want to drown out everything around me at night. I turned the fan on high speed, plugged the Sony’s buds into my ears and turned them on. I put them in ANC mode and the fan all but disappeared. All that remained of the noise was a faint, higher-frequency hiss (distinct from the ANC hiss which I will explain later). Of all the phones I have used, this set and the Bose are the only ones to wipe out that much noise. I also went into the bathroom and turned on the ventilation fan to test, and these phones again wiped out a large majority of the fan noise. For this fan, the Bose sets have a very slight edge but you have to be looking for it to notice.

The main difference between the Bose sets and these is the utter lack of that weird pressure sensation with these. If you don’t like that sensation but you want very high ANC, these are simply excellent. Like a lot of ANC phones, these generate a faint hiss that you really won’t notice unless you’re not feeding any sound at all to them and you’re listening for it.

The sound profile is also quite solid. Usually with ANC phones, because of the cancellation of certain bandwidths the phones compensate by twiddling the sound profile to fill in what was dropped, and usually this means overcompensation in the bass range (if you use Dre Beats, you know exactly what I mean). Heavy bass gives me headaches so I avoid headphones where the bass has been given too much boost. With these, Sony did not overdrive the bass at all but it’s still very solid and full - love it. The midrange is very warm and rich and music has the right depth. The highs are very bright and clear but not piercing. Overall, I am very pleased with the sound profile - not audiophile quality but closer than most.

In terms of design, these are a wireless earbud product with a neck harness. So, these are neither on-ear or over-ear phones. The harness and slack but adjustable wiring to the actual earbuds ensures that they can be set up so they won’t tug or pull when you’re working out, running or otherwise doing physical activity. Being wireless, there’s no cord to tangle up either. And, one size really does fit all which is a problem with some regular phones. The neck assembly has a leatherette padding that is soft and will not chafe.

The Bluetooth functionality works great. I paired these to my phone and they paired and connected in less than 5 seconds which is really all I could ask. After a full power-off, I turned them back on and they immediately connected to my phone again. I have no complaints there.

One of the really interesting features of these is the ability to turn off the ANC and use them without any cancellation, but they have another unusual mode that I have only seen in one other pair of phones - they have an “ambient sound” mode that you can turn on that dampens the feed in the buds and slightly increases the surrounding noise without turning off the ANC. Assuming the volume is not turned up too loud, this allows for carrying on a conversation without turning off the feed. I will say, though, that listening to my own voice coming through in this mode is disconcerting.

I do not know yet how long the battery in these lasts. So far I have not run them all the way down.

Included in the box are the phones themselves, a conversion cable so that they can be used with an audio jack (handy when Bluetooth is not an option), a cable for charging, an in-flight audio adapter, several silicone tips fo the buds so you can get the size right, and a protective carry bag.

The carry bag is the only complaint I have with the whole package - it offers little protection from drops and crushes. If you only are concerned about keeping everything together and keeping the set very clean, the bag is acceptable, but if you need better protection that consider getting a third-party hard case or use the original packaging box.

Sony got these right and even at the price tag these are easy to recommend. They’re comfortable (more comfortable than I expected for ear buds), they have excellent sound and the ANC function is outstanding. I prefer these to my Bose phones and will be using these instead.

Growing up I always had a radio in my room. Times are a little different now and I tend to get my music from the Internet, but there are still times when local radio stations are a better choice - particularly during power outages or when getting local news. I have had very good fortune with Sony electronics and computers in the past so I was eager to try this AM/FM tuner and had high expectations. It did not disappoint me.

Let me very clear about this unit - it is for AM/FM receiving only. It does not play MP3’s, it doesn’t play CDs and it doesn’t stream from the Internet. It’s just an AM/FM tuner. It does this quite well, though - better than most other tuners I have used in the last several years.

Right out of the box, this unit looks nostalgic. It has a classic AM/FM radio look and feel, very similar to a radio my father used to have in his workshop when I was a kid. This is a big plus for me, just for the fact that it takes me back to my childhood.

I plugged it in and turned it on, and I immediately tuned to one of the [relatively] local stations. It picked it up and played it very clearly, better than most other tuners I have used in the last 4-5 years. It is definitely better than the car’s radio. I “surfed” the dial and found other stations that I have listened to in the past but thought were out of range and this little radio did a good job of picking them up and playing with minimal static. That’s really all I could ask. It’s not a miracle radio though and it cannot pick up FM stations hundreds of miles away, but it has better range than most I have used recently.

I like that it can be used on AC power or on batteries. That will be handy during weather events.

I can’t find any real reason to complain about this tuner. It works great and looks great too. It is a little on the pricey side which is par for the course for Sony electronics, but it is a fine tuner that is worth its asking price.

I have worked with a lot of Bluetooth headphones, all of which have their strengths and weaknesses. These headphones by Panasonic are on the less expensive end. The question is whether they are worth the asking price. In my opinion, they could be better and are still priced a little high.

Comfort-wise, I do not care for these but this is a personal preference. I like a headphone that fits tightly and presses down on my head, and these are very light-fitting. They adjust well enough and there should not be too much trouble getting these to fit almost any head, but keep in mind that they’re not the type that clamps down tightly.

The build quality is sub-par. These are very lightweight and feel quite flimsy and fragile.

I found an issue in the sound profile. The bass is good and not too heavy, and that’s good news for me. I dislike strong bass which is good for giving me headaches. The midrange is on target too and the music has some depth. Where the problem lies is in the highs. When listening to music I noticed some distortion in the highs. It’s not in-your-face and it doesn’t ruin the listening experience unless you are really fussy about your music. These will be fine for listening to speech, though.

I had no trouble connecting these to my laptop via Bluetooth. These come up quickly and connect without any issue and are ready to go in seconds. These aren’t the absolute fastest connecting phones I have worked with but they are among the faster ones I have used.

There’s no protective case for these phones in the box, not even a sleeve. These do fold up nice and compactly but I am not sure what is the point without a case in which to store them.

As I write this, the asking price for these phones is $60 which is a bit high in my eyes. If the sound profile was perfect, or if the build quality was higher, I would be more amenable to that price but the truth is that less expensive phones can be found that have a better sound profile and are constructed more solidly - and they have a case.

These are not bad phones, but I think they leave much to be desired. The build quality is mediocre, the sound profile is imperfect and the cost is a little high for what is in the box.

I selected this mouse with the thought that it would be a good travel mouse. I like the feature set, specifically the ability to recharge the mouse instead of replacing the batteries. So far, I have had no issues with this mouse. In the price range, it’s a good one.

The mouse comes in a little mesh bag which sets it up nicely for use as a travel mouse. I can toss the whole in my bag and the USB dongle will stay with it even if it slips off the mouse.

The mouse quickly connects once the dongle is plugged in, and I have not had any trouble with it. It’s responsive and does not skip or stutter.

One of the things about this mouse that stands out to me is actually the shape. Most mice are somewhat arched but do not have enough arch to fit my hand properly. This one is much more arched than most. I still prefer my trackball, but I do not have any issue with using this mouse because the fit in my hand causes less cramping for me.

Charging this mouse is fast and easy. It comes with a USB cable and it charges up quickly when plugged in. I have not drained the mouse all the way down and recharged it so I cannot say for sure yet how long it takes to charge it up from empty.

I had forgotten how nice it is to have a side-scrolling mouse...

This is an inexpensive mouse but that doesn’t mean it’s cheap. It works well and it seems to be well designed. It’s rechargeable which means no spending on batteries, it’s shaped nicely to fit the hand a little better than many and it connects quickly.

I have worked with a lot of headphones, active noise canceling (ANC) phones in particular. ANC phones are interesting in that while they are good at stripping out white noise they frequently do not sound quite right because they twiddle the sound profile, usually in the bass range, to compensate for the sound frequencies they filter out. Also, there are varying levels of ANC, the standard to which others are compared is Bose. This headset by Jabra came as a huge shock to me, both for the very balanced sound profile and the aggressive ANC function.

This headset is on-ear, not over-the-ear. Usually I am a bit wary of on-ear headphones as they tend to be a little uncomfortable. These have very soft, leather-like pads and they are actually quite nice – for a while. After about an our of wear they start to get slightly uncomfortable for me, though taking them and shifting them a little makes them fine again.

The ANC function is VERY aggressive, approaching the same level as Bose but not quite. It is able to wipe out the sounds of the A/C, a fan, engine noise and more. Like Bose, when these are first turned on the ANC gives the wearer a sensation of pressure on the ears. Using this without feeding in noise, it is possible to enjoy relative quiet when traveling, reading, studying or enjoying similar activities.

The sound profile is on point. The bass is present and unmistakable, but it is not pushed forward so much as to dominate the whole profile and drown out the midrange. The midrange is bright and warm, giving music the right depth instead of making it sound like it’s either in a tunnel or in a barrel. The highs are very good – solid but not piercing. Jabra has nailed the sound profile where a lot of others have screwed up.

This is also a headset for talking, and call clarity when using with a mobile phone is very good. I have had excellent results using this headset and it has worked extremely well for me. There is a caveat, though – because this headset covers both ears, it is not suitable for use while driving in many jurisdictions. It’s great when in the office, but know your local and state laws if you plan to use it in a motor vehicle.

There are two ways to use this headset and connect it. It has built-in Bluetooth and it pairs and connects very quickly with my phone. It also has a USB dongle for connecting to a PC, though it can be connected to the PC via Bluetooth too. My observation there is that volume levels are reduced when connecting to a PC via Bluetooth.

The headset comes in a crush-resistant case and includes the USB dongle and a USB cable for charging.

I can find little about which to complain with this headset. It does get slightly uncomfortable for extended wear, but it has great ANC and a very balanced sound profile. As a headset it works great for talking, too, and the Bluetooth pairing is fast. This has already become my favorite set of headphones for streaming music, though because of laws where I live I cannot use it as a hands-free set while driving.

A NAS is a great way to add storage for the whole network where everything can be reached from any system connected. It is not as simple as a USB mass storage device like a thumb drive, of course, but it addresses a completely different issue. So far, this drive has proven to be a good one, though its reliability remains to be demonstrated over the long haul.

I have the 8TB drive, and it is great for dumping huge numbers of videos, music, documents and other media needed across a small network. It is fairly fast too, so streaming video from the NAS to any given device on the network is reasonably smooth as long as the network can handle the bandwidth (keep this detail in mind if you are wanting to stream video over a slower wireless network - the lag isn’t necessarily the drive’s fault). The drive is very quiet, though not silent, and so far seems to stay acceptably cool.

I did learn that it does not work all that well in a USB drive enclosure right out of the packaging. I have an enclosure that is capable of handling drives up to 8TB so I decided to try an experiment with the drive when it first arrived. I put it in the enclosure and connected it to my Windows 10 laptop. The system saw the device, and it even saw the drive and recognized the model and serial number, but it was unable to access the drive or even format it. I had more success with my Linux system which recognized the drive and was able to access the partition table and display drive parameters. I did not repartition the drive or create a file system for my experiment though I believe it would have worked.

Time will tell if this drive will be reliable over the long haul. Based on my experience so far, it has worked out well and I have had no issues. It’s the largest drive I have worked with and can handle a LOT of data. If you need wide open spaces for your network storage solution (or you are willing to fiddle with it to get it working as a USB solution) this is a good choice.

My parents used to have a Polaroid camera and it was everything that we remember those old cameras for – it spat out a white square of plastic that slowly developed into a grainy, faded-looking picture within a few minutes, it was bulky and it had a very distinct sound. It was a great old camera but when Polaroid quit making film for it it became a paperweight. It's nice to see that some of these old cameras are available with film again. That said, there are some oversights with this package.

I will start with the two negatives (no pun intended). First, the way the camera was packaged for shipment was sub-par and the package was partially crushed when I received it. It did not appear to be damaged beyond the packaging, but it was a disappointment to open the package and find the merchandise box partially crushed. Second, the camera comes with no film or batteries at all. So, the camera by itself is still a paperweight. It would have been nice to have at least a lower capacity pack for film to get started.

The camera came out of the box without a mark on it. It looks to be brand new, in spite of being an older unit. Some of the other reviewers have complained that the camera they received either was scratched up or was partially damaged, but mine is pristine. It's a simple, straightforward device too, and it does not require much thought to use.

In use, it works just like it would have when new. It fires the flash, spits out one exposure with that same distinctive sound I remember and the film develops in front of you. The exposure still looks grainy and old when it is all done, but it is a real photograph that does not need a separate printer or software to get a hard copy. This is not the kind of camera a photographer would use, but rather it is for the tourist or enthusiast.

Why would you want a camera like this? For me, it is a trip down memory lane to a time years ago, when candid pictures were a part of daily life and the exposures were lined up on the pinboard for all to see without needing a computer or tablet. It is not going to make pictures that look like they could be in a magazine, but it will produce pictures you can enjoy right away.

I have a small stand similar to this one that I use for my phone when I am at the office. It allows me to see who's calling when the phone lights off and it gives me a very consistent place to keep my phone where it is out of the way and in a safe place – no more misplacing my phone. The idea is good, and the design is good, but I have one issue with this stand that keeps it from being ideal.

This is a small, aluminum S-shaped stand with a plastic kickstand, designed to hold a tablet, phone or e-reader upright so that you can see the screen without holding it. The kickstand is adjustable with the push of a button and it has almost 360 degrees of movement (though it does not really need much beyond 100 degrees to be useful). It has rubber grommets to make the surface anti-slip and to keep it in place. So far, so good.

In the tray of the stand is a rubber insert that serves two purposes. First, it also provides slip resistance so that your device does not move easily. Second, it prevents damage to your device's screen which is important – metal on glass is usually a bad idea when the idea is to keep away scratches. I have used another stand like this that does not have the rubber insert and the first time I put in my phone the metal lip caught the screen protector and cracked it.

Be aware that there is not enough clearance between the tray bottom and the surface on which the stand is set up to allow plugging in the device without either cocking it at a weird angle or turning it on its side (or upside down). This is typical with this type of stand and I cannot count this as a flaw.

The one issue with this stand is that the rubber tray insert is not permanently attached and it is not secured in the tray at all. When the stand arrived the insert had separated completely and was loose in the box. It does slip back in without issue, but it won't necessarily stay there when you move the stand in transport. Without glue or some other method of modifying the stand there is no way to secure the insert more securely, and this is an unfortunate design flaw. It's not a deal breaker, and it does stay put when the stand is set up so the stand is very usable, but care is required to ensure the insert does not fall out when moving the stand.

Other than the tray insert not being securely fastened to the stand, the is a fine little stand and it works well. It's small, easy to pack and move and it provides a stable and easy way to set up even a larger tablet so that it is upright without having to hold it it place. It will see regular use in my house.

I have worked with a lot of Bluetooth speakers and I have seen a good variety in features and sound quality. I have a set of Monster headphones and they are excellent; I expected the same from this speaker. It’s a good speaker, but it has a weakness in the sound profile.

It pairs and connects quickly and without any issue. I was able to connect it to my computer without any problems and it was ready to go in less than 20 seconds. In terms of connection speed via Bluetooth, this one is slightly faster than most.

I really like the fact that the speaker has a slider switch for power instead of a button you have to hold down. It makes knowing the speaker is on very simple and it also makes it very simple to power off. This is a big plus to me and is one of the best features in my mind.

I tested the sound quality fairly extensively and make a few important observations, most of which were positive but there was one important issue. The speaker has good volume (controlled by the source) and excellent operational range - I went as far as 30’ and there were no cut-outs or crackles, a good sign. The sound profile though is slightly problematic. The bass is strong - very strong - and is enough to dominate the whole sound output. Many speakers and headsets are heavy-handed on the bass, so this is not totally unexpected but is a bit heavy for my tastes. The highs are good and everything is clear and crisp. The midrange is very flat to the point of being practically non-existent, likely because the bass is as high as it is. Because the midrange is so flat, the output has a tendency to be dull and lifeless.

This is not a bad speaker and it is a decent choice if you want a small and strong speaker. But, be aware that the sound profile is unbalanced.

I listen to a lot of music, usually electronic music though I listen to a little of everything. I have worked with a lot of different speakers and I have gotten very sensitive to the strengths and weaknesses that speakers bring to the table. I had high hopes for this speaker – I have always had excellent results with Yahama products so I expected the same from this speaker. It has not disappointed me.

The speaker itself is about the size of a cantaloupe – not huge but not tiny either. It's the right size for a bookshelf or as part of a larger sound system.

I did not completely understand what was meant by “MusicCast” until I started working with this speaker. In short, it is a wireless speaker that communicates over a wireless network (not Bluetooth). Using an appropriate device (like an Android tablet) the speaker is easily connected to the network and the software on said computing device allows for turning the speaker on and off and for streaming music to it. My service of choice is Pandora, and I had no trouble at all streaming a channel from Pandora to this speaker. The software comes into its own when you have more than one speaker, all of which get controlled separately and can stream different music from the same source device. So, given a sufficient budget (these speakers are not cheap), you can have different music playing in different rooms, all controlled from the same device.

The application is not perfect though I have been able to do everything I want with it – play music from local storage, stream from a service, increase/decrease volume and twiddle the sound profile a bit.

The sound quality is excellent, particularly when given a little volume. The bass is solid but not overwhelming which is great – the trend of late is to overdrive the bass which drowns out the rest of the sound profile, so having the bass not overpowering the overall profile is a big plus with me. The midrange is excellent as well and the music has the right depth as a result. The highs are bright and crisp. At lower volumes, the bass washes out which is has been the case with every speaker I have used. At higher volumes, I was unable to get the speaker to distort.

I am very happy with this speaker. I primarily use with with my tablet to stream music from Pandora, though it is useful for playing music from other sources too. It is expensive, but the sound quality is definitely there. If you like the idea of being able to add multiple speakers to your sound array and you want to design your sound system from the ground up, this is a good choice.

A long time ago I had access to a Polaroid Instamatic camera. It was great - snap a picture, it spits out a sheet. Wait about 2 minutes and what you have is a printed photograph. Polaroid is gone now (though the name gets licensed over and over again), and with it went all of the film for the camera that made it so useful. This new camera by Fuji brings back some of the fun of instant photos, though it is by no means perfect and it suffers from some of the same issues the older Polaroid camera had.

The idea is very straightforward - point-and-shoot, and the camera ejects an exposure that will develop over a few moments and will be fully developed in approximately 2 minutes. This is great for social events and is a fun way to share candid shots. The camera is very lightweight and it is small too so it is easy to pack and carry with you.

There are a few issues with the camera, though, some of which are very much like the old Polaroids of days gone by. The images do come out a bit grainy and are definitely not high resolution. If you are looking for images with nice, clean edge detail and bright, vibrant colors, this is going to disappoint you. Also, the images are really small, a little bigger than a passport picture but not by very much. And finally, the film is relatively expensive, a pack of exposures coming with only 10 slides and costing about $0.60 per exposure.

On the plus side, the camera is very easy to use and the camera body itself is not very expensive at all.

There are trade-offs with this camera. On one hand, it is super convenient, it’s fun and it’s relatively inexpensive. However, exposure quality is mediocre, pictures are small and on a per-picture basis the exposures are somewhat expensive. To me, the fun factor weighs heavily in favor of this camera and offsets some of the negatives. For social gatherings and recreational events, this is a fun camera and will serve well. Do not expect to have high-end results, though.

I have worked with several tripods and I have concluded that there are really two distinct classes of camera tripods: there are heavy durable tripods that are designed to be stationary most of the time and take some abuse, and there are those that are much more lightweight and are designed with mobility in mind. There is some that are somewhere in between but to be honest I have seen few of these types. This particular tripod falls under the more lightweight category and is a decent one, though there is one feature about it that gives me some pause.

This is a very lightweight tripod and it comes in a nice nylon case, making the whole thing well suited for travel. The whole weighs under 5 lbs. which is great when you have to pack it for moving or need to toss it in the car. No complaints there.

It’s easy to work too. The legs work via locking latches and extend in three segments, and I am able to so this with one hand (though it is much easier when using two hands). When the legs are fully extended and the head is raised to the maximum height, the whole stands about 5’ tall which is good for a majority of uses. If you need a taller tripod, please keep this in mind.

The head is very smooth and it gives full motion to the camera. It is comparable to most tripod heads I have used in that it allows motion in three directions so that the camera can be oriented in just about any desired direction (though not inverted of course). Motion is smooth and does not require a lot effort, though it is tight enough to prevent the camera from moving when it should not. The head can be “locked” in place via tightening knobs to keep it firmly in place.

My one complaint with this tripod is the feet. These are hard plastic feet that can be adjusted to balance the tripod slightly, but each has a hole in the bottom which exposes the end of a leg – a sharp point that is all metal.
