This is a double-edges sword. On one hand, the feet can allow the tripod to easily move and slide on hard floors if adjusted properly which might be the goal. On some hardwood flooring, though, they gauge the floor and leave permanent marks. I have hardwood flooring in my house and I am extremely careful with this tripod, but this is the only one I have used that poses this problem.

I like this tripod, especially for travel and mobility. It is very lightweight and easy to adjust, and of course it is quite affordable. If you have hardwood floors, watch the feet; otherwise, this is a decent tripod that is worth consideration if you need one that travels well.

If you own an iPhone, iPad or one of the newer iPods you are familiar with the need for lightning cables. These are basically special USB cables that are reversible and are specific to Apple electronics. The problem with these cables is that they can be expensive, especially if you go with Apple-branded cables. There are some good third-party cables available, and they represent a good value when compared to Apple cables. I get offered a LOT of lightning cables for review and I have noticed an unpleasant trend: most vendors hawking their cables to not mention MFI certification at all, anywhere, and this is important. This particular cable is clearly marked in the description as certified, so it is worth some consideration on that basis alone when compared to many of the others available.

These come in a two-pack, and they are a little more than 3’ in length. These have hard plastic plugs on the end and the length is insulated with a vinyl sheath for protection. So far these have shown no signs of fatigue at the plugs and they work very well. I have been able to charge my phone as well as connect it to iTunes. I attempted to pull the shielding away from the plug and was unable to do so, so I see no risk of exposing the wires inside the casing.

I mentioned the certification above, and I will restate that this is a very important feature. Because these cables are certified, they are guaranteed compatible and will work. If you use a cable that is not certified you might get messages on your phone or tablet that the cable is unrecognized and it might not work as desired. I have worked with non-certified cables and sometimes they work while others do not work at all. I have never had a certified cable fail me.

If you are looking for a less expensive alternative to Apple-branded cables, make sure you select a product that has been certified to work. This two pack of cables is a good choice; so far, they have given me no trouble at all and they have worked well for me. They are definitely compatible and are made well too. And, getting two of them instead of just one in the package means you can have one in the office and one at home.

I have been looking for the right phone holder for the car after the one I had been using for a good while finally broke on me. The one I had was great; it had a strong suction cup and a large-opening clip that held my phone securely and could also be used as a holder for my TomTom. Since it broke I have been looking for a suitable replacement and I had the opportunity to work with this car mount. Rather, this is a set of car mounts. So far it has performed well for me and it has kept my phone secure while I am driving.

There are three separate mounts in this package. The one I use most is the short dashboard mount. I have it mounted on a weighted movable base that I can slide to either end of the dash while I am driving. It holds fairly well and it has not come loose while I am driving. I did discover that the suction cup released after several hours though, which is a problem I have seen with other mounts when using this same base. The second one is a windshield mount with a flexible mounting arm. This is the most flexible and versatile of the mounts, though I am not a fan of this type of mount as the phone tends to jiggle and bounce when the car is in motion. The third one is an air vent mount and I do not use this one as my air vents do not cooperate with it, though it seems to be ok with most vent systems.

The mounting brackets are spring-loaded sliders and they provide a good bit of tension when holding the phone in place. The brackets seem to be tight enough to survive the “shake test” for most typical situations though the phone can be shaken loose if you shake the mount hard enough (though this becomes an unrealistic test). It requires two hands to open the brackets which is a good sign that they will hold.

The brackets attach to the different mounts via ball joints which give solid flexibility and allow for angling the phone properly. One of the problems I had with another mount was that the ball got chewed up by the bracket assembly so I look for this when I see these types of mounts, and so far the brackets have mounted properly and have proven to be well designed.

Most car mounts are of a single type. This is a set, though, so you get not just one type of mount but three that you can use simultaneously, for the price of a single mount. These are made well and they work well, so at the price point this is really hard to beat.

I have worked with other Rii keyboards and every one of them has worked out well for me. The ones I have used prior to this one have been well suited for portability and are smaller than a standard-sized keyboard. This one is a little bit different – it is still small and it has a nice footprint, but it includes an integrated touch pad. It is also rechargeable, which is not new but it is different in how it works. I am using it to type this review on my Linux laptop.

First things first – it is compatible with Windows as well as Linux and Android. I will assume it is compatible with OSX but I have no way to confirm this as I am not a Mac user.

This is a wireless keyboard that comes with a USB dongle as well as a direct USB connection that allows it to charge when it needs it. I had hoped that the USB wire would allow for not only charging but for use as a wired keyboard, but this is not the case – the wire is just for charging and nothing more. A Circular Polarizer Lens (CPL) filter is a useful tool for the photographer that generally is used to reduce light during long exposure times. The idea is that it can be used to take a longer exposure of something in motion without washing out, and in the case of moving water it can make the water seem almost misty and magical. I have a CPL lens for my dedicated camera, but this one goes with the Bitplay SNAP! series of cases. In this context it is a great lens for deepening colors and reducing glare.

This lens is small, designed to attach to the SNAP! case threads. If you do not have the case, this lens is very unlikely to work for you.

It works by having two glass lenses, one that is fixed in place and one that rotates. As the lens is rotated, the light coming through the pair fades due to the polarization. It is easily tested by looking through this lens at a flat-screen monitor like a laptop screen.

One of the issues with a CPL filter is that often there is an uneven fade; this lens does not seem to suffer from this problem as much as with other CPL filters I have used and I have gotten consistently even shots with minimal bright spots.

While I haven't yet messed with my phone enough to know how to increase the shutter speed, I still have been able to take shots with reduced glare. Much like polarized sunglasses, this lens is suitable for dealing with glare and reflections, and it works well.

I am pleased with this CPL filter. It works well with my phone and it is does exactly what it is supposed to do. If you have a SNAP! case for your iPhone 6 and you are looking to “up your game” when it comes to taking pictures with your phone, this is a lens that will serve you well once you learn to use it and get the hang of how it works.

As a child one of my favorite things to do was to look at things under a microscope. I vividly remember gathering a water sample from a swamp near the house and looking at a sample and finding my first paramecium. It has been years since I have owned a microscope, but with this microscope I can see how things have advanced and changed. This one does not have the same magnification as that microscope I had as a child but it is a lot easier to use and I can still see things with it that I cannot see even with a good magnifying glass.

This unit looks more like a drill press than a microscope, in terms of the design. The scope itself fits on a metal shaft and two turning knobs make it easy to raise and lower the scope in relation to the base. The base has two clips for holding down your slides or paper or whatever else you want to look at through the scope. There is no eye-piece on the scope – the image is viewed on a computer screen instead and the connection is made via USB.

Included with the scope is a software CD and this must be installed to use the scope. Installation is quick and painless. I installed under Windows 10 64-bit and had no issues. After installation I launched the software immediately.

The software consists of a view/capture application and a supplemental application for saving your work. The main part of the view & capture app is a live window that shows what is visible through the scope. As the object or slide on the scope base is moved, the image updates in real time. I found it a little awkward to line things up just right at first but I finally did manage to get things in the viewer just as I wanted them.

I started with a gray piece of paper that I thought was solid gray, but I found that the gray is actually a micro dot pattern like magazine print. More interesting was the corner of a $5 bill showing not just the print pattern detail but the fine fibers in the paper. A penny, cat hair and a very close-up view of a microfiber cleaning cloth all proved to be interesting subjects. Attached to this review are some of those detailed images, my favorite being the penny. I have not yet gone to the culvert near the house to gather water samples.

The software allows for two different capture types – photo or video. I have only played with the photo capture so far but it it very straightforward – click the photo button, either on the application interface or on the USB cable where the light level can be adjusted and the image appears in a list on the right side of the application window. If you double click the image you can save the image to the hard drive, zoom in on it and do a few other operations.

Linked to a tablet instead of a computer, this is a great travel scope to take with you. It is well-suited for classroom use as well as for use in the office.

I like this microscope. It is very easy to use, it does a good job of magnification and images are nice and clear. It is very different than the microscope I used growing up, in ways that I like. It's so much easier viewing on a screen than looking through a viewer, making this more fun to use too.

I have worked with several K&F Concept lenses and filters in the past and I have had excellent results with them. I am still very much a beginning photographer and I am still learning as I go but I have learned a lot in the process. One of the things I have especially come to appreciate is the fisheye effect. Up to this point I have only had the ability to work this out via software, so I was pleased to have the opportunity to work with this fisheye lens. So far I have had a lot of fun with it and I love how it works, though I have again learned a few things along the way.

A fisheye lens is somewhat similar to a magnifying glass with a great deal of distortion. The center comes out clear and the edges are distorted and warped, giving the effect of looking through a lens that is very thick in the middle and thins out towards the edges. Straight edge objects like sidewalks become warped and bent.

This particular lens is a chunky and hefty fellow, actually comprised of two lenses instead of just one. There is a large macro lens that can work independently of the fisheye lens and it is very good for taking very close-up shots. The fisheye lens attaches to this macro lens and relies on it.

I took several shots with the fisheye lens and I discovered something I did not realize though it is fairly obvious now. When using the minimum amount of zoom, the distortion is maximized and you get the most effect. The more you zoom in the more dampened the effect though it is still noticeable. I used the lens to take two pictures of the case in which the fisheye lens packs, one zoomed in all the way and one zoomed out all the way. For the one zoomed out, you can see the warping effect on the blinds over the windows and you even can see the entire image framed in a black circle. The image zoomed in has minimal distortion.

I should state that this particular lens is designed for 58mm threads. Make sure your camera can use it before you buy it. If you have a different thread size for your lens, buy the right sized fisheye for that lens.

This is one of the most fun lenses I have. It works great and it does a good job of giving the distortion you want with a fisheye lens, and it is not particularly expensive. I am very pleased with it and am looking forward to working with it for many years.

[[VIDEOID:9c7f474d82697dfd8035b3c7cf95ccc5]] I am a longtime graphics tablet user, having started with a Bamboo small. Since then I have had several tablets including a Bamboo Fun Pen & Touch, am Intuos4 and finally an Intuos5 Medium. All of the tablets I have used have been Wacom tablets; this is my first experience with another brand, and it is the first time I have even heard of Huion as a brand. To me it makes sense to compare this tablet with my Intuos5, with which it actually compares quite well for about 20% of the cost.

My test system for testing this graphics tablet is a Dell laptop, with an Intel i7 processor and 16G RAM, running Windows 10 and Corel Painter X3.

Comparing this tablet to the Intuos5 it is approximately the same size (both are medium tablets). They both look very similar at a glance and there are some distinct similarities in the pen and pen holder as well. In operation they are both similar but there are some very distinct differences, and each one has advantages over the other.

One of the differences between these two tablets is that the Huion tablet has a numbered gauge across the top of the writing surface and includes a replacement surface in the box; the Wacom does not. The gauge is not a big deal but it does make a nice measure if you are looking for consistency in length of lines. The replacement surface is another matter – it is easy to damage the surface and over time it does get scuffed, so being able to apply a new surface is a huge plus to me.

The pens are different and there is give and take with them. The Wacom pen is sealed and does not need batteries or recharging. It is also reversible and both ends can be configured for drawing. Typically one end it set up as an eraser. The Huion pen is rechargeable and is not reversible. I prefer the Wacom pen, but I like the feel of the Huion pen and it works well.

The pens both come with a stand, extra nibs and a nib extractor. The Wacom stand is slightly heavier, but otherwise they are functionally equivalent.

The software is obviously different, and I have been experimenting with the Huion software to learn how to configure the buttons. The Wacom software is a little more intuitive, btu I have found the Huion software to be a bit more versatile and it provides better control. Speaking of buttons, the buttons are a little different between these two tablets with the Wacom providing fewer buttons but providing a scroll wheel.

Both tablets have 2048 pressure levels, and the only real way to test the pressure levels and drawing capabilities of each is to use a drawing application and start experimenting. I loaded up Painter and selected some acrylic brushes and started playing. I was able to get very similar results using the same brushes and the application had no issues with recognizing the pen or the position on the writing surface.

Operationally, these two tablets are very similar. However, the Wacom is more expensive – a lot more expensive. The Huion tablet costs roughly 20% of the cost of the Wacom and to be honest when I compare these two it is hard to justify the cost of the Wacom when the Huion tablet works as well for so much less.

Working with the Huion graphics tablet has been an eye-opening experience. It compared beautifully against a Wacon tablet of similar size and capability. I am very pleased with this tablet and can heartily recommend it as an excellent alternative to more well-known brands.

The primary lens I have on my camera is a good 18mm-55mm lens and it does great for capturing images that are a foot or more away. When I get much closer than that my camera is unable to focus properly and I end up with a crummy shot and I either have to give up or back up so that it can focus – not what I want most of the time. These magnifying lenses are a good solution, but there are somethings you have to keep in mind when using them.

I will start with a statement that should be obvious: make sure you have the correct lens size when you are purchasing add-on lenses like this set. This particular set can be used only with a lens where the thread size is 55mm. If you have a lens that has a different sized thread, you should consider looking for this kit in a different thread size. You can use a ring adapter, but getting the right size at the start is better.

There are four lenses in this kit, a 1x, 2x, 4x and 10x lens, each increasing in power as the numbers suggest. You can somewhat view these as magnifying glasses for your camera, but that metaphor is not completely accurate. They do magnify the image for you, but they allow a closer shot as well and you can get very close to your subject when you have one of these attached to your lens. Perhaps a better way to describe them is to realize that they make your camera very nearsighted and your camera can see close-up well and distance not at all when using these lenses.

The main thing to remember about them is that as they go up the scale in strength they introduce a lot more edge distortion. This is most obvious with the 10x lens. If you take this lens and hold it so that you can see things through it clearly in the center, you cannot help but notice a large area around the edge of the lens that is distorted. The effect is less then you get it close to something on which you wish to focus but it is something to keep in mind. If there is too much distortion, use a less powerful magnification lens.

These particular lenses have a little bit of heft to them but they are not what I would consider heavy. Because they are glass they are a bit more substantial than resin or plastic lenses.

Overall, these are nice lenses. I have been able to use them for taking very close shots that I otherwise would not be able to take with my camera, such as ridge detail on a penny or dot patterns on magazine print. These are not real-world examples but they definitely show off the capabilities of such lenses. If you are looking for good magnification lenses for your camera, this is a good set that works well. Just make sure you have the right thread size before you buy.

Using an HDMI cable I was able to use my laptop to project my desktop and subsequently my videos. Done correctly, this projector is a fine second screen and makes an excellent presentation screen for PowerPoint (this requires setting up the desktop to extend the display on the second detected monitor - this projector - and then tell Powerpoint to use the second display for playing the slide show). It works very well and I am pleased with it.

There are two manual controls on the side of this projector. One controls the focus and the other slightly adjusts the tilt of the image on the surface where it is being projected. The focus is unable to get a clear image if you set the projector less than 6'-10' from the projection surface - not too bad of a distance.

On thing you have to remember, though - this unit puts out heat and lots of it, though less than larger projectors. It can quickly warm up a 10'x10' room so consider ventilation when using this or any other small projection device. I was a little surprised too that when the projector is shut off the fan stops instead of running a little longer to cool down the light - not a big deal but noticeable.

I like this projector. It travels well, it has a lot of options for inputs, the controls are intuitive and the picture is bright enough for smaller audiences.

I listen to music all day at work and I also enjoy listening to music at home and as such I spend a lot of time with headphones on my head. This is one of the more unusual headsets I have used, more in terms of their appearance than for their features or quality. These are decent headphones with some very interesting features though the sound profile is a little off, particularly in the highs.

I received the blue and yellow headset and these definitely look like headphones for kids. They almost look like toys, though in use they have revealed themselves to be a bit better than toys. The main features they offer are Bluetooth connectivity, FM tuning, direct audio connection via 3.5mm cable and hands-free connectivity.

When I received these, they were completely dead and needed to be charged up. It took me a little time to realize they were not broken, but once I plugged them in to charge the problem became very clear. I was then able to work with them. So, if you receive these and cannot get them to work, try plugging them in first.

I was able to pair these to my computer and they connected without trouble. The headphones identify themselves as “KB-2600”. When I had them connected to my computer they worked fine and they did not stutter or skip which is all you really can ask for. I did not try testing the range.

I discovered, quite by accident, that this headset has a full-blown FM tuner and it can scan for channels and make channel presets. It actually works surprisingly well and I found myself listening to a station coming from 50 miles north and it was surprisingly clear. Most headsets I have used to not have an FM tuner so finding these to have a tuner was a pleasant surprise.

I loaded up some music and listened very closely to the sound, and unfortunately I found an issue with the sound profile. The bass is good; it is about right, not overdriven and not soft. The midrange is slightly strong but still quite good. The problem is in the highs which sound muddled and flat. When listening to vocals the sound is not particularly sharp, instead sounding far away. It is fixable with an equalizer, but with small music player or phone an equalizer may not be available.

Comfort-wise, these are actually more comfortable than their looks would suggest. I personally like a headphone that clamps a little tighter on my ears but these are better than some of the other sets I have used. The pads on each phone is a mildly firm leatherette material that is comfortable and does not heat up as much as one might expect. The headband itself has a very soft pad on it that provides a very nice cushion between itself and the head.

These are very interesting headphones and they have some cool features. Except for having a deficiency in the high range, these work well and they are quite comfortable. If you get a two-color unit it is a very good choice for younger listeners.

I have come to understand the value of a good camera strap. It is more than just a designer item and more than just a simple strap to keep the camera hanging around your neck. It needs to be strong enough to keep the camera secure and it needs to be long enough to allow for grabbing the camera and taking a quick shot instead of having to struggle with getting the camera from around your neck and risk missing the shot by a second or two. The strap that came with my camera is functional but much too short and I expect it to rip eventually. This strap by Orota is a much better strap than that provided with my camera.

This is a well-made strap. One side is a heavy weave not unlike a car’s seat belt but not as smooth and shiny. It is also quite a bit thicker than a seat belt and will have no issue with supporting the camera. Sewn to it is a decorative layer that is also a heavy weave, similar to but not exactly like canvas. These are stitched together with heavy thread and I see little risk of them separating.

Each end is clamped with a leather reinforcement that is held in place with four metal rivets. The leather ends each hold a metal buckle with the thinner nylon straps that actually connect to the camera. Looking closely at each component I found no loose threads, no uneven seams, no flaws in fabric or materials. There is nothing about this strap that suggests it will fail under daily use.

This is a much longer strap than what came with my camera, measuring a little less than 3' long. I like the fact that with this trap attached to my camera I can lift my camera and quickly get the shot I want and I don’t have to take it from my neck in order to focus on it. I can hold it far enough from my face to actually focus on the camera. This is a very big improvement over my old strap which was short enough that I could not get the camera in front of my face at a comfortable distance.

This is a very well-made strap and I am very pleased with it. It is stylish, well constructed and it is long enough to make it much more useful to me than my old strap.

An IP camera is an inexpensive and straightforward way to add a little extra security to your property, whether it is watching a door, monitoring a hallway or even just keeping an eye on the dog while you’re at work for the day. This is one such camera by Foscam, and it seems to work fairly well in my testing. There are a couple of minor issues I have seen, though nothing that I would consider a showstopper.

This is a small and lightweight camera, about the side of a baseball, and it is hinged such that it can be angled in a range of about 300 degrees of coverage if it is placed properly though in practical use (meaning, when it is placed on a wall and anchored to it) it is likely to be positioned more like 70-90 degrees. It also rotates on the base, so it can be configured to point to just about any target from where it is anchored.

The base itself is detachable and the whole camera can be popped off the base with no tools. To me this represents a concern. It means that someone can simply take the camera from the mounting place if it is low enough, using no tools. I like being able to rotate the camera on the base but I also like knowing the camera is not going to get taken easily.

Setup of this camera is very easy and I was able to get it connected to my network without too much effort. That said, I struggled a little bit with the Foscam software and it took me a little while to get the software talking to the camera. I have had this trouble with another Foscam camera, and the problem seems to be the software - very specifically the IP Camera Search Tool utility - and not the hardware or the network. I was able to find the camera in the monitoring client.

Once the camera is connected and available it can be logged into directly. There, the user has some control over a multitude of settings including firmware updates, login credentials and more. I like the interface even though it is somewhat basic as it is easy to navigate and is completely accessible from a web browser.

The monitoring client software allows for more control, which includes concentrating on a single camera if there are more than one connected, scheduling, playback and more. In addition to the software that runs on a computer, users can connect to it via smartphone if they have an iPhone or an Android. Windows phone users are unfortunately out of luck.

The camera resolution is very good and is detailed with fairly accurate colors. This certainly is not the same as a camcorder, of course, but it is sufficient to recognize faces even at a fair distance. The night vision (infrared) is excellent and is sufficient that I was able to read a sheet of instructions that was held in front of the camera.

I do not like the LEDs on the camera, though... It is very hard to place the camera inconspicuously and have it remain unseen in the dark when it lights up with a ring of LED lights. This is the one major issue I have with this camera that I think needs improvement. It’s not a complete deal-breaker, but consider the possibilities when an intruder sees the camera and knows he or she is being recorded. These can be turned off in the settings and I highly encourage doing so.

The camera has a micro SD slot near the hinge where storage can be inserted. It is unfortunate that there are no cards in the box though this is a minor gripe. I used an 8GB card for testing and the camera was able to record to it without trouble and I was able to control this from the monitoring client.

This is a decent little IR-capable security camera. So far I am pleased with it, though there are some minor quirks. It’s a relatively inexpensive camera and is an easy way to monitor areas of your house and record what is going on when you can’t be there.

I have always been intrigued by discrete video cameras and I really like the concept of having the camera embedded in a pair of sunglasses. I was interested in giving these glasses a try and so far they have been great. They video quality is better than I expected.

At a glance these appear to be basic sunglasses with really wide arms. They are not especially stylish but they do not look bad either. The surprising part for me was that they fit very well and completely cover my eyes and form a wind barrier for me. Most sunglasses I have tried leave some gap around my eyes so that I do get a little wind when wearing them - no so with these.

These serve as a Bluetooth receiver and they seem to work well in that regard. When set to pair they identify themselves as “MS2 Bluetooth” and when I paired them to my Windows phone they paired and connected without issue, both for audio and voice. The product description says these work with Android and iOS phones but do not mention Windows phone. So, for the record: they work with Windows phones.

The sound quality for music is not great but it’s not bad, either. The highs are great and are very detailed. The midrange is somewhat flat and as a result the music sounds a little hollow but not unacceptable. The bass is weak. Now, all of this said, these are not designed to be a constant-wear set of headphones so the emphasis was not poured into the sound quality. If you listen a lot to music and plan to use these all the time for that, these just won’t do the job. But, for the day on the ski slopes or occasional use outdoors they are just fine.

The main feature of this set of sunglasses is of course the embedded video camera. The quality is actually better than I expected and it produces a decent video, though certainly not as nice as a hand-held dedicated camera with anti-shake. The sound is not bad either, though if you are moving or are outside when it is windy you will pick up some wind noise, but it is not terrible most of the time (all bets are off if you choose to wear these on a rollercoaster or on a speed boat). Color is bright and vivid, and the detail is there.

These come with 8GB of storage. Installed in one arm of these glasses is a Class 6 8GB card. According to the product description these can support cards up to 32 GB, but I have not attempted to put a different card in there at this time.

These come in a hard, crush-resistant case and are in a small microfiber bag in the case. The case is lined in a velvety material that will prevent scratches if you scrap the bag. Also included are the detachable ear buds and silicone inserts of different sizes so they can be fitted better.

The sunglasses themselves are polarized and are UV-coated so they provide very good eye protection when in the sun. These are a great choice if you are a fisherman and you want to capture highlights from a day on the lake - the UV coating protects your eyes and the polarization cuts down reflections on the water. These will also serve well if you are looking to spend a day at an amusement park, but be aware that there is no anti-shake so if you want to use these on a rollercoaster expect a very jumpy video.

I like these sunglasses. They do a good job of protecting my eyes and they fit very well, they record video very nicely and they have acceptable sound quality. Overall, I am happy with them.

I have worked with and used a large number of headphones and headsets. There are some significant differences between various models and brands which include comfort, sound quality and noise isolation (or active noise cancellation for some of the more expensive headsets). I was eager to see how well these Panasonic earbuds would work out, especially since the last Panasonic headset I had was a dud. These have proven to be much, much better than my last Panasonic headset and are better in a lot of ways to most of the other earbuds I have tried. They are not perfect, but they come close.

Right up front I will state that these are strictly earbuds, not a hands-free headset. If you are looking for a headset for talking, this isn’t it.

Style-wise these are very attractive earbuds, with a dark gray housing and red trim. The cabling is round wire with thick insulation. The round wire is more prone to tangling than the flat ribbon-style cables that have become more popular, but for me I prefer the round wire.

When it comes to comfort these are more comfortable than many I have tried. They fit my ears reasonably well and I have not had problems with them jabbing me or slipping out. I can pull them out by the wire which is good from my perspective as it means if I catch them on something they will pop out of my ear instead of pulling. I have been able to wear these for a couple of hours without any discomfort which is a good thing.

The most important aspect of any set of headphones or earbuds is the sound, and this one gets it really close to perfect. The highs are very clear and bright and I am very happy with how well vocals sound when listening. The midrange is balanced nicely and the music has some depth as a result without sounding hollow or like it is coming from a tunnel. The bass is strong - very strong - and while it is a touch heavier than I like, Panasonic did a good job of not wiping out the whole sound profile with just the bass. If you like earbuds that boost the bass, this pair does it right.

These also have very good noise isolation, or passive noise cancellation. I have worn these for a couple of weeks while at my desk with an air purifier running less than two feet from me and they do a good job of blotting out the sound of that purifier. I do have active noise cancelling headphones too and those do a better job of killing the sound from that air purifier but at a much higher cost and for the difference in sound reduction it’s not an appreciable difference to justify the cost.

Included in the package is a carry pouch and more silicone ear inserts.

I am very pleased with this set of earbuds. They are a bit pricier than the typical set of earbuds I have seen and used of late but they do a great job of blocking ambient sound and they sound great. I am not a huge fan of the bass boost but I seem to be in the minority, and to Panasonic’s credit these buds boost the bass correctly - meaning, the rest of the sound profile is very solid. If you want a set of really good-sounding earbuds with a bass boost, this set is among the better ones I have used.

I have been shooting a Canon 50D DSLR for several years, mostly outside or with stage lighting. Occasionally, I also have been using a small camera-mounted flash, but it is weak and very limited. To improve my flash photography, I decided to try the Mago Speedlight by Pixel. This is an excellent, mid-priced flash with loads of features.

The Mago Speedlight comes with a nice soft case and a fold-out manual which guides you through the setup of the flash and includes screenshots of the back LCD. It also includes a small stand which is great for use in slave mode, and a clip-on flash defuser. The flash uses 4 AA batteries or an external power supply (not provided). It is even upgradable via a USB port hidden in the battery compartment (not tested).

The controls are easy to use after some experimenting. The manual really helps as there are so many features. The buttons are solid and the display is easy to read, with an optional green backlight.

The flash head can be tilted up and down, or rotated left or right. It also includes a built-in defuser and a white card reflector. These are very useful if you are not bouncing the flash off of a ceiling or reflector.

One interesting feature is an LED model light that can be turned on/off easily via a dedicated button. This light is quite bright and very useful for setting up your shots.

I tested the flash on a Canon 50D with 20mm and 50mm lenses and somewhat cooperative subjects (my kids). After learning the controls, I took several excellent pictures.

The flash supports E-TTL mode, manual mode, and multi-flash mode. I tested all three.

To test the multi-flash mode, I set the flash to 5 bursts at 500 HZ and took a picture of fan blades, resulting in a very interesting effect.

As a final test, I put the flash in slave move (S1) and put my old flash on the camera. This flash worked great as a slave flash and I took some interesting pictures using both flashes. I also used S1 mode to slave the this flash to the camera's on-board flash. Note, I did not test the wireless flash mode (a smart slave mode) as I do not have another flash that supports that feature.

I work with a lot of headphones, headsets and earbuds. I am very partial to one very special set of headphones that I own, a pair of Monster Inspiration phones that includes active noise cancelling (ANC) and this is the pair of headphones against which I compare all others. Although I have worked with many sets of very excellent headphones it takes a lot for me to really rave about a specific set. To be that awesome, the headphones have to be very, very comfortable, have brilliant sound, be made well and have at least good passive noise cancelling if not ANC. These phones by Geega are nothing short of outstanding and actually complete very well with my Monster phones.

These are some of the more comfortable phones I have used. They are completely over the ear phones and cover my entire ears so there is no pinch. The earphones themselves are padded with a soft leatherette that is almost buttery soft and the headband is covered in the same material. These are very easy to adjust to get the fit just right. I can wear them for long periods of time and they do not pinch or get uncomfortable though they do get warm after about an hour. Because they are over-the-ear they provide some measure of passive noise cancelling.

The sound profile is excellent. The bass is at about the right level - not weak and not too forward so the bass response is very good. When the bass drops, you know it but not because it causes a headache. The midrange is very rich and full and the music has amazing depth, better than many others I have used. The highs are absolutely brilliant, bright and crisp. I would stop short of calling these audiophile headphones, but the sound profile is every bit as good as a pair of $350 Sennheiser headphones I own - better, actually, and it makes me sad to know I spent that much on those phones when I could have spent a lot less for these. I intend to connect these to a Bluetooth transmitter and connect them to a professional sound mixing board to see how detailed the sound is - I will update this review when I have done so.

I have these paired to my tablet from which I stream Pandora to them. They paired and connected without issue on all of the devices I have tried - my laptop, my phone and finally my tablet. They identify themselves as “GEEGA S204” and on all three devices I tried to connect I had no issues at all maintaining the connection.

These phones come in a nice, hard protective case that provides good protection from crush damage. There is a mesh pocket inside for keeping the included USB cable for charging and the AUX cable for alternate input.

The range on these phones is 20' - 30' which is very much in line with most phones I have used. Interestingly, they did not stutter and cut out, they just completely cut off when I passed that threshold. I am not sure if this is just a function of my environment or if they really are that sensitive at the threshold.

Overall, these are simply outstanding. I have not found any other set of Bluetooth headphones with the same level of comfort or sound quality. These are the best wireless phones, of any type, that I have ever used. These are my new reference point for wireless/Bluetooth headphones and are the standard by which I will judge any others. I will still use the Monster phones, for the ANC function and for comparison against other wired phones, but these phones by Geega will be used for listening in my home office where I enjoy listening to music most.

I have always liked the video footage taken by bikers as they barrel down a mountain trail or through a wooded area on their bikes (or the crazy base jumpers wanting to capture the drop). It gives a really good sense of what the rider was seeing when riding and you catch every bump in the road, every acceleration and deceleration. I have never used on of these little cameras before now so I was very excited to have a chance to evaluate one of these cameras. So far I am very happy with it and it works well, though I have learned that those with big hands and fingers will struggle a little bit with it.

This is not just a camera, it is a complete kit with the camera, a waterproof housing, cables, mounting brackets, double-sided adhesive pads - everything you need to use this little camera in just about any outdoor activity you might want to capture. I will write mostly about the camera but will touch on a couple of the accessories as well.

Except for cameras designed to be hidden and concealed this is the smallest and lightest camera I have ever seen or used. This is of course required for a device like this that is intended to be used on the go. It very easily can be slipped in a pocket or a bag or purse. It comes packaged in the hard plastic frame that is the waterproof case but even this case is small enough to fit in a purse or smaller bag.

I will say this - read the included manual! The manual is not perfect but it is better than what comes with most electronics and it gives a very good rundown on how to use this little camera. I had no clue at all what to do with this camera until I looked through the manual. I suspected it was touch-screen and I was right. Even though the screen is touch screen and easy to navigate the interface is only semi-intuitive. It is also complicated by the fact that there is an anti-scratch cover on the screen for shipping and if you do not peel this off the screen is a lot less responsive. This is where I had the most trouble - trying to work around the plastic sheet over the screen when I didn’t really even notice it before.

This camera has a lot of the same capabilities of a good phone camera. You can take still pictures, video and also play back that which you have recorded. The camera can snap stills up to 12MP resolution and the video recording can go all the way up to 1080P. These equate to very good image quality when used properly. There are a million little settings for these modes too, from white balance, ISO, anti-shake, motion detection and a lot more. Many of these will be familiar to anyone who uses their digital camera for anything more than just casual shots.

In testing my images and videos came out ok. I am still learning how to balance all of the settings on my big camera so I am no expert, but what I was able to produce was acceptable, particularly the video. I did manage to get the date set correctly and displayed in the corner of the video, I got the lighting right and color straight. I spent too much time playing with the zoom and I learned I am very adept at shooting videos of my hands.

This is a rechargeable device and a standard micro USB cable is provided for charging.

I ran into one issue with the camera and it related to the fact that I have huge hands and the camera is so small. I found that the only way I personally can work the touch screen is to use a stylus. Using my fingers I am unable to pinpoint the spot on the screen I want to touch and I got very frustrated trying to get certain things done on the screen. If you have really big hands, consider using a stylus on the screen.

There is no storage included in the package. The camera takes a microSD card so you will need one to save any pictures or recordings.

The waterproof case is a perfect fit for this camera and it seals wonderfully. It snaps closed without effort and it keeps the water out. It is supposedly good for submersion up to 30m (according to the description). I have not had an opportunity to test this.

There are a number of mounting solutions in the kit, including mounting screws for attaching to a selfie stick, bicycle frame/handlebars and helmets. In the case of the bike mount, it holds very tightly and a good series of bumps is not enough to rattle it loose.

Having never had a sport camera like this I have no basis of comparison but so far I am happy with this little camera. It is very compact and lightweight and it does a great job of taking pictures and video (though it is obviously not a full replacement for a dedicated point-and-shoot or a dedicated video camera). It’s inexpensive too (a LOT less expensive than GoPro) so I think it’s a great option for someone wanting to capture their adventures.

Heat is the main killer of computers and computer equipment so keeping a system cool and ventilated is a big deal, especially when involving systems that see heavy use. Laptops are just as vulnerable as larger servers and require the same precautions. One of the main solutions for heat dissipation and ventilation for laptops is a chill pad (a fan-based platform that moves air under the system) and this one by AMNIE has been outstanding. I have been using it for about two weeks on my personal system and likely will swap it over to the system in the house that sees the heaviest use.

This is a good-sized pad, able to comfortably handle laptops up to 17”. It has a total of 4 larger fans that move some serious amounts of air, and fans are paired two and two between a pair of switches. The frame is painted metal mesh and offers good support to the laptop it holds.

The switches that control the fans are dial controls and they provide variable fan speeds for each pair of fans they control. There are no graduations so you can set the speed anywhere within the range to suit you, though having that much control is probably not all that necessary. The fans run very quiet but on the highest speed setting really move the air. When maxed out and all four fans running at top speed the fans blew cooler air from between the frame and the laptop, telling me I had the speed up much higher than needed. For my particular system under my typical use load, it seems I only need to turn them on about half way.

I have worked with some chill pads that have flaws in either the fans or the bearings and they make awful amounts of noise. So far, the only noise this pad makes is a low-frequency hum. It is quiet enough that even with lower-end noise canceling headphones I can cancel out the noise completely. This pad is not silent even on the low end of fan speed but it is very quiet all the way through the range of speeds. I have been able to leave the fans on full speed all night and sleep through the sound.

I have not measured the temperature difference between when the fans are on vs. when they are not, but I have noticed that the internal fan does not kick in as frequently when doing video rendering as when the fans are off. It does turn on and it still hits high speed on occasion but it is noticeably less frequently.

Sometimes it is necessary to take a picture of something on a solid background, often white for contrast but also sometimes black for lighter-colored objects. Most of the USB cables I have are either 3' cables or are really short ones that come with electronic devices. One of those things is that a cable can be too long in some cases, though this is a failure in organization, not in the cable.

These are shielded in woven nylon which is great; the nylon is stronger than soft plastic shielding and gives the cable a little more stiffness but does not make the cable so stiff that it’s awkward to run. I tried one of these with my phone and it worked just fine, I was able to charge the phone and move data between it and my laptop. I did not attempt a speed test.

There is a big difference between 3' cables, 6' cables and 10' cables. If you need a 6' cable, a 10' cable will leave you trying to figure out what to do with the extra 4' of cable. In my case this meant having to use a twist tie to bunch the cable up in the middle. This is not a criticism but rather a suggestion - get a cable that’s the right length for the job. If you need a 10' cable, these have worked great for me.

These are nice USB cables. They seem to be made well and they work as expected. If you need a really long cable, this is a good choice.

I have been learning more about photography and as time has permitted I have been improving my skill as an amateur photographer. I have worked with other types of filters, in particular CPL and FL-D filters, but before now I have never worked with ND filters. I have been able to achieve good results with it and so far I am pleased with this filter though I know I have more to learn about it.

A neutral-density filter is used to reduce light reaching the aperture without fiddling too much with the colors. This allows one to get creative with shutter speeds. This particular filter is adjustable and turns on the lens body face, allowing the photographer to increase or decrease the amount of filtering done. At the lowest setting the filter does very little filtering; when turned up to the maximum filtering level very little light gets through and a moire pattern appears so I do not recommend turning up the filter to this level.

To get a feel for how well this filter works I took my camera outside as a big thunderstorm approached and took some pictures of one of the cloud formations. I selected two pictures from that set, one where I did not use the filter and one where I did use it on about 1/4 strength. Although the filter evenly reduced light levels, the color contrast in the filtered image is much more pronounced and obvious.

The most common use for this kind of filter is to reduce the light levels, then take an extended exposure for a scene with motion, such as a waterfall.

This is a very nice filter and I could not be happier with it. It is very easy to use and it really works well.

Right out of the box, these are striking phones that are quite attractive. When it comes to the build quality, the strongest feature of these phones is the cord - I am exceptionally partial to woven tangle-free cords versus plastic coated wire.

The difficulty I had with these phones initially was the sound profile. The bass is exceptionally heavy, so heavy that it drowns out the highs quite a bit and the result is a sound that is muddy and unclear. FOSCAM is a well-known name when it comes to security cameras and security equipment and they make a good variety of security solutions for home and business use. The F19803P camera is a wireless IP camera that is weatherproof, has night vision and can be accessed via smartphone. One configured and set up on the network it works great but the setup process can be a very painful one.

In the box is the actual camera, the antenna, power adapter, mounting kit, installation software and an Ethernet cable. The camera housing is roughly the size of a new roll of bathroom tissue - very small, compact and lightweight. The mounting kit is a small but solid painted aluminum bracket plus the screws needed to secure it. When mounted properly, this camera can be very inconspicuous.

Following the included directions, I installed the software first and then hooked up the camera to the router. According to the included documentation the IPCamera application should immediately see the camera and from there one can select the camera, log into it and manipulate it as needed. This did not work for me and the camera never did appear. I tried downing my firewall, I tried connecting to a different router and even tried directly connecting to the camera and still was unable to see it. I finally managed to reach the camera by opening the FOSCAM client software and telling it to search for cameras. When I did this, the camera finally appeared, and the IPCamera application showed it too. This works but runs contrary to the documentation.

I did get into the camera finally and was able to change the username and password. I also set up the wireless network settings and found other settings to adjust like IR timer, time source and more.

I found that the camera’s administration settings can be accessed as needed through the IP address and specifying port 88 (unless the port is deliberately changed). I strongly encourage assigning a fixed IP address to the camera via DHCP through the router; otherwise, the IP address can change and accessing the camera gets more difficult. I learned this the hard way, when I had the Ethernet MAC defined but not the WiFi MAC in my router’s DHCP table. My fault, but this was made more difficult by the IPCamera application still not seeing the camera and I had to let the client software scan again.

I made one more mistake and reset the camera via the reset button and it cleared everything I had set already: user name, password, everything. I was concerned that I would lose everything again with a power failure so as a test I unplugged the camera for a few hours and plugged it in again, and fortunately it retained its configuration.

The camera cannot see my 5G network, only my 2.4G network. However, even though my computer is on the 5G network it still can access the camera. Both networks are handled by my one router so I assume that this is normal. If you have a 5G network, make sure you also have the 2.4G network configured or keep the camera connected via Ethernet. The fact that it does not support 5G networks is not necessarily a problem but is worth knowing beforehand.

Once I made it through the configuration (which was all of two hours, most of it trying to figure out how to talk to the camera), the client software allowed me to add it to the configuration and stream a live video feed from it. The video quality is actually very good and when not in IR mode is in full color. When streaming IR video the image is straight black and white, but the image is very clear. Testing with the camera indoors I killed all the lights in the room and the IR kicked in, my intent being to see how clear the image is. The image is clear enough to read text off a white sheet of paper when angled right. Specifically I held up the instruction manual to the camera at about a 2' distance and was able to read the front page without difficulty. The only complaint I have with the IR is that it does not seem to kick in early enough; when in a dimly lit room the camera still tries to use non-IR and the result is a very dark feed. I have found no way to adjust this in the camera settings other than to set the IR to cut on at a specific time which may or may not be the most useful thing.

I like the fact that this camera does not need a specialized hub to work and can be run from a PC or MAC instead. This makes the system a lot more flexible and easier to manage.

The real power of this camera comes in the client software. It allows for adding additional cameras (the screen settings suggest up to 64 cameras) and monitoring all of them at once on one screen. Some of the camera settings can be manipulated such as setting up recording times, setting alarms and more. Adding a camera is as simple as running a search and then adding the camera to an area. There is even the ability to play back the video that has been recorded built right in.

This is a nice security camera and it works well. It has very good IR capability, it works wirelessly and has full-color video that is clear and workable. Configuring this camera can be very unpleasant, though once configured it’s a great solution. If you need a good outdoor wireless camera and you have some patience for an install that’s not necessarily smooth, consider this one.

Fishing is one of the activities I have loved ever since I was very young and able to hold a fishing rod. Though I have used several types of fishing reels my personal preference is spinning reels. There are a number of reputable brands available and I have tried several - Lew’s, Quantum, Daiwa, Mitchell’s, Shakespeare and more. I received a Triton 3000 spinning reel for test and evaluation and have been thoroughly pleased with it.

This reel has some heft to it, very solid and tight. It’s more substantial than many reels I have used but it’s also not the largest or heaviest either. In terms of size and weight, it falls in the middle of the pack of reels I have used for freshwater fishing and it’s a bit on the small size compared to many saltwater reels I have used. I have larger hands and the size it about right, but someone with smaller hands might find a smaller size (like the Triton 2000 or 2500) a better match. In terms of assembly, there is nothing loose or flimsy on this reel at all and there is nothing that required tightening or adjustment right out of the box (which has been a problem with some others I have used in the past). Overall, this is a solid and well-assembled reel.

Appearance-wise, this reel is absolutely gorgeous. It is a deep shade of purple, almost black, with chrome and nickel colors on the spool, bail and handle. Appearance is not really all that important but it certainly does add to the package, and this is a reel that you won’t be embarrassed to break out in front of others. It relies on simple elegance, not bright flashy colors to make its statement.

This reel has a good-sized spindle on it and it can hold a good amount of line. I put at least 150 yards of 8-lb test on this reel and there’s a lot of room for more. The spindle is tall, not deep.

Ok, on to the really important stuff - how does this reel perform?

This reel has 10 ball-bearings for forward reeling and the reel is about as smooth and quiet when retrieving as could be. Cheaper reels (cheaper meaning lower quality) tend to grind a little bit when retrieving or they make substantial amounts of noise, and some reels even have a clicker in them to mask the sound when retrieving. Some also feel hollow when retrieving, but the Triton feels solid and smooth without a hint of inferior build quality. As nice as the reeling forward is, one of the most important features in a good reel to me is a zero-reverse clutch and this reel has it down. When engaged, the reel will not reverse even a little and to me this is worth its weight in gold.

One very real issue I have seen with some spinning reels is a poorly shaped bail that interferes with the distance when casting. If the bail is too shallow and does not allow enough clearance to allow the line to fly freely off the spindle, it can seriously impact casting distance. Fortunately, this reel has a very wide bail that has plenty of clearance around the spindle and it does not impact the cast at all. I get very good distance when casting as a result. Instead of concentrating on distance, the angler can instead concentrate on accuracy (and after years of practice I am still working on improving my accuracy).

I tested the drag and am pleased with it as well. When tightening the drag the dial does not get more difficult to turn like on some other reels and the drag gradually makes the spindle harder and harder to turn. It is not a graduated turn, meaning it does not increase in steps so there is essentially a limitless variance in how tight the drag can be adjusted. The dial remains easy to turn all the way through the turning range until it is tightened completely, at which point it just stops.

When reeling, either forward or backward, this reel remains balanced and does not wobble much at all. It is hard to notice wobble when the reel is attached to a rod so I tried something when I had not yet attached the reel to a rod. Holding the reel in one hand by the assembly and giving the handle a good spin, I was able to feel the reel gyrating very slightly but not appreciably. I tried the same with another high-quality reel and it was similar. This is not the case with cheaper reels which may or may not balance.

I love the fact that the reel is mounted on an arm long enough to prevent the bail from whacking me on the knuckles when I retrieve. A reel mounted too close to the rod due to a short arm can have this unpleasant effect and I look for this problem specifically so I can avoid it. I also appreciate that the handle is far enough from the reel body to avoid hitting my hand.

In the box with the reel is a velvety microfiber cloth bag for storage and transport when the reel is not in use. This is the only reel I have ever had that has come with such and it’s a nice touch. The bag is useful for keeping the reel clean and also for keeping supplies with it, like a small container of lubricating oil, an extra spool of line or even an extra lure or two (though this is no substitute for a tackle box).

I am very hard-pressed to find anything to criticize about this reel. It is a solid and well-made, looks great and works like a dream. I believe I have found my new primary reel.

I have a 10" tablet and it primarily gets used as an e-reader and as a music streaming device. I have tried suction mounts to attach it to a window and that works fine but the window cannot move and when the window is cold the suction mount lets go. This flexible mount for tablets is a very good solution for my needs and is far better constructed than suggested by the product description.

This is a simple mount in concept and design. It is flexible coil tube with a screw-on vice clamp attached on one end and an adjustable frame-style bracket attached via a ball joint to the other. In the box the unit comes unassembled and requires less than two minutes to put together. When finished, the whole thing is approximately 3' long.

Everything about this mounting stand suggests that it is built to last and is designed to hold up under heavy use. The item description here says it will support 2.2 pounds but it will support a little more than that (though I would not try to put much extra on there, particularly if the coil is horizontal).

The coil attaches to the vice clamp via a threaded machine screw assembly and it has enough threading to allow the coil to turn 360 degrees without becoming detached. This allows the tablet to be swung around a work area in an arch without having to really do anything that requires any effort. While this is great, what really caught my attention is that the clamp itself can be screwed to the coil in two ways at 90-degree angles (top or side) so that the clamp can be attached to an anchored surface that is either horizontal or vertical. This is one of those design decisions that just makes sense but I have seen very few manufacturers make this kind of effort.

The coil is covered by a very heavy plastic sleeve which protects the tube and makes flexing the tube easier on the hands.

The mounting bracket is connected to the top of the flexible tube by a ball joint, similar to the kind of joints many GPS navigators use in cars to attach to the suction base. When I first attached the bracket to the coil I put it on upside down, which is not a big deal except that the weight of the tablet worked against the joint and it tilted downward slightly. The bracket itself is a standard slider with a lever that presses against the slider which then catches on teeth on the frame to lock it in place. I wanted to see if these headphones could compete with a set of phones that cost more than 10x more. I was amazed that these phones do compete, and quite nicely, for a fraction of the cost. The Monster phones do have a richer midrange and come with ANC, but the sound difference between them is marginal when considering the price difference.

These are certainly not perfect headphones but for the cost they are nothing short of excellent. You can find better headphones out there but expect to pay more. These are a great deal.

One of the issues with some tower cases is the placement of USB ports. Some of the newer cases have USB ports on the front but often these are USB 2.0. Even when there are 3.0 ports on the front of the case it seems there need to be one or two more. AVANTEK's 5.25" drive bay USB add-on hub adds three USB ports as well as a 2.4A charging port.

The hub has two internal plugs. One is for power and one is for the USB bus. Be sure that your case and motherboard can support USB 3.0 and has the proper plugs.

Once installed, the three ports are immediately available to the operating system and they work like the other USB ports on the system. The USB speeds are best realized with something like a USB 3.0 storage device like an external hard drive, though USB 1.1 devices like mice and keyboards work just fine on this hub too.

What makes this hub interesting is actually the 2.4A charging port. This is very convenient for charging a cell phone, a tablet or similar device. My chosen device for testing chargers is a Magellan Roadmate GPS navigator, which is an ornery device that will not charge when powered on unless using the car charger that came with it. I selected a high-speed USB cable and plugged in my navigator and it charged up quickly when powered off. However, the navigator slowly drained faster than it charged when powered on. This was expected though it was worth a shot.

I am especially encouraged at how solid this device is - the ports are securely soldered to the PC board and the board itself is mounted on several posts to the frame which makes it much less likely to flex and ultimately break. I applied some direct pressure to the PC board (not a realistic scenario in use but a good test before installation) and the board really did not flex much at all.

I can't find any real issues with this hub. It's a solidly built device, it mounts easily and once connected provides 3 USB ports and a charging port on the front of a computer tower case. It is reasonably priced too which makes it a very good buy.

Drive carriers and enclosures are a convenient method for converting internally mounted drives to USB connectivity. This particular enclosure is for 2.5" SATA drives and supports USB 3.0 speeds. So far I have gotten excellent results with it and am pleased with it.

This is a tool-free device; no screwdriver or wrench is required to open this enclosure or install a drive in it. The cover slides off with a little pressure to expose the plug for the drive and the drive simply pops in. In the box is a foam pad that attached to drives that are not thick enough for a solid fit when the cover is replaced. Once assembled with a drive, this is a solid and compact enclosure that feels a lot like a Passport drive though it looks a lot nicer and feels a little more substantial.

I plugged the drive into a machine running Windows 8 and the system immediately recognized the drive and the partitions on it. I was able to use the drive without issue.

I tried a couple of different configurations for accessing this drive under Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL). First, I tried to access it under RHEL running in a virtual machine. I was unable to get the hypervisor to expose the drive to the OS which is a configuration issue, not a compatibility issue. To determine this for sure, I plugged the drive into a machine that runs RHEL natively with the GNOME desktop. RHEL immediately recognized the drive and opened a Nautilus window with the filesystems on each partition exposed and I was able to navigate the filesystems without any issues. I could not ask for better results.

I put a 500GB SDD in this enclosure and plugged it into a USB 3.0 port and got insane speeds. I could not be happier.

This is a great drive enclosure for 2.5" drives and it works great under Windows as well as under Linux. For the price, this is a great enclosure that works very well.

I purchased these replacement pads for my Bose QC-15 headphones as the old pads were torn and needed to be replaced. I selected this set of pads based on the positive reviews here on Amazon with the thought that they would be the same as the original pads. While they look the same, they are indeed slightly different.

First things first - these pads are fairly easy to install though they do require a little persistence to get them to snap into place. The earphones themselves have small tabs around the edges designed to snap the pads' bases into place and hold securely, and if the pads are not snapped down they simply will not stay securely. The inner foam and cloth shield that covers the electronics is easy to install but I had trouble with the double-sided tape that holds them in place - the adhesive did not want to release the cover strip and I had real difficulty peeling that strip away without ripping the actual cloth.

Once in place, the phones look exactly like they did when they were new, but I found three differences. First, the phones no longer fit into the case as easily as they once did. Instead of just turning the cups to lay flat and simply putting them in the case, now I have to mess with them slightly to fit into the case properly, though they can be made to fit. More noticeable, though, is that the pads are not as effective as the originals for passive noise canceling. A fan that I have in my office used to be canceled out almost completely with the combination of passive and active noise canceling but is now more audible than when the original pads were in place. I would not say the difference is enough to render the earphones' ability to cancel noise completely compromised, but they are definitely not the same. Finally, these replacement pads are just a little less supple and soft than the original pads. It is not all that noticeable until comparing the original and replacement pads side by side. You have to really be looking closely for the difference to notice it, but it's there.

The difference in noise canceling ability is most noticeable when working in an environment with reverb. I use my phones to monitor sound coming through a professional sound board because these have always done an excellent job of eliminating reverb and leaving just what comes through the sound board. With these new pads in place, I can now hear a lot of reverb, even when I press the phones tight over my ears and have ensured that they completely cover my ears so it's not a gapping issue. The material is different, plain and simple.

These are not bad replacement pads by any means. They are very good, they are comfortable and they do make these phones look brand new again. That said, they were not manufactured by Bose and there are some differences. When considering the cost difference between these and Bose parts, the trade-offs balance out favorably. If you have to have an exact match with the original pads, these are very close but not 100% identical. If you are satisfied with a [roughly] 90%-95% match, these pads work nicely for a lot less than original manufacturer pads.

The point-and-shoot camera market has taken a nosedive due to the prevalence of camera phones that produce high-quality images. It is difficult to buy a mobile phone that does not include a camera, and since mobile phones have become so commonplace and essential anymore there's little need for the point-and-shoot camera for most users. However, what phone cameras lack is the ability to make optical adjustments like zoom and winde-angle - all of these adjustments are done via the phone's ability to digitally enhance the image it takes. The BTOOP lens kits change that and add capability to your camera phone.

The concept with this kit is simple and is very similar to add-on lens kits for more expensive cameras. A lens is attached to the camera lens that enhances the zoom, creates a fisheye effect or adds wide angle capability. The lenses attach by a clip that attaches to the camera with a hole over the lens and a thread where the extra lenses attach. It works better than I would have expected and the image quality does not suffer from this arrangement.

This lens kit comes with three lenses. My favorite of the three is the fisheye lens which works surprisingly well and makes great distortion effects. It is particularly effective for emphasizing the center subject in the image. The wide angle lens also works well and creates photos that have more area covered in them. This lens is ideal for landscapes and skylines. The third lens is the most amazing of all, the macro lens. Using the macro lens I focused on a penny and was astounded by the ridge detail I could see. I took the lens off the phone and put the phone back on the penny and the phone never could focus on the penny that close. The macro lens is absolutely wonderful for very close-up shots.

The kit comes with a small pouch for carrying the lenses and clip, and the pouch doubles as a microfiber cleaning cloth. It's washable too so it can be run through the wash when it becomes soiled.

This kit also works well with built-in tablet and laptop cameras. Taking video with the fisheye lens in place on my laptop is a fun use of an afternoon...

This is a very nice kit for easily and very affordably extending the capabilities of your phone's camera. It's very simple to use and it adds optical effects that cannot be achieved to the same degree with a phone's software enhancements. It's works well and I am happy to recommend it.

I did a good deal of research to find the right camera. I wanted a solid camera with a generous feature set but I didn't want to spend a huge sum either - my budget was roughly $500. At Christmastime the NX300 went on sale, enough of a sale to put it in my price range. After doing a little more research to make sure I had found the camera I wanted, I committed. So far I have been very pleased with it.

Every digital camera I have used before this one has been a point-and-shoot camera, the best of which was actually another Samsung. These types of cameras are great for casual use like a day at the amusement park or making memories on a day trip, but for making really exceptional photographs these cameras are usually ill-suited. Either the focus is flat (meaning everything is one-dimensional), the zoom isn't granular enough, the color is wrong or something else is off just enough to make the picture not quite perfect.

The Samsung NX300 is a "prosumer" camera, meaning it's a high-end consumer and low-end professional camera. Unlike point-and-shoot cameras it has an interchangeable lens system and can be manually focused. It has a good number of features I have not seen on less capable cameras too, such as Wifi connectivity, the ability to add color filters to the lens and much more. I'll hit the highlights.

Without the lens in place, this camera is about the same size and weight as a point-and-shoot camera, maybe slightly larger but not appreciably heavier. Adding the lens adds some bulk and heft to it but it's not as large as something like a Canon Rebel or a high end Nikon. To me this makes this camera a lot easier to carry around than some other models with which it competes, and that can be important when traveling. That said, if not used to working with a camera that has interchangeable lenses there's more to carry (particularly if you use more than just a single lens). A good camera case is a good investment.

This camera has several modes of operation, each optimized for specific shot types and accessible through the spin dial on the top of the camera. The one I use most when experimenting is Auto, which does most of the adjustment for the user and tries to calculate the best settings given the lighting and conditions. It's a good, general purpose mode for most situations. Smart mode is a good choice too, which has presets for a good number of predefined situations like optimized face shots, panorama views, night shots, light traces, silhouettes and several more. Of those smart settings, "Beauty Face" makes adjustments to portraits to compensate for imperfections and this is a great feature. There is a mode for giving the lens the highest priority when it comes to adjustment and that's the mode that gives the user the maximum control over zoom and focus. Manual mode gives the user good control over what to focus on automatically but the camera maintains most of the control. Shutter priority mode allows the user to adjust the shutter speed which is great for when a faster shutter is needed (like an action shot). Aperture priority mode adjusts the aperture width and thus the amount of light allowed in. Program mode seems to be roughly equivalent to Auto mode; I am still learning about that one.

The menu system on this camera is accessible through a nice touch-screen interface, providing access to all manner of settings. I will not go into great detail on the menu system as to do so would make this more of a novel instead of a review. I will say this, though - it is very easy to accidentally make changes when using the menu system if handling the camera in any but the most careful of ways. Just picking up the camera when it is turned on must be done with care as it is almost too easy to touch the screen and make changes without intending to do so. It's fantastic that the screen is sensitive and can be so easily manipulated but it's so sensitive that care is required.

One of the greatest things about this camera is that it can take pictures that have a 3-dimensional quality to them. The main subject of the picture in the foreground is clearly in focus and the surroundings at different depths are in varying levels of being out of focus, and this gives the photo a depth that usually is very difficult to achieve with a point-and-shoot camera. I spent an afternoon playing with the camera just experimenting with this and was thrilled at how natural and easy this camera makes it to take this kind of picture.

Built into the camera is the ability to connect to a Wifi network for uploading images to a smartphone or to share online. This is a nice-to-have but it is not a feature I personally need.

The lens system on this camera is what makes it shine. I bought the 18mm-55mm OIS lens with the camera and this is my first exposure to smart lenses.
