Also, I cannot get the screw to tighten all the way; there's always a bit of looseness at the end, and I'm afraid it will defeat the purpose of having such a rugged lanyard when the screw will come undone and the plugs pop out.

Great to have on a backpack, though. I just have it strapped to my backpack with the thicker lanyard.

The headphones themselves are comfortable and easily adjustable, the range is nice, and the sound quality is great, but the controls themselves are frustrating. The pairing says that you hold until the light flashes blue then red, and I did this. But what happened to me is I held it and it flashed blue once then it would flash red repeatedly. The manual said nothing about repeated red flashing so I assumed it was in pairing mode and I was confused as to why it wouldn't appear on my phone. After a while, I realized that if I held the pairing button longer after it started flashing red then it would flash blue and red alternately and then I could pair. I still have no clue what the red flashing means. Also, the way the skip/volume is set up is weird and temperamental. You hold the button to change the volume and press once to skip or go to the previous song (depending on which volume buttons you press), but sometimes after letting go from holding the volume button the song will change anyway. I think it would be more efficient to switch to press to change volume and hold to change song to prevent accidental switches. I have yet to try a phone call but if the volume/song switch buttons weren't so annoying this would be a great product.

Amazingly sturdy cable. Monoprice rarely ever disappoints for the price, and that still is true in this case. Works great, too; most of the HDMI cables are similar. It all depends on the cabling with how they perform, in my experience.

This one is definitely going to be the longest you'll need for a home living room setup. Monoprice, for the price, always delivers.
This one is super thick, so if you prefer something with more manageable angles then I'd suggest Mediabridge.

Since we mounted our TV we like to use as few chords as possible. This way they are neatly tucked along the wall and down into the entertainment center where all our entertainment equipment is housed. So the main HDMI cable runs down but of course we have more components that require a cable than the one connected to the TV. Our solution? A signal splitter. Thankfully, we have only three output connections so this one seemed perfect. Plus, it touts 4k signal, even though most pre-4k HDMI boxes should be fine, but it's nice to have that in the title just in case.

What I use this mostly for is the cable box and a couple of video game systems. As for the cable box, seems to work fine; no dropped signals that I've noticed, nor any degradation in quality. As for game consoles, I have the PS3 and the Wii U hooked up to it. SAme: no noticeable quality degradation nor input lag.
Now, to put it to the real test, I hooked up some retro consoles that have been modded to output native HDMI; that means they'll be HDMI with no lag. Considering I have this and two HDMI cables connecting the console to the TV, I was curious to see if there truly was any lag.
With older games, timing is everything, especially on the 8-bit consoles with platformers and fighters, like the NES. From what I could tell, there was absolutely no lag, not to mention signal loss. The buttons responded as though I were using a normal NES on a CRT.

So yeah, I'm pretty satisfied. It's a bit light and doesn't have heavy pads on the bottom to prevent it from sliding around. With so many cables, and the ability to use the remote control, it should be a bit more stable on the surface.
I haven't used the remote as the detections are instant. No need to manually switch the inputs, at least from my experience. Also, I didn't need to use the power adapter; the power from the HDMI cables seemed to be sufficient, and the detection was not complicated by the lack of adapter. Weird.

Got this to mount a 42" Samsung TV onto our bedroom wall. It is very basic and doesn't require too much knowledge if you've mounted TVs before, but mine didn't come with instructions. I looked online and there are no available instructions, so I had to figure it out from similar mounts and reviews online. The only biggest problem I had was with the screws; I didn't know what width I needed to drill a pilot hole as many PDFs online had different numbers, but I found the right size and drilled away.
Unfortunately, the drill I have wasn't strong enough to drill these all way, but I was able to use a socket wrench to finish putting them in by hand.

The mount is decent, but, again, instructions would've been helpful. For instance, I couldn't tell if the spring-loaded bolts at the bottom of the mount, once the TV is hoisted up, were to be tightened after positioning the TV or left alone. I tried tightening them only to realize they were to be left alone. About five minutes wasted.
I tilting the mount more but really you get about a half-inch's worth of movement.

Otherwise, fine. Fantastic for the price, and more of a fixed mount if you need it.

I run during the summer and run outside. I hate carrying heavy items with me, like water bottles and phones. I feel they sort of hinder my performance, though I realize it's probably more psychological than physical.
Still, I'm not going to mess with a run I've been accustomed to for nearly twenty years, but I do wish, more often than not, that I had some way of tracking my run and how many miles I've done *exactly* while being outside. Sure, I can track the mileage by checking my phone before and after, but it would be nice to have a tracker on me without adding any psychological weight. I used to have a Polar watch that worked fine, but it died some time ago and I never bothered to get a replacement.
But finally I did.

With this one, I'm able to wear the watch without toting my phone along and it still carries all the features and tracking as if the phone were connected to any other tracking watch. While this watch is used for a number of cardio activities, I use it only for running. There are "pages" of exercises you can track, but for a quick run the default is set on the bottom left button--very nice to have, especially for me. Not sure if you can change the default on there to another exercise, but for me it's perfect and I haven't bothered looking up how to change it.
But curious to check out the full features, I ventured into the different pages (or screens) the watch has to offer. During my course, I found that the buttons were *very* stiff. This might be to prevent accidental presses during exercise, but I found that I had to press almost twice has hard as other electronic watches for the watch to recognize my press. But, from my uses so far, I've pressed it mostly to view all the screens when testing out all the features. When actually running, I do no more than a few presses before and after each run. The network had trouble activating itself in the beginning, but that's because I was fiddling with it outside. It kept trying to set itself numerous times when I actually ran outside, but I always dismissed it. Once, however, I was under the open sky I let it connect and it has had no problem or delay connecting ever since.

After every run I am able to sync it with the Epson app, as well as RunKeeper. People have complained about the Epson app but I find it neat and useful.

Overall, it's a great little watch that accurately records my runs and uploads them without the use of the phone during the workout. I'm able to review it speedily on my phone right after, and I love that I can now track my progress without the burden of added weight. It's pricey for sure, but considering I don't need my phone and my previous watch lasted me ten years, I'm sure this watch will be a great investment that will last me hopefully for another decade or so.

We have had a couple of MBPs before getting this one, and those two have sustained minor injuries over the last 10+ years. But since this MBP will be used between two people this time, we decided to get some sort of protection for it besides the padded sleeve. This one was far more expensive than others, but I love the colors and that I could see a majority of MBP. It snaps-fit into the MBP. They're a bit stiff and the snap sounds like it damages the computer, but obviously it's supposed to protect it I guess that's normal.

The kit comes with two filters that fit over the MBP as well, in case you're worried about having full coverage. Though I"m not sure if there are any films to remove from them; they come with tabs that you have to remove--like from phone screen protectors--but they remove nothing when I remove them. I lifted them up and out and just the tabs took off. Weird.

It's very pricey for what it is, but it looks sleek and doesn't add much bulk. I like the blue accents in the inside, though they're barely noticeable when on the computer.
The bump at the bottom where you rest your thumb when using the track pad takes some getting used to. I've been used to the groove of the MBP for years, which has been improved with each subsequent model, but this one tries to make it easier to find the notch but at the same time throws me off because I'm not used to it.

It's a nice case; maybe a bit pricey, but I love the colors. Just wish the Thule logo was more subdued.

I use this with my Note8 and so far have used Poweramp, Spotify, YouTube, and Audible through them. It worked wonderfully and I got no hiccups from the signal. I used it while running and stationary at my desk. No distortion and the sound is very good, considering the price.

The clip works great and stays on my shirt while running. At this time, I have run on the treadmills. I don't like it, but it's much too cold at the moment to run outside in Chicago (I don't like layering). I don't expect it to differ much, though, when I start using it outside in the summer.

As sunglasses, they are phenomenal. They even fit my slightly narrow face. I own a pair of Gascans that I've had for almost eight years and they are my favorite pair of sunnies. Wanted something now that I'm starting to run more and the sun can sometimes cause a harsh glare.
So nice sunglasses with the ability to track my exercises? Sure; why not.

As sunglasses they fit a bit loose on my head, but with the same material that I used on my Gascans I was able to make them tighter by fitting some foam on the hinges; this way they wouldn't (and didn't) loosen while running.
They fit great and are an excellent addition to my running routine. The sun isn't as vibrant as of this writing, but I will continue to use these throughout the winter as the sun's glare on the snow will be an issue.

I tried these on without the smart devices enabled at first to get an idea as to how the sunglasses were by themselves. The box comes with all the electronics apart from the glasses, and the glasses come in a nice semi-hard shell with the additional lens inside. I then equipped everything in one bout.

The earphones fit okay, but they did tend to slide out at times during the few times I've used this so far while running. No issue in terms of when I'm in the gym, however. Syncing from my phone has never been an issue, though I hate carrying it with me.

As smartglasses, they're okay; nothing revolutionary, and it's up to you if you want to pay the premium price for something your phone already can do, provided you take it with you. As the coach doesn't do as much as I'd like as of this writing, as I already have most of my workouts set. I suppose it may not be entirely geared for me as the only exercise I do outdoors is running; the rest is all in the gym.

The music does tend to cut in and out, and I wound up just shutting it off completely after a while. I may look into more comfortable replacements, too.

As sunglasses, these are phenomenal. The perfect sunnies for triathlons, methinks (when they're not wet). But as for smartglasses, a novel idea but needs improvement.

For $80, this tablet is actually pretty good. It's about the same height as my Note8, but almost double the width. Still, the tablet-exclusive apps on the Google Play Store work without issue on it, though of course you're going to sacrifice some viewing due to the smaller scale.

When I got the tablet I knew it wasn't going to be anything spectacular. At $80, I knew it wasn't going to compete with the devices I was used to, but it still was nice to have to act as a tablet to play my tablet-exclusive games on and for the kids to use to play their games. The screen of course isn't the sharpest, and out of the box it isn't as sensitive in all areas. Two of the first games I installed were a couple of pinball apps, and the screen had a hard time detecting my presses on the left side.

The screen is quite sharp considering it's a "low-end" tablet, and the feel is very solid. Has a nice textured back to it which makes me reconsider if I'll get a case. The screen does retain fingerprints easily but a quick wipe on a shirt resolves all issues.

There is a microSD slot which is a nice addition; I can transfer any transferable games to that since this tablet has only 16 GB (less considering there's only 14.-something and some of that is taken up by the OS).

Operating the OS is super sluggish. Takes four times as long to do something as it would on a beefier device. But actual in-app operations aren't as bad. A little more sluggish than on a beefier device, but not enough to notice that much.

Since this tablet doesn't have a phone speaker at the top, the actual main speaker is located in its stead. As a result, you get a nice, loud, crisp sound whenever you watch a movie or play a game.

All in all, a fantastic little tablet for the price; I hope the missing sensitivity spots are temporary. The screen isn't as smooth as others, but I'm willing to forgive that for the price.

First time using a hybrid smartwatch. I have used fully fledged smartwatches before, but never a hybrid. I was curious as to how they worked. Did they have a mini screen? Did they play notifications? Or was it just a simple vibration gimmick and time and date were synced to the phone? (Answers: #3.)

Anyway, when I got the watch I was impressed right as soon as I opened the box. It was and is beautiful. I love a rose gold tint when it's more copper than pink. Really, many of the rose gold colors geared for men is more of a copper color; not sure why companies are naming them "rose gold." It sounds nicer? Going with the Apple trend? I dunno.
Either way, I like it.

The strap is made of premium leather. I own many leather watch straps, and I love the way this one feels. Light, but solid and soft. The rose gold accentuates it handsomely.

Now, on to the device itself, which, as I stated, is my first hybrid smartwatch.
I have a Note8, and so I've used only an Android to pair with this watch. I don't recall if the box states it works with iOS (I've placed the watch in my drawer and the box is stored in the basement, so I don't feel much like fetching it), but with Android it works fine. I say fine because I did experience some small hiccups which I will discuss further.

The instructions included were bare, but really you're to install the app on your phone and follow the instructions from there. In the quick-start menu you'll get the watch running in less than a minute. The hands move as you set the watch, and everything is synchronized correctly.
The app does all the work for you; you can assign shortcuts to the buttons on either side of the crown, set the notification functions, and so on. For me, I set the upper one to check the alarm and the crown to check the date.

The watch is beautiful on the wrist. I like to wear it with warmer, redder colors, and it fits beautiful with the entire ensemble. The time so far has always been synchronized, but I have noticed some slight hiccups while paired with my phone.

The notifications don't always show. I have one contact set to my favorites, and that one always shoes (both hands move to 1 and the watch vibrates when I get a call or text from the favorite, and subsequent favorites will be moved to 2, 3, etc.). However, I do not always get notifications for texts from others. From my understanding, the watch is supposed to vibrate for texts and calls, even if they're not part of your favorites, but I get notifications almost always just for my favorite, and not the others. I don't recall any notification for an incoming call, whether from my favorite or others.

As a hybrid smartwatch, I like that I can see my steps through the complication, and see the date and alarm settings (though I hate that the date isn't a complication; instead you have to assign on of the three buttons to check the date). However, because it doesn't always detect notifications I'm still perplexed as to utilizing its full functionality. I hope it's just some sort of glitch that will fix itself with...time.

Got these for my daughter to use when she has screen time with the iPad or one of our phones. They come in a very nice box with a window display inside the front flap. Included inside were the micro-USB charging cable and the 3.5mm-3.5mm headphone jack--both made of threaded fabric. Very nice.

The headphones didn't come pre-charged so we charged them right away. The sole LED on the 'phones turned red during the charge. Once they were done, we paired them first with my Galaxy S5--it was detected right away. Next we paired with our ancient iPad 2, which also detected the headphones immediately. My wife carried them to a doctor's visit and it paired flawlessly with her iPhone 7.

They are very attractive as headphones; the sound is decent. About right for this price range. They fold for storage but ours didn't come with a carrying case of any kind (not sure if one is supposed to be included). The volume doesn't reach very high, but I guess since this is for our daughter anyway that's a non-issue for us, but still something to point out.

I am not an audiophile by any means. I have Rockbox installed on my iPod video classic with a FiiO amp attached, all loaded with FLAC tunes. I listen to Spotify at work. That's the extent of my musical needs.
I have Audio-Technica headphones, and dream of some day owning custom Kaisers. That's my background.

I was pretty excited to get these. Right after ordering, I watched a few YouTube videos on them, and read up on Head-Fi. For the price, 1More seems to deliver outstanding products. Needless to say, I was pretty excited.

The box finally came and I was found to be very impressed with the presentation. You get a nice, magnetic box housing the IEMs, a leather(ette?) pouch, and multiple choices of ear piece tips. For starters, I found that the ear piece tips pre-attached to the IEMs were the most fitted for me, but I still do not find them perfect. They slide down a bit when in my ear, so there is some loss of sound. I will have to buy some aftermarket ones.

The microphone is also sub-par. This is the first time I've used a mic with headphones, and most of my calls could not catch my voice properly. I would get complaints that I sounded muffled or far away, and so I've resorted to using the phone mic most of the time. The mic buttons work flawlessly for playback features, however.

As for the sound, it's fantastic. With four drivers, I can hear so much more--and so many more flaws! I usually transfer music files into FLAC, and so I have pretty good sources for music. I've been using both my Samsung Galaxy S5 and Rockboxed iPod Video (equipped with a Fiio E11), and the sounds are great, but I'm noticing some files that weren't transferred correctly. I cannot connect to my computer speakers at work as the speakers do not have enough power to juice up the Quads, so be sure you have a more recent device or one with enough power to drive these IEMs.

I also use them on my Wii U's GamePad for Breath of the Wild, and they're actually better than my Audio-Technicas, even with the sliding ear tips. I hear a lot more, and sound is very important in the game.

All in all, amazing value for the price. The ear tip issue is more personal as my ears simply don't fit perfectly any of the ones provided, but I do wish the mic worked better.

I really like these headphones. The presentation of the setup is done really well, especially considering I've never heard of this brand before. The box comes in a sleeve which removes easily, and the box separates to reveal a lower portion which doubles as a headphone stand. That's really neat! Though I won't use it as I prefer a more dedicated headphone stand, I think it's nice of them to offer it; you can even fish a charging cable through a hole so that it can charge while it's standing.

Comfort-wise, the headphones are really comfortable. I was able to find a good height with them on my head and had no discomfort after wearing it for over an hour.
I had no issues connecting to my phone right away. I have an S5 and it picked up the headphones almost instantly.
I was not able to connect it via my Samsung smart TV, but that may be due to the TV's limitations rather than the headphones'.

The sound is very good, and, despite being wireless, there is no noticeable lag. When I say lag, I mean hearing the playback while monitoring the pace of the playback on the screen.

Now, for the touch controls. Overall, they work really, really well. I think the design of the track-skip and volume is gaudy and detracts from the overall aesthetic of the headphones (for being black, these headphones are otherwise a real eye-pleaser).
However, I did notice on mine that the volume doesn't go very high, and that there's actually a very loud beep whenever I hit max, and it's actually really, really abrasive on my ears. At first I thought it was a one-time thing, but it keeps happening whenever I want to raise the volume and I think it's not loud enough, only to find that I'll reach max pretty quickly.

Otherwise, they're great headphones, connect flawlessly, and are very comfortable. I think the right earpiece, which contains the touch area for track navigation and volume, is a bit tacky and detracts from the aesthetic, but that's a personal preference.
These were my first pair of Bluetooth headphones and honestly I wasn't impressed. They didn't work very well and the sound was muffled. Wouldn't spend your money on these.

These were super easy to install and so far have lasted great on trips to and from Wisconsin (we live in Chicago). They're extremely durable so far, and have held fine in slight rain and regular wind conditions. I usually ride in the city so have easy access to hide from the elements, but it's still nice that these will take a beating every once in the while when I'm on the long expressways.

The sound is loud and I'm always able to hear my music, whatever I'm playing. So far so good and at the price I'd say these are a great option for "lower" end bike speakers.

After countless times of the ps4 controllers dying on me due to short battery life, media use on the ps4 was beginning to be a bit of an annoyance. Thankfully, the PDP universal ps4 remote has come to the rescue; well, for the most part. First and foremost, let me say that for the price, it does everything it needs to do and does it well. All of the buttons feel solid and are easy to use, the construction is good, the back is nice and grippy, it is lightweight and because it is a universal remote, it also works on your TV and other electronics. When attempting to use it with my TV it quickly synced itself without issue however I should note I have a Sony television.
If you are looking for a basic remote for Blu-ray movies and Netflix, this is it. It completely solved the battery issue I had with the ps4 remotes, as it has not died on me once. If you are a Hulu user however, you can stop reading, it simply isn’t good enough for Hulu as it can behave somewhat erratically and will not go out of Hulu menus once in them. Outside of Hulu however I have not had a problem with the controller and it functions great with anything else I may need.
There are some minor issues with the remote, for example in order to change the volume you have to switch to the TV controls and then switch back to the ps4 to work with that. It may have just been my controller, and it was easily worked around (use both controllers) but some may find that an issue. When price is factored in, I would say that for the most part, the small annoyances are just that and most users will be able to overlook them. If I had to give a star rating it would be a 4 out of 5 star product. Half a star off for lack of Hulu compatibility and another half off for the little kinks it still has, overall a good product.

The main feature we wanted from this was to pull the photos from our iPhone without having to sync all the time. Sometimes our phone gets filled so quickly with photos and videos that we can't take any more and we're not near our syncing computer. That's where this comes in handy.

In order to use it fully, you have to download the compatible app (which is free), connect the device, and let the app and device access your photos, contacts, and calendar. We have a few microSD cards lying around, and so far our brands (Kensington and SanDisk) worked fine, even though the packaging is adamant in having you buy their brand of cards. ;)

The app itself is pretty easy to use, but I'd rather have the main syncing buttons appear on the first page. When you open it up the app is split into three "pages" that you can swipe through to select. At the top are icons to select the app and card memory (though I'm not sure why you'd back up the phone to the app over the card), and then at the bottom you get features to sync to other apps. Those aren't why we got this product, so when you swipe right you get the buttons to sync the photos, contacts, and calendar. You can sync selected ones or sync them all to the card. We usually just select all, even if we know only pictures and videos have been added since the last sync; we just like to be cautious.
Syncing takes only a few minutes. To confirm that all the photos and videos have been synced, I removed the memory card and plugged it in to both my computer and an Android device. I was able to navigate the folders in the card without issue (that is, no restrictions as I thought there might've been since it was an Apple's synced history going into Windows and Google machines) and see all the photos, etc. You can also navigate the folders via the device in the iPhone, but the thumbnails sometimes take a while to load.
Initially I didn't think the videos were backed up, but that's because they didn't have that little play icon on them as other videos usually do. When I scoured carefully through the dates, however, I found them all, and no noticeable resolution loss. Perfect!

So far this is exactly what we wanted and it works just fine.

After a year of owning my first Android, I've had my 32GB SanDisk used without issues. At least, that's what I had thought until I popped in the Samsung. It could be a variety of reasons (using Samsung cards with a Samsung phone, having a newer card, etc.), but the Samsung card, I've noticed, works a bit smoother and faster with my memory.

I store all the apps I can onto my memory card, have quite a bit of music, books, and photos/videos, and they all load efficiently and far more quickly than my previous cards was capable of. Maybe it's just that the card is new, but I'd like to think it's because I'm using the card with a correspondingly same-brand phone.

This sucker is strong, no doubt, but my phone is heavy. I have an S5 with an Anker battery case, and the stand, while strong enough to withhold the phone up, cannot grip the magnet as well, as such, the phone does slide down during my car ride, so I have to keep readjusting.

That said, the actual features are fine, even if the speaker on my phone isn't the best (seriously, who thought having the speaker on the rear of the phone was a good idea?). You may find that many of the reviews for the app say it's not great, but be aware that the app requires either this stand or Logitech's ventilator mount to operate. With either of those, you'll be good to hear all the features.
I tend to use the car radio more for music, so the lack of musical options on the app isn't a downer. What makes it indispensable for me is the heavy-duty stand to use Waze and to pick up or send the occasional call. Thus far, after a week of using, I've not had any issues with the phone.

The suction works fine, even if the dashboard isn't perfectly flat. It grips on without any wobble.

In my last review for the GolfBuddy CT2 device, I noted that I'm not a very avid golfer. I'm still not, but that doesn't mean I wasn't able to give this a thoroughly tested and detailed try.

The other I had was made to store in pockets, but that doesn't mean this one is any different. This one is about just as small, and easily fits into the caddy and pockets I used. Overall, working it was simpler as I used to the other. Just as the last one I reviewed, this was used about a couple of times, though I plan on using this one a few more times at the very least.

Nevertheless, it has about half the screen ratio compared to my other device, as this is meant to be worn around the body and supplemented as a watch of sorts. The menus are easily navigable with one hand (with only a couple of fingers necessary, at most), and all information is there with just a few presses.

I used with the same friend who helped me out last time, although this time I didn't need his help, especially since I had this on me at all times, so I had to force myself to use it and learn.

I don't golf as much as I'd like these days, but for the couple of games I participated in recently I decided to bring this along. I've never used a rangefinder before, so using this was a nascent experience, to say the least!

Another reviewer here mentioned watching the introductory video offered on the company’s website. I did so, though I used the instructions as well. The video I watched before my first use, and kept the instructions with me during the games.
The video was far more helpful than I initially thought as it went into the gadget's features into great detail without being exhaustive (they even put a Table of Contents at the beginning of the video so you can jump around). Even though it made using the device far more intuitive, I found that, when it came time to actually use the device, I still fumbled through the screens; I often had the button configurations mixed, and so many times I’d enter screens which I didn’t intend. I’m uncertain if this is something to do with the design of the gizmo or if they all are like this. I s’pose I’ll just have to become accustomed to it.

During one of my games, I had a friend of mine use it with me, and he got the hang of it faster than I did; his experience with other golf GPS devices was minimal, but it still was more than what I had. He was able to memorize the shortcuts better than me, and that helped me while I watched him navigate.

While it’s a great learning experience for me considering I've used it only a couple of times, it was very nifty to have and helped a ton. The backlit feature is nice, but if you’re golfing early in the day you probably won’t need it much. It’s light in its weight, no doubt, and convenient to stash in any pocket. The dot-matrix display makes the experience much easier to read and manipulate; truthfully, I did think that most of the screens are organized very well from screen to screen, image to text. The company seems to have excelled in this area.

I realize I became far more serious in my game with this than before; I'm not a very competitive person, but something like this will be very useful for those who take the game of golf more serious than a stroll through the field. I'm sure that, if you've used these before, the layout and button configuration is a breeze. I'm new to this world (not golfing itself, of course), so the whole experience of using these is a tad overwhelming. I just keep telling myself that it’s like adding the map features from my golfing video games to the real world!

We got this to replace our old camera, which had been knocked over. It worked well enough, but the antennae kept falling apart after the incident, and by that time it was well past its warranty.
We didn't realize how much more that one had than this model, especially considering they're both around the same price.

Right out of the box, though, my wife and I noticed how sturdy this one seemed. It's small, but it has some weight and over the past month we haven't had it budge from its spot at all. We use ours as a kids monitor. As such, we don't mind that this stands out. It's bright white, and has LEDs for night vision. When we need to, we use it as a security camera when we're away for long periods of time. It'll make do.

Compared to our previous camera, this one was a LOT easier to set up. Because it has its own app, the camera and our phones synced perfectly and instantly. Before, we had to pick and choose from various apps since the camera didn't have its own. It was cumbersome and confusing, so we welcome this change. As far as IP cameras go, this one was easier to set up. I would still like to use this camera on a browser, but I haven't ventured into that, if at all possible.

It doesn't do as much as my old camera at the same price (namely, rotate), and the cloud feature makes me wary to the point that I turn it off when I don't need it, but it's a good, sturdy little replacement for our previous model.

I've been wanting one of these since I first discovered them on a tech blog last year. I have a bad habit of being a grumpy morning person; part of it is going to sleep late, the other part is the way I wake up.
So I then discovered that some alarm clocks wake you by showing you artificial sunlight. Perfect, I thought.

I was excited to get this set up when it arrived. I found the box a bit light, but I got out the pieces and assembled everything straight away. The settings were very easy to get done, even though the buttons seemed confusing at first.

There are touch buttons on the light part, as well as alarm and volume buttons on the base. The lamp itself is a bit light, however. I mean weight-wise. It tips over my nightstand quite a bit.

And that brings me to the buttons. My daughter, two, loves to touch gadgets. This is no exception. If you plan on getting this, put it somewhere where kids can't reach. Even at her slightest touch the settings are constantly reset, so I have to put them back. As of right now I have to reset the settings again, but I do love the clock and I find myself in a better mood in the mornings.

But not when I see my daughter reaching for the clock as I get up.

The light glows after some time, and really gets a good light in my face. The days are getting warmer here in Chicago and so the sun is shining more and more through the windows. Still, I'm able to utilize this alarm to get the sunlight less offensive.
The speaker on it is really clear for the size; maybe I'm just surprised at how well speakers have gotten in alarm clocks.

Overall, great. The lowest brightness for the clock isn't too bad. You can't really see it when the bedroom light is on, but at night it does get a little brighter than it seems. On my nightstand I put a pillow there to block just above the digital clock so the numerals get blocked out but I still get the light from the actual wake-up light.

Overall I'm pleased with it. I could have some heft to keep it more stable, and I'd prefer harder-to-press buttons (both for my toddler and my snooze tendency). Still, it's a lot better than using my phone as my alarm clock, especially since I don't like bringing in phones into my bedroom, thus allowing me to get to sleep right away.

Got this to locate our car, and honestly it works. Left it in the glove compartment and checked in on it over the holidays periodically. Between lots of holiday shopping, eating at restaurants, and going to the theaters, we did lots of parking and had to find our car on a regular basis.

The first few times I forgot I had it, but when I looked it up I was able to find the car right away. I haven't lost reception yet, so I don't know how long the utility will last.

But for now it's a great convenience.

I'm a burgeoning audiophile and I'm always eager to try new cans to add to my listening experience. A while back, say 2007 or so, I jumped into the deeper waters and decided to upgrade my stock Apple ear buds (why I didn't sooner is beyond me). I haven't looked back since, and continue to look forward this very day.

But do these headphones do my ears and music justice?

Right now my arsenal consists of some Sound Blasters I use for my computer and my trusty ol' Sennheisers which I've had since 2007 (the selfsame headphones with which I used to help me jump from Apple), along with Monoprice ear buds I keep at work. I'm not the most professional audiophile, but I sure as heck can tell some differences in quality, especially if the sound source is in FLAC.
Unfortunately, I'm not the most ecstatic about SMS Audio's STREET by 50, especially at the higher premium for Star Wars branding.

I've always been wary of celebrity-endorsed products; never trying Beats, I've been bombarded by them on the streets of Chicago by the candy-colored headbands on people's heads. I've always wondered about their integrity, until a fellow flesh-and-blood audiophile renounced them after she had used her ATH -M50s for some time. I took her word for it and never considered using Beats.
But me, being the Star Wars fanatic, had to try the SMS Audio. When they arrived I admit I was impressed by the fancy packaging. For $200, the headphones arrived looking like it.
They came in a slipcased box that was a little difficult to remove as the vacuum-sealed enclosure proved a tough fit, but they open up sweetly after that.

There are some nice manuals that come with, along with some neat little Star Wars stickers and papers. There's even a cleaning cloth and nice soft zippered case. The headphones came folded inside the case.
When I opened 'em up and took out the included removable cable and tried them on, I was a bit dumbfounded and how uncomfortable they felt around my head with such soft ear pads. I'm not sure if I need to break them in longer, but I've been using them steadily for a month and so far I haven't noticed a difference. My ears ache after just 20 minutes.

The sound was very disappointing at first, though I admit it did warm up (or down?) after a few weeks. But are they a large improvement over my $30 Sennheisers? A little, but not considerable. I can hear more background noise--that is, in the music--but there's not much balance as I have to turn up the volume to notice any huge improvement. There's a bit more bass than I'd like, but not enough to drown my ears in it.

I like the fact that the cable is detachable, but the ones they included feel a bit cheap and they tangle easily. I HATE the fact that they have the buttons, something which I've always hated since the iPhone came standard with them. But that they are removable altogether makes up for the buttons, as I'm able to change them out with custom, and higher quality, gold-plated cables.

The colors are fantastic; honestly, they were the reason I was drawn to them, but they look metallic in the press shots whereas, when you get them, the material is actually plastic, forcing the colors to be a lot lighter, more matte, and cheaper in feel. I'm all for matte, but I had hoped the headphone band was metallic; alas, it's plastic.

So that's my take on the cans. Take them or leave them. They're nice headphones, and I've gotten plenty of complements on them both from friends and at work, but at the steep price tag I can't recommend them, especially when you can get far superior headphones for much less (like the revered Audio-Technicas).

I use SanDisk for all my memory card needs as they've always been very reliable. But Samsung, of course, is a fine manufacturer of electronics, so I thought I'd give them a try.

This microSDHC card comes with an SD adapter, but I never use them as I already own a SanDisk USB adapter that plugs in any size SD card.
I've been using the card with my SanDisk Clip Zip (the treachery!) and haven't noticed any lag. The card is read just as quickly as SanDisks themselves, and it's always handy to have an extra card around.

The case is slim and is fairly comfortable to hold, the lego plate isn't that much in the way. It is easy to snap on, only slightly difficult to take off, and the edge of the case slightly goes over the rim of the iPod. Although it is small, you can build on the lego plate and. If you have the right bricks, you can literally build up and over, you can create a stand for your phone out of legos. However, the sound and lock buttons, and the headphone and charger stations are very exposed. Other wise, it's a very good case.

Works well with my wife's MacBook and our TV. We connect her laptop to a Mediabridge HDMI cable, which then plugs into our TV, and the resolution is stunning.

It's very sturdy and complements the HDMI's thickness, and doesn't seem like it'll tear or rip if it's accidentally tugged on too forcefully.
Or if our 2-year-old daughter happens to snatch it away when we're not looking.

We have a TP-Link router, so getting an extender of the same brand seemed to fit the bill in extending our Wi-Fi issues. We live in a 150-year-old apartment building with very thick walls. The cable for the TV and Internet is located in the living room, whereas my office is on the completely opposite side of the building. There are about three walls in between, so my Internet was shoddy at best. I have an iPhone, MacBook Pro, a Toshiba PC, and some handheld gaming consoles, and the only one to get decent service in my office was the MBP.

I ordered the signal extender and stuck it into our bedroom, which is the halfway point from the router to my office. Setting up the device was extremely easy, and took all of a couple minutes (half of which was me making sure I did it right). At first, I noticed no boost in Wi-Fi to my office. Before, the strength of signal reaching back there was about two or three bars on my Toshiba PC, and the first or no arc on my iPhone. However, after going about my business, I found that my Toshiba PC only once has dropped under three bars, and sometimes even reaches its full signal strength--but that's happened once. My iPhone is about the same, but sometimes it does show full signal strength as well.

I never get any more disconnected webpages in my office, and I can go about my work and non-work without having to worry about taking the power off my PC and dashing to the living room.

Only once in the past month or so has it lost signal, but it picked up right away. It also acts as a nice nightlight with its warm blue glow, illuminating the path to the door so I can get out for a quick midnight getaway to the throne room and back.

I use this primarily for my PS3. Since the system comes with only two USB ports, and there are a healthy amount of accessories for it, the ports usually get hogged up. Cue the Belkin hub.

I've got the Eye and my Turtle Beach headphones plugged into the first port with the hub, while the second remains free for charging. It's been working fine this past week, and it's small design lets met tuck it away to the side of the PS3 without worry, save for the USB connections plugged in, obviously.

It's kinda stupid that the connector for the hub is on the same side of the ports, making it kind of awkward, but what are you gonna do?
The lights flash to show which connections are in use. Overall a nice little hub. We'll see how it stands in the long run.

Got this one to use in my office. I used to have the standard 6-outlet bar for my computer and gaming setup, and an additional 3-outlet plug with USB outlets on the wall. I found that I was constantly plugging and un-plugging devices on the 6-outlet one, so I decided to get one that has a couple more.

I like this one in particular because it has the right amount I need for now. The last two toward the bottom are spaced a little wider than the rest, which is perfect for my bulkier plugs, namely my shredder and my MacBook Pro charger.
Haven't had the chance to use the phone plugs as we don't have a landline (Who does these days?). We purchased a multi-printer with the fax option, so maybe that'll get some use in the future.

Overall, great. This is my third or fourth Belkin surge protector, and I'm pretty satisfied with them all. They feel heavy-duty and sturdy, so I don't see them wearing out any time soon, no matter where we place them.

About a few weeks in after using this, I noticed that the switch would be turned off every so often. It was strange, because it hadn't happened to any of my other surge protectors. I asked my wife if she had accidentally turned it off while walking around the area, but she said no. It was really frustrating, because my chargers and alarm clock would turn cease to operate because of this, and I'd have to turn the switch back on every time and recharge my devices and reset my clock.

One morning, when I put my one-year-old daughter down so I could get my breakfast, I noticed she immediately shot for the surge protector and switched it off.
Must be the shiny red light.

Sorry for the lengthy review.

I love this sound bar. Five stars for the audio. No doubt about it.
I consider myself relatively gadget-savvy, but certainly not tech-savvy. I love gadgets, but I'm an idiot when it comes to sound and sound-related technology. I only recently stopped using ear buds altogether and switched to my Sennheisers as my primary listening `phones.

My family and I live on the third floor of a three-apartment house, and not once did I ever consider getting surround sound. I have the speakers for it, as they were hand-me-downs, but I don't want to set them up lest I receive the wrath of my neighbors. That, and I don't even have the connections necessary on my TV (my TV is two years old; the speakers are far older than that). I recently heard about sound bars (though the PS3 one that came out a while ago caught my eye before), and thought that might be a better fit for me.

I don't normally track Vine orders, as they usually get delivered on Tuesdays. But I was so excited about this one I kept looking on UPS's website, only to be disappointed to read that it had not been delivered on Tuesday; when I got home, my hopes were ultimately crushed when I found the "undelivered" sticky on my mailbox. What's one more day? I signed the note and left it for the UPS man.
When I finally got the package the next day, I realized why they needed a signature: the box was huge! And there's no outer box, so all that's delivered is the product in its factory packaging, as if you bought it from the store yourself. Everybody and they momma are going to know what you ordered. But, thankfully, I don't have to worry about theft in my neighborhood too much.
So when I unboxed it, I was surprised to see how little real estate the actual sound bar took. Initially, I was surprised to see how big the box was, as I didn't think the bar itself was too big. But then I realized the box was oversized to accommodate the subwoofer.

Instructions were easy enough, but the HDMI set-up was a pain. There's a disc with the manual, but I would prefer if LG's website lets you download it (as of this review, they still don't have it up). Out of three HDMI cables I had lying around (two from the same brand), only one worked. I have two Mediabridge cables, one six- and the other nine-feet, and a cheapo one which came with my Comcast DVR. Only the Mediabridge six-foot cable worked, for some odd reason, so that's the one currently connecting the sound bar.
Nevertheless, the Internet capabilities are going to be wasted on me, I'm assuming, as I already have services such as Netflix on my PS3, and I don't see myself switching to the sound bar any time soon.
I haven't tried the other apps, so I can suggest getting this model without the Internet capabilities for the cheaper price tag. Really, you're paying $100-$150 just to have Wi-Fi on it, when many most likely have such services on other devices.

There's an optical cable included for the audio, as well as a wall mount. I won't use the mount till we buy a house, so I can't say much on that.

I love that the subwoofer is wireless. I knew where I wanted to place the sound bar and subwoofer before they arrived, and I was pleased that I was able to put them exactly where I wanted. I have a 47" Toshiba, so the sound bar and TV are perfectly matched.

My initial sound tests were Game of Thrones, Arrested Development, and Dexter's Laboratory (I'm a kid at heart), and the sound was amazing. I've never used other sound bars, but, considering this isn't a 5.1 surround sound system, I was blown away. The sound was perfect, exceeding my expectations. As I mentioned, I'm a newb to the audio world, so forgive my ignorance and bliss. I'm perfectly content with my sound bar, though, as our current "surround" sound system.

My wife didn't like it at first--and still kinda doesn't--as she thought "it's too loud," but over the first weekend, when we watched The Last Stand (awful movie, by the way), she changed her mind. She said it was like being in a theater--at least, the next best thing.

The bar itself is great, but the subwoofer really adds that punch where you can *feel* the sound. I have the subwoofer next to the couch for extra oomph.

All in all, I love it. I give the audio itself five stars, but I'm taking one star away for the Internet services. Honestly, I don't see the reason for paying the extra money when the other model with audio only is just as good. I still haven't used the video options, but will update this review if I ever do.

The remote is a bit large for just a sound bar, as I'm using only the power and volume buttons, as well as the occasional input button for Bluetooth. The latter feature is nice, but don't go moving your iPod/iPhone/other streaming device around, as the connection breaks easily. But when it's still, the music quality sounds great.

After getting this sound bar, I no longer care what my neighbors might think.

Before this stand, I used another Fellowes one for my laptop at home, and it proved its worth--for a while. However, with my new desk setup, I needed something which I could use while changing the height and angle of my laptop screen in a way the old stand simply couldn't. I have a Unicomp keyboard and Logitech mouse which I prefer using, and my "home" laptop needed a better stand.
Enter this Lift.

I've seen many angled laptop stands, and that's what I had in mind when I wanted to switch my old one out. Plus, my old one was better suited for the monitor at work, so I wanted to take that when I had the chance. Finally, I had the opportunity to get an angled one, so I jumped on it.

I'm not using this stand with my laptop by itself. I'm using it as a supplemental to "lift" it up with my home desktop setup being my keyboard and mouse. For that, the stand works marvelously. The angle and height are just about right; I no longer have to arch my neck uncomfortably forward. Plus, I can take my old stand to work and finally have proper posture there too.
I can't see using this by itself. My hands would quickly become painfully uncomfortable. Heck, I can't stand using keyboards with their built-in mini stands. I honestly don't know why they're there; the angle cramps my wrists very fast.

So for my use, I think the stand is great. There's even some empty real estate near the back to put things under, and it seems sturdy enough overall. It's currently holding my Toshiba 17" Windows PC, which is snugly fit.

My five-month-old daughter loves this thing. Well, so far. We've had it for a couple weeks, and bust it out whenever we're home and she's awake, and we have some free time (which is hardly ever, but still). When I realized the apps uses with this is the same as the [[ASIN:B0080D58GA Fisher-Price bConnect Digital Soother]], I just flipped it over to the mirror and let her play with the toys.

My complaints are that the mirror is embedded behind the clear film (which would prevent the baby from touching the phone), so the reflection is milky. Also, because of her size, the mirror doesn't reach her face when she plays with the toys, so it's kind of useless anyway.

We don't really use the straps on the sides to hang the toys as her little arms won't be able to reach them on either side when she's lying in the middle, so we just hook `em all on the centered rings and she likes them just fine.

It's easily portable, though I question its price-point. It's worth $20, in my opinion. Also, if you have newer iPhones or iPods, they won't work due to their elongated size.

But my daughter could care less (yes, sarcasm), and for her it's a lot of fun. My gripes come from the paying adult's point of view.

If you're like me and have many gadgets and other electronic devices around the house which use long amounts of cables (or a surplus of cables at that) and usually toss out the plastic ties they come with, these Velcro ties are a boon to the household. I actually didn't realize I needed them so much until I ordered them just for some TV cable ties, and then found myself wrapping cords from my video game controllers to cable box cables to whatever. They're mostly used around the TV, since video game concoles and other devices are hooked up to it, but I plan on using some more with my computer cables and accessories.

They might be a bit pricey at $18 for 25, but I find them to be well worth it, and would even buy more once I ran out. I like that the whole sides are taken up by Velcro, so you can tie it as tightly as you want without any part of it hanging. I personally ordered the 8" size, but might go one size smaller next time since most of the cables I've used them on didn't require so much length.
Still, I'm glad I have them, and have already recommended them to people. You really don't know how useful they are until you get them.

I'll update this with more use.

So far, the alarm clock radio proved exceptionally. The power of the sound is fantastic, and easily rivals the other top brand iPhone/iPod docks out there. The buttons don't stick, and seem to last a while (had this for a couple months now). The light is a nice hue, not too bright in the night time.
The dock itself does protrude out to allow iPods of varying sizes and inside cases, so we'll see how durable it is in the long run.

Perhaps if the sound was better, or if the price was lower, these would be great headphones. The design is slick, and actually comes fully black-gray brand new (I know they "customize" over the years, but the blue on the cans in the Amazon picture threw me off).
The stretchiness is great, and I don't fear that the headphones would break easily if, say, someone accidentally sat on them. Nonetheless, I do have some gripes.

First, the sound is absolutely awful for $100. There was some tinny noise, and because the headphones have a hard time adjusting to my skull, I couldn't get the right position for the full sound effect. It's a shame that headphones of this price can't even beat my $20 Sennheisers (which is no jab at my beloved Sennheisers). Another issue I had is with the cord. I understand that it's certainly non-tangable, but it comes with a longer cord that makes absolutely no sense. The longer cord isn't the major issue, though; it's the short cord that extends from the headphones: it's so short, it can't attach to *anything* without requiring the longer cord. Maybe if you were on your bed and the iPod/music device was on your chest it would work, but I imagine people aren't buying these cans for bed use. The longer cord is absolutely fundamental to using, so I don't know why they even bothered separating it from the cans themselves. They should've made the shorter cord longer and the longer cord slightly shorter.

While the design is superb, I'd look elsewhere if you want good sound quality.

I was ecstatic to receive these headphones because, while I like to do some gaming before I go to bed, my wife gets shuteye earlier as her workday begins at the "buttcrack of dawn" (her expression); but while the TV is located next to the bedroom, the volume has to be kept at a reasonable volume so as not to disturb her beauty rest, which leaves me, then, with little to no volume.
Therefore, these headphones seemed like a lifesaver for the PS3, but when I first received them, I could not for the life of me get them properly connected. Like everyone else, it took me a while (days, unfortunately) to realize that I would need to use the RCA cables from the PS3 to use these to their fullest potential.

To start off, and due to the fact that I couldn't get them hooked up the PS3 first, I'll explain testing them on the Mac. They work terrifically. I tested out a bunch of music and some videos, and the sound was supreme. The software is a digital download from their site, and necessary to fully utilize the headphones' capabilities. At times it sounds a little overwhelming, but tweaking it to your standards with the software helps to alleviate that. It even lets you save profiles in case someone wants to set the settings to their own preferences.

After one charge, I've yet to recharge the headphones and been using them for days. Once I was able to wrap my head around the fact that I'd have to dig for my RCA cables from the PS3 box, I plugged them in, followed the slightly confusing instructions that came with the headset, and played away. True, the sound isn't the greatest in terms of clarity, but it suits basically nonetheless. For the price, you're probably better off getting other headphones that are specific to consoles. While these headphones advertise as being cross-platform, the Mac/PC audio leaves much to be desired from console hearing.

With that, the customer service is marvelous. I placed a comment on another's review before posting mine about the console frustration I was having, and I received an email a few hours later from a customer service rep from the company, asking me to get in touch with them about the issues I was having. With some patience and instruction, I finally realized that the HDMI cable just isn't enough to use these.

If you want some good cross-platform headphones and don't mind sacrificing quality for consoles, these are excellent; if you do more computer gaming than console, then go ahead. However, if you want some headphones that are superb for PS3 and/or 360, I'd suggest other ones. I didn't get to test these on the Xbox 360 as I don't have one, but from what I've heard don't even bother.

I've heard about these foam tips for quite some time, but staved off as the gel ones that came with my [[ASIN:B000FUESSU V-MODA Bass Freq Earbuds (Bling Bling Black)]] worked just fine. The bass is great, and the gel bud tips enhance the sound even further.

Nevertheless, I decided to order these just to see what the fuss was about. Many other reviewers seem to give them great reviews, so I, what with me being a bass freak, decided to give them a whirl.
At first they're excellent, and fit extremely comfortable. After a few wears, though, they seem to lose their greatness and tightness. HOWEVER, and this is a big however, they once again expand to perfectly fit the inside of my ear. Not sure how that happened, but they went back to how they first fit, but even more comfortably.

If that's not the case for everyone, and the foam tips just collapse with time, then I'd say avoid these. BUT because with my experience they retained their fit inside my ear, and were indeed customized over time to fit perfectly, then I tout these to the extreme. Just go to the product page and make sure they fit your earbud headphones. They're a bit pricey, yes, so not necessary if what you have works fine; they just provide more comfort and enhance the bass for me.

I ordered this to match my [[ASIN:B003ZX8B0U Garmin nüvi 1350LMT 4.3-Inch Portable GPS Navigator with Lifetime Map & Traffic Updates]], and the accessories are wonderful. I was on the hunt for a good, simple case since my wife just tosses the GPS on the floor after use (don't ask; I've tried), and hopefully lengthen the life of the unit.

The case is a bit tight at first, but with a bit of time the fit becomes glove-like. The additional accessories, while not entirely necessary, are perfect for frequent travelers, and I've yet to have one of them malfunction. They're basic, but that's the point of AmazonBasic's line. This is my third product from Amazon's own, and I can say I'm a happy consumer.

I got these for my sister for when she goes to college, and here's her take on 'em:

I have been using these speakers while watching television episodes on Hulu and, of course, when listening to music. They have a really high maximum value and so far I've heard no buzzing because of playing them loudly. There is a separate wired volume control that, I've found, really comes in handy so you don't have to reach for the speakers every time you need to adjust the volume. The speakers themselves are very small and don't take up a lot of space which is something I really enjoy. The wires to each speakers are definitely long enough so you can place them a good deal far apart for a surround sound effect. All in all, I have enjoyed the speakers and will hopefully continue to when I take them to college.

This is a review of the product by the person I got it for:

Definitely is the actual size as shown on the box. Nice, compact size with a requirement of only one USB port. Installation was easy to follow and complete (follow the folder-finding path on the manual though, and don't just start clicking files when the hard-drive shows up under "My Computer"). For not being a particularly tech-savvy person myself, it was fairly easy to transfer files from my old hard-drive to the new one. Fast access; doesn't slow down my computer like my older one did. Completely satisfied with the product; very user friendly.

What more can I say that hasn't already been about the Wave design? It's comfortable, ergonomic, easy to use, and helps me to get my keystrokes in faster. Sure, it's no IBM Model M or Unicomp Customizer, but it's the best quiet-key keyboard I've used so far.

The Unifying feature is neat, as I have the Anywhere Mouse MX (which is great, by the way), and makes hooking up lots of Logitech devices that also utilize this feature a cinch.

No need to get this if you already have the Wave, but if you don't, or you're absolutely dead-set on getting this for the extra features (via software) and Unifying setup, then this is a great keyboard to consider. It's easy to use right out of the box; had no issues whatsoever (batteries included, too).

This is the first Logitech keyboard I've gotten, and now I see why Logitech is considered to be a proficient manufacturer in keyboards and other computer-related paraphernalia.

Without installing any such programs or software, either from the website or from the included disc, I plugged in the USB receiver right out of the box, followed the easy-to-setup instructions engraved on the back of the keyboard, and away I went. I was able to type flawlessly at the office, and the keys are very smooth and quiet. Even though it's just a keyboard, I kept opening up different programs to test out the typing. Pure joy! (For a nerd like me, at least.)

I guess the only gripes I have, and I noticed it almost immediately, is that there are no lights to indicate locks for the numbers, caps, or scroll. It's a minor gripe, but a gripe nonetheless since I have to utilize the Caps Lock every so often at work.

When I used the extra buttons for various computer software, I found that the respected programs opened up right away. There was some stall, but that was the result of my slow, crunching computer.
The mouse worked just as it should.

Now, I have to admit, what I really wanted to get this keyboard for was my Wii at home. I know, it sounds nerdy.
But the keyboard I was using before was an old office wired one that was given to me. That one worked fine, but I wanted a wireless one. So, I took home this MK300 keyboard and USB receiver, plugged in the latter into the back of my Wii console, opened up the Internet Channel and found, to my delight, that the keyboard worked flawlessly.
There was some range betwixt the keyboard and receiver--about ten feet or so--but it made no matter: my sitting spot isn't too far from the console, so it's not like I'm going to be typing in a completely different room.

Since this keyboard works so well, I was hoping to use it on a Mac. I've yet to buy the MacBook Pro--which is why I'm stuck with the Wii's Internet Channel for now--and since the specifications for this certain keyboard doesn't include Apple's OS, I'm assuming that there is simply no way around hardware setups (ever tried?) and will have to resort to something else, when the time comes.

All in all, though, if you're looking for an excellent wireless (not Bluetooth) keyboard at a relatively inexpensive price tag for any PC machine or Wii, look no further. The MK300 works like a charm.

I was skeptical at first to purchase this item. I read many reviews here on Amazon.com before I decided to give it a try. It had more good reviews than bad so I ordered it hoping that the reviews that spoke of how easy it was to set up as an Access Port were reliable. I am happy to say that I love this product. It was as simple as plugging it in to a wall outlet and an ethernet jack. I had several ethernet connnections in my apartment but wanted to have wireless Internet access for the i-Touch I recently bought and for my laptop computer. I set the switch to AP, plugged in the a/c adapter and connected the supplied ethernet cable and voila, I had wireless Internet. Now the signal is not super strong, but from one room to the next you will have no problems. I don't want the neighbors stealing my signal anyway. I didn't have to install any software or go through a modem or router, I only had to "connect" to d-link on my i-Touch and laptop when they picked up the wireless signal. I would definitely recommend this product to anyone just looking to make a small area wireless. I cannot attest to the other capabilities of this device because I am only using the one feature.

These two big gripes aside. The watch is good and likely the best choice going into 2023 for pure Android Wear OS users (not looking at Apple or Tizen overlay users.)

Its not perfect and Pixel users will benefit the most when paired to this watch. Its lost most of the lag recent watches from other Wear OS brands. Has all the sensors the majority of buyers could want based on watch tech right now. It swipes, it plays well with the apps made for it. It gives you the info you ask of it. There are even a few nice 3rd part accessories now to avoid Google Gouging for proprietary bands. And there are few quirks I hope they iron out soon. Mainly, when the phone is in Bedtime Mode. Make the watch do it too, or add that Zen Mode feature to the watch also. It sucks to have animals tripping the security cameras outside dinging on my wrist and killing my sleep score. The snooze/do not disturb button on watch fails too easily and you have turn it on/off manually everytime.

As many claim, the battery sucks. Sort of. I can go up to 36+ hours on a slow day, and many others can too. It will depend on too many factors to list. But basically your popularity with notifications and thinking you need the screen always on are the biggest battery hurdles. Most can get use to touch to wake. And maybe only having text, phone, front door doorbell and one email be allowed to bother your watch with notifications. Do you really need to know what cousin Billy had at Dairy Queen when he posts the same pic/vid on Facebook, Instagram, Tic Toc and YouTube, etc. Find a nice balance of wrist information along with what sensors you need checking if you are still alive. You can start the day and track everything till the next morning when you charge it again while you shower and get the next day started. It charges quickly. And most other Wear OS watches have the same daily charge requirements. Nobody on Wear OS is winning on battery. Or Turn every setting all the way up and have a spare charger puck ready for a mid day juice. If you go that route. I suggest a quick release band to ease the removal of the watch.

So, its not up to the level or price of the Ultra Apple Watch. And if you don't care for Samsung. Your love for stock Android will eventually lead you back to this watch. Unless you forgo ECG sensors. The price will drop soon. Cases are minimizing the fragility of an ALL glass jelly bean design. But when comes to keeping your phone pocketed and yet still have info relayed in a useful way. Pixel Watch is the best current albeit not perfect solution for now.

It should be the answer most need to try magnetic connector for their devices. And if your cables were already good for data/charge, these shouldn't change that unless you are using some very high spec stuff.
Ever since wearing out PS4 controller charge ports from the necessity of plugging charge cables that often get tugged from excited gaming, pets and just forgetting you are tethered. I now ONLY use higher end magnetic cables and dongles like these for charging my PS5/Switch/Steam Deck/Retroid or any other item that needs frequent charging where the connector could be damaged by movement. For home use and travel these are worth the purchase if you want to extend the life of USB-C charge ports.

BTW, can't mention the brand here since this "Sheeast" brand only seems to sell the dongle and no cables (starts with K and sounds like a Hawaiian dance). But for magnetic cables for data/charging that are not total garbage. Only buy the elongated, almost rectangle magnetic cables. Like the shape of these dongles. AVOID the circle cables. And don't be careless and let the magnetic ends drag on the floor. They will collect metal and crud and become useless. Be good to your stuff!

Just have trouble getting used to the side marble and it wasn't great for gaming and the others were cheap and felt low quality.

Brings us to the Kensington Orbit. For me, it is as close to the Marble as I have found so far in a wireless version. Good range and plenty response options. Ball is in the center where I prefer to have it. 2 buttons the way a mouse was meant to be (although a couple tiny programable buttons would be nice at this price). Yet not all is perfect, but I am coping with it. The tricky bit for me that hinders a higher rating. First, the right click button is too big. There is no where for my pinky finger to rest without clicking. Please revise the design just a bit for the base to ride a bit higher or the button to get a bit smaller. Or add a flip up piece to partially cover the button to prevent pushing it (likely to 3D print something for my use). Who needs the right click button to be so prominent. Secondly, It might be me, but the sliders/scroll on either side of the ball are not great. They hesitate and don't react to my touch too well, but it might be me with rough fingers.

I will keep the mouse because it works well for what I need right now. But, Hey Kensington, consider a revised model that has room for the finger to rest somewhere on the right that does no result in a button press. Can't be the only one. Or maybe that is a different model you already sell? My choices were limited when I ordered.

The bags are good for almost any remote you might have for a tv or sound system built in the last 20+ years. While I was pretty sure the bags would be that crunchy plastic you see on Easter baskets or grocery store flowers. I hoped it would be a bit closer to something softer or maybe silicone like. The heat shrink works great and fits all my remotes well. The downside is you end up with corners of hard plastic with sharp/pointy edges after the shrink (tried multiple methods or sealing and still rough corners). And getting the air out is near impossible. You end up with a balloon around your remote and some of the buttons can't be pressed (a plus if you are just storing things). Or you put a pin hole in the plastic and the seal is tight, but maybe too tight after you get the full heat shrink smooth. One remote of mine has a frequently used button 2 in from the side and it is hard to use now.
You get a lot of bags and it might be trial and error to find the balance if you plan to use the item you shrink wrapped. Its a good product and serves the purpose I wanted it for. Just wish they could come up with a softer less crunchy plastic.
Hair dryer is all you need to shrink the plastic. I also sealed the ends with a vacuum sealer. These bags can't be vacuum sealed though, too smooth.

We mounted one on each of our Lectric Xp bikes. With a few real thick zip ties (the ones included are useless) they fit perfectly and solidly in the bike rack. And once you load your cargo or in my case mount a thin board on top of the rack. There will be no access for anyone to reach or destroy the alarm if it goes off. It is the perfect fit and hiding spot for those with a similar bike or rack set up. Although, I know some hide it in the seat above the post. It has enough air gap to hear the horn/alarm and can't be messed with or even found/seen.

Now as for how well the alarm works. It arms and works great as a bell with the 3 tone options. No idea if it will deter thieves. But I know I would not be able to waste much time trying to cut any locks with this alarm blaring for the 30 seconds it takes to reset.

You can see in my photos that it fits perfectly flush on the rear rack. So it is easy to place cargo on the rack and not touch the alarm. I installed it facing down to the fender. There is only a 2 inch gap between the fender and rack so the alarm does not touch the fender and not enough room to reach alarm this way either. Once I mount the wood panel to the rack. It will be totally covered and unreachable to the average person. Sure it will add a extra step should I need to change the batteries. But minor detail. And should this post reveal a way to defeat the location. Still likely to get enough eyes on the thief to show anyone around that a bike is being stolen. Bike is only used in daytime and mostly for trail riding.

For the price. This is a worth it expense to try for a well rounded security in conjunction with one or two bike lock methods. We have three!

A few years ago, our cable provider stopped airing MLB games. To say my husband wasn't happy is an understatement. Because we still under contract with the company, we weren't able to switch cable providers. He was able to watch some games at friend's homes or at a local sports bar. But MLB plays games almost on a daily basis and the start times can be late if played on the west coast. He wasn't able to go to friend's homes or the bar all the time to watch the Phillies play. He decided to buy a new radio so he could at least listen to the games. He went out and spent a good amount of money on a VERY nice radio with tons of features. He was ready to listen to his first game on the new radio, sat outside in a comfortable chair and turned on his new radio. And heard static. Nothing but static. We live less than an hour from Philadelphia yet his radio couldn't even get a Philly station so he could hear the game. His radio got exactly ONE station. Our local station that plays music, no sports. Turns out, where we live, surrounded by mountains and heavy forest areas isn't a great place to get radio reception. Fast forward to now. When I saw the offer for Dingmi's excellent reception transistor radio in my VINE queue, I decided to try it. My plan was to return it if it didn't get radio stations. When it arrived, we plugged it in and turned it on and began to check out the radio stations, anxious to see if any other than our local station would come in. And boy, did they ever! The first station we came to was located in Ocean City, MD, nearly 200 miles away. It came in as clear as can be. We picked up stations in New York, Ohio, West Virginia and New Jersey as well...ALL crystal clear without static! In addition to the excellent reception, this radio is a nice size yet incredibly lightweight! All of the dials are clearly labeled and simple to use. They all turn with ease. They're also very secure and will not break or fall off any time soon. The AM/FM stations are easy to read as well. The radio also has a nice size antenna that is easy to raise/lower. The radio can operate via 4 D batteries (not included) or via the power cord (included). The AC power works great. I did put 4D batteries in but don't use them to power the radio. I have them in there in case of a power outage. ( And we experienced one a few days after the Dingmi arrived, thanks to a snowstorm. We were able to listen to the weather and storm warnings until the lights came on again. Prior to having this radio, we wouldn't have had one to use. ) The volume allows you to play the radio as loud or as quiet as you chose. There is an earphone jack on the side of the radio (earphones not included) for private listening as well.

This is an exceptional radio. I am SO glad and so relieved we have it. We get fantastic reception and tons of stations from all over, even with mountains, huge pine trees and heavily wooded areas all around our home. Its lightweight and so easy to operate. This radio is perfect for outdoor use, home use, campers, RVs, take on vacation...perfect for just about any local. It definitely is worthy of gift-giving as well! I absolutely recommend the Dingmi portable transistor radio. I don't just recommend it...I HIGHLY recommend it! (BTW...I'm happy to say, MLB games are airing once again in our home! We're with a new cable company! lol)
